items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
In many maritime and farming traditions, work songs use call-and-response: a leader sings a line and the group answers. Ethnomusicologist Adaeze Okafor examined 400 transcribed work songs. She sorted them by the size of the crew that sang them and by whether the task they accompanied, such as hauling a rope, required workers to move in unison. Okafor concludes that larger crews favored call-and-response, but only for tasks that demanded synchronized movement.

Share of Song Lines in Call-and-Response Form (%)
Crew size | Synchronized tasks | Unsynchronized tasks
Small (2–4 workers) | 30 | 25
Large (10 or more workers) | 70 | 27
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Okafor's conclusion?
choices: Large crews doing synchronized tasks used call-and-response in 70% of lines, the highest share of any group.
For both synchronized and unsynchronized tasks, large crews used call-and-response far more than small crews.
Small crews used call-and-response at similar rates for synchronized and unsynchronized tasks, 30% and 25%.
For synchronized tasks, the share rose from 30% to 70% with crew size; for other tasks, it barely changed.
items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: crew size raises call-and-response for synchronized tasks, and it doesn't for unsynchronized ones. You need the crew-size comparison in both columns. It's 30% to 70% for synchronized tasks and 25% to 27% for unsynchronized ones, which is the 'only for' pattern.

A.why: This is accurate, but a single top value doesn't show a crew-size effect, and it doesn't address the condition that the effect appears only for synchronized tasks. You picked the most striking number instead of the comparison the claim requires.

B.why: For unsynchronized tasks, the share went from only 25% to 27%, which is not 'far more.' This choice also states the broad version of the claim and drops the 'only for synchronized tasks' limit Okafor sets.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares task types within small crews only, so crew size never varies. You compared the wrong pair of cells.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus: Folklorists have long debated why oral tales become more uniform over time. Rhea Castellanos studied one widespread tale, counting how many distinct endings appeared among variants collected in coastal and inland villages in the 1880s and in the 1950s. Printed tale collections reached the coastal villages around 1900 but did not circulate inland until the 1970s. Castellanos hypothesizes that printed collections reduced the variety of endings by giving tellers a single fixed version to imitate.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Castellanos's hypothesis?
choices: In the 1880s, coastal and inland villages had the same number of distinct endings, with 12 recorded in each.
Coastal villages fell from 12 distinct endings to 4, while inland villages fell only from 12 to 10.
Inland villages had fewer distinct endings in the 1950s than in the 1880s, dropping from 12 to 10.
Coastal villages had more distinct endings in the 1950s than inland villages had in the 1950s.
items.explanation: Use the passage to decide the direction first. Between the 1880s and the 1950s, only the coastal villages had print, so if print reduced variety, endings should drop sharply on the coast and change little inland. The coast falls from 12 to 4, while inland falls only from 12 to 10. That contrast links the decline to print.

A.why: This is accurate, but it describes only the starting point, before print arrived anywhere. A shared baseline doesn't show what print did. You chose a true statement that doesn't test the hypothesis.

C.why: This is accurate, but the inland villages never had print during this period. Their small decline is the comparison group, not the effect of print. You read the wrong pair of bars.

D.why: In the 1950s, coastal villages had 4 distinct endings and inland villages had 10, so the coast had fewer, not more. You reversed the comparison.

items.subtype_name: Density and per-unit quotients (including working backward)
items.stimulus: A music conservatory keeps its collection of $4{,}800$ handwritten opera scores in a climate-controlled vault. The vault has a floor area of $60$ square meters.
items.stem: What is the density of manuscripts in the vault, in manuscripts per square meter?
items.explanation: Density is the amount divided by the space: $\frac{4{,}800 \text{ manuscripts}}{60 \text{ m}^2} = 80$ manuscripts per square meter. The units read manuscripts per square meter, which is what the question asks for.

A.why: You divided the area by the number of manuscripts ($\frac{60}{4{,}800}$). That gives square meters per manuscript, the flipped quotient, not manuscripts per square meter.

B.why: You made a place-value slip when dividing. $4{,}800 \div 60$ is $80$, not $8$. Check it: $8 \times 60 = 480$, not $4{,}800$.

D.why: You multiplied the manuscripts by the area. That gives manuscript-square-meters, which is not a density. Density is a quotient, amount ÷ space.

items.subtype_name: Density and per-unit quotients (including working backward)
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist studying a silicified tree trunk finds that the petrified wood has a density of $4$ grams per cubic centimeter. A fragment of this wood has a mass of $96$ grams.
items.stem: What is the volume, in cubic centimeters, of the fragment?
items.explanation: Because density = mass ÷ volume, volume = mass ÷ density: $\frac{96 \text{ g}}{4 \text{ g/cm}^3} = 24 \text{ cm}^3$. The grams cancel, which leaves cubic centimeters.

A.why: You divided the density by the mass ($\frac{4}{96}$) and so flipped the quotient. The units would be $\frac{1}{\text{cm}^3}$, not cubic centimeters.

C.why: You subtracted the density from the mass. Density links mass and volume by division, not subtraction.

D.why: You multiplied the mass by the density. That rearrangement is invalid: the units come out as $\text{g}^2/\text{cm}^3$, not cubic centimeters.

Because these cells are already stationed where many infections begin, they can respond to a returning pathogen before circulating cells arrive.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about tissue-resident memory T cells?
choices: They travel continuously through the blood and the lymph nodes.
They stay in one tissue, so they can respond early where infections begin.
They respond to a returning pathogen only after circulating cells arrive.
They are the most abundant type of memory T cell found in the body.
items.explanation: The text says these cells stay in a single location and, because they are stationed where infections begin, they can respond before circulating cells arrive. This choice combines where they stay with what that lets them do.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Continuous travel through blood and lymph nodes is true of most memory T cells, and 'However' introduces the group that stays put.

C.why: The text says these cells respond 'before circulating cells arrive.' This choice reverses the order.

D.why: This sounds scientific, but the text never compares how many there are of each type. Nothing in the passage supports calling them the most abundant.

items.stimulus: Most faults beneath the Harlow Basin stay locked for decades and then release their stored strain all at once in a sudden earthquake. The Tessel Fault behaves differently. Instruments placed along it record steady movement of a few millimeters every year. In more than a century of record keeping, no large earthquake has been traced to it.
items.stem: Read only the sentences about the Tessel Fault. Taken together, what do they tell you about it?
choices: It moves slowly and steadily instead of slipping in large sudden earthquakes.
It stays locked for decades and then slips all at once in one earthquake.
It is one of several faults that lie beneath the Harlow Basin region.
It is unable to produce an earthquake of any size, now or in the future.
items.explanation: Three sentences are about the Tessel Fault: it 'behaves differently' from the others, it moves a few millimeters every year, and no large earthquake has been traced to it. Put them together and you get a fault that creeps steadily and does not slip suddenly. This is the core move behind real questions that ask 'Which choice best describes...' or 'What does the text indicate about...' one named item: find every sentence about that item, including the one that sets it against its group, and combine them.

C.why: This is true, but it describes something the Tessel Fault shares with every other fault in the basin. The question asks what the text tells you about this fault in particular, and the important point is how it differs.

D.why: The text says only that no large earthquake has been traced to the fault so far. It says nothing about small earthquakes or the future, so 'any size' and 'in the future' go further than the text does.

items.stimulus: Nearly all of the moons circling the planet Ostra travel in the same direction that the planet spins, and they follow almost perfectly circular paths. Pell, one of the smallest of these moons, is the exception. It orbits Ostra in the opposite direction. Its path, however, is just as circular as those of its neighbors.
items.stem: Read only the sentences about the moon Pell. Taken together, what do they tell you about it?
choices: It travels in the direction opposite Ostra's spin along a nearly circular path.
It travels in the same direction as Ostra's spin along a nearly circular path.
It travels in the same direction as Ostra's spin along a long, stretched path.
It travels opposite Ostra's spin because it was captured from somewhere else.
items.explanation: Two sentences describe Pell. One says it orbits in the opposite direction, and the other says its path is 'just as circular' as the others'. So Pell is an exception in direction only, not in shape. Real 'Which choice best describes...' questions often turn on exactly this: you have to know which feature makes the item an exception and which features it still shares with its group.

It was built of timber and, like the others, has since been replaced.
It is the oldest stone bridge still standing anywhere in the country.

items.stimulus: Hydrologists monitoring forty springs in a limestone upland found that nearly all of them respond to storms in the same way: within two days of heavy rain, their discharge surges and their water turns cloudy with sediment. Hollin Spring is the exception. Its discharge rises by about as much as the others' does, but only after roughly three weeks, and its water stays clear. The researchers attribute both differences to a single cause: water reaching Hollin Spring travels through a network of fine fractures that slows its flow and strains out sediment along the way.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Hollin Spring?
choices: Its discharge surges within two days of heavy rain, and its water turns cloudy with sediment.
Its discharge rises about as much as the other springs' does, but later and without turning cloudy.
Its discharge rises less than the other springs' does because fine fractures restrict its flow.
It is the spring that hydrologists most often study to learn how fractures filter sediment.
items.explanation: Put together every sentence about Hollin Spring. Its discharge rises 'by about as much as the others' does' (same size), 'only after roughly three weeks' (later), and 'its water stays clear' (no cloudiness). Choice B combines all three facts and adds nothing the passage doesn't say.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. A fast surge and cloudy water are what the other springs do, and the passage introduces Hollin Spring as the one that behaves differently.

C.why: You mixed up the two things that could differ, the size of the rise and its timing. The fractures slow the water down, but the passage says the rise is about as large as at the other springs. Only the timing changes.

D.why: This sounds scientific, but the passage never says how often anyone studies Hollin Spring. It only explains why the spring behaves as it does.

items.stimulus: Of the thirty-one recorded versions of the tale of the fox and the miller, all but one end with the fox caught and shamed. The exception, recorded in 1894 from an inland weaver, lets the fox escape with the miller's grain. Some scholars have treated this ending as evidence of a distinct inland tradition. However, the collector's notebook records that the weaver was telling the story to her grandchildren and that she "softened several tales that evening." The variant's ending may therefore say more about that night's audience than about any regional tradition.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the 1894 inland version of the tale?
choices: Its ending provides strong evidence that inland communities told the tale differently.
It ends, as the other recorded versions do, with the fox caught and shamed by the miller.
Its ending was softened by the collector, who revised several tales recorded that evening.
Its ending may have been adjusted by the teller for the young listeners who heard it.
items.explanation: The weaver was telling the story to her grandchildren and 'softened several tales that evening,' so the passage concludes that the ending 'may' reflect the audience. Choice D puts those facts together and keeps the passage's hedge.

items.stimulus: On a river island, ecologists have tracked eleven native bee species since 2015. Ten of them nest in burrows in the soil; the eleventh, a mason bee, lays its eggs inside hollow plant stems. When a flood submerged the island in 2019, burrow-nesting populations fell sharply, while the mason bee's numbers held steady. Two years later, however, a grass fire swept across the island. The soil insulated the burrows, and the ground nesters were largely spared, but the fire consumed the dry stems, and the mason bee population nearly collapsed.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the mason bee on the island?
choices: Its choice of nest site shielded it from one disturbance but exposed it to another.
Its population fell sharply after the flood, as the burrow-nesting species' did.
Its nests in the soil protected its eggs from the heat of the grass fire.
Its population is likely to disappear from the island within the next few years.
items.explanation: Collect both events. Nesting in stems kept the mason bee's numbers steady through the flood, and the same stems burned in the fire, so the population nearly collapsed. One trait protected it in one disaster and exposed it in the other, which is what choice A says.

B.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The burrow nesters declined after the flood. The mason bee's numbers 'held steady.'

C.why: You put the mason bee in the wrong category. It nests in hollow stems, not soil. The soil protected the ground nesters during the fire, and the mason bee nearly collapsed.

D.why: The passage says the population nearly collapsed after the fire. It makes no prediction about whether the bee will disappear from the island.

items.stimulus: In a three-year drought trial of twelve wheat varieties, agronomists found that yields of eleven fell by a quarter or more compared with irrigated plots. The variety Kesterel was the exception: its drought-stressed plots produced nearly as much grain as its irrigated ones. Its grain, however, contained noticeably less protein under drought, a shortfall that matters to bakers, who pay premiums for high-protein flour. Whether Kesterel is a sensible choice for dry regions, the researchers conclude, may depend less on the field than on the market a grower sells to.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about Kesterel?
choices: Like the other varieties, it yielded far less grain on drought-stressed plots than on irrigated ones.
Its grain held its protein content under drought even though its yield declined sharply.
It kept its yield under drought, but the grain it produced there was lower in protein.
It is the variety best suited to dry regions among the twelve that the agronomists tested.
items.explanation: Kesterel's drought plots produced 'nearly as much grain' as its irrigated plots, so its yield held. But its grain 'contained noticeably less protein under drought.' Choice C combines both facts and gets each one the right way round.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The eleven other varieties lost a quarter or more of their yield. Kesterel is the one that did not.

B.why: You swapped the two measures. Under drought, Kesterel kept its yield and lost protein. This choice says the reverse.

D.why: The researchers leave the question open: whether Kesterel suits dry regions 'may depend' on the market. Calling it the best-suited variety ignores the protein drawback the passage raises.

items.stimulus: Most antibodies that people produce after infection with henipaviruses, a family of bat-borne viruses, attach to the tip of a surface protein that mutates rapidly, so a new variant can slip past them. Researchers have now described an antibody, designated R7, that instead binds the protein's stalk, a region that was nearly identical in every related virus they examined. In laboratory tests, however, R7 neutralized the virus only weakly. The team suggests that R7 may prove more valuable as a model for designing broadly protective vaccines than as a treatment in itself.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes R7?
choices: Like most antibodies, it binds the rapidly mutating tip of the virus's surface protein.
It neutralizes the virus more strongly than antibodies that bind the protein's tip do.
It has already served as the model for a broadly protective vaccine now in use.
It likely still attaches to variants able to evade most antibodies, despite its weak effect.
items.explanation: Variants escape most antibodies because the tip mutates. R7 binds the stalk, which was nearly identical in every related virus examined, so it would likely still bind those variants. That is a small inference built from two sentences. The passage also says R7 neutralized the virus only weakly. Choice D keeps both points and the hedge 'likely.'

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Most antibodies bind the tip. R7 'instead binds the protein's stalk.'

B.why: The passage says R7 neutralized the virus 'only weakly.' Binding a stable region is an advantage, but it doesn't make R7 a stronger neutralizer, and the passage never compares its strength to other antibodies'.

C.why: The team only suggests that R7 'may prove' useful as a vaccine model. Nothing in the passage says such a vaccine exists or is in use.

It was woven in the 1870s with natural indigo the mill purchased after 1868.
items.explanation: Put together every sentence about the blue swatch. • The star Orvane-3 has three known planets.
• All three were discovered by the transit method, which detects the slight dimming of a star as a planet passes in front of it.
• Planet b is a rocky world slightly larger than Earth and completes an orbit every 4 days.
• Planet c is a gas giant that takes 211 days to orbit the star.
• Planet d, the outermost of the three, was detected in 2024.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the orbit of planet c. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: All three planets that orbit Orvane-3 were discovered by detecting the slight dimming of the star.
Planet b, a rocky world slightly larger than Earth, completes one orbit of Orvane-3 every 4 days.
Planet c, a gas giant, takes 211 days to complete one orbit around its star, Orvane-3.
Planet c, a gas giant, is the outermost of the three known planets that orbit Orvane-3.
items.explanation: The goal names one planet and one feature: planet c's orbit. C makes planet c the subject and gives its orbit directly. It takes 211 days to go around Orvane-3.

A.why: This covers the whole planetary system and how it was discovered. The goal asked about one member of the system and one feature of that member.

B.why: This gives the right kind of detail, an orbital period, for the wrong planet. Check which planet the goal names before you match on topic.

D.why: The notes say planet d is the outermost planet, not planet c. This choice gives planet c a position the notes assign to another planet.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lucía Merino is an epidemiologist who has worked in public health for over three decades.
• In 2004, she founded a national registry for tracking outbreaks of foodborne illness.
• In 2011, she was appointed director of the national public health institute.
• As director, she expanded free tuberculosis screening to every regional clinic.
• In 2019, she received an international award for her leadership of the institute.
items.stem: The student wants to describe an accomplishment of Merino's from before she became director of the national public health institute. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: In 2004, Merino founded a national registry for tracking outbreaks of foodborne illness.
As director, Merino expanded free tuberculosis screening to every regional clinic.
In 2011, Merino was appointed director of the national public health institute.
In 2019, Merino received an international award for leading the health institute.
items.explanation: The goal has a time limit: before Merino became director in 2011. The only accomplishment in the choices from before that year is the foodborne-illness registry she founded in 2004, so A meets the goal.

B.why: This is a real accomplishment, but it happened while she was director, which is after the point the goal names. You skipped the word "before" in the goal.

C.why: This sentence describes the appointment itself. That is the event the goal uses as a cutoff, not an accomplishment from before it.

D.why: This award came in 2019, eight years after she became director. It also honors her leadership of the institute, so it falls in the wrong period.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
Notes:
- Sprint coaches disagree about whether static stretching before a race slows runners down.
- Physiologist Lena Ostrowski studied 24 college sprinters.
- Each sprinter ran 40 meters twice: once after static stretching and once after a light jog.
- On average, times after static stretching were 0.04 seconds slower.
- Ostrowski concluded that a light jog is the better warm-up.

Goal: describe the study's method.
items.stem: Which sentence gives exactly the detail named in the goal?
choices: Each of the 24 sprinters ran 40 meters twice, once after static stretching and once after a light jog.
The sprinters averaged 0.04 seconds slower after static stretching than they did after a light jog.
Ostrowski concluded from her study that a light jog is a better warm-up than static stretching.
Ostrowski's study proved that static stretching before a race slows down every sprinter who does it.
items.explanation: The goal names one stage of the study: the method, meaning what the researchers actually did. Only A describes that, with who ran, how far, how many times and under what two conditions. This is the core move behind 'describe one specific detail' questions on the Rhetorical Synthesis questions: find the single note that matches the noun in the goal and pick the sentence built on it. Study notes always run background, researcher, method, finding, conclusion, so you can go straight to the one stage the goal asks for.

B.why: This sentence is about the right study, but it reports the result, not the method. You saw the study's numbers and stopped there without checking that the goal said 'method.'

C.why: This is the conclusion, the last stage of the notes. It mentions the two warm-ups, but it tells you what Ostrowski decided, not how she ran the test.

D.why: The notes give an average for 24 college sprinters, not proof about every sprinter. This sentence also describes a result rather than the method, so it fails twice.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
Notes:
- Beavers build dams out of branches and mud.
- A single dam can hold back a pond more than 100 meters long.
- In winter, young trout shelter in the deep, still water of beaver ponds.
- Beavers feed mainly on the bark of willow and aspen trees.

Goal: describe how beaver ponds help young trout.
items.stem: Which sentence gives exactly the detail named in the goal?
choices: Beavers, which share their streams with trout, feed mainly on willow and aspen bark.
Beaver dams, built from branches and mud, can hold back ponds over 100 meters long.
In winter, young trout shelter in the deep, still water that beaver ponds provide.
In winter, young trout avoid the deep, still water that collects in beaver ponds.
items.explanation: The goal ends with the exact content it wants: how the ponds help young trout. Only one note answers that (trout shelter in the ponds' deep, still water in winter), and C is built on that note, with the trout and the ponds in the main clause. Practising this helps with Rhetorical Synthesis questions whose goal ends in a specific phrase. That phrase points to one note, and the right answer is the sentence built on it.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. It names trout, but only in a side clause, and the main clause is about what beavers eat. Mentioning the right word isn't the same as giving the right detail.

B.why: This sentence describes how big the dams are, which is accurate but says nothing about trout. You picked a true fact about the general topic instead of the one the goal named.

D.why: This reverses the note. The trout shelter in the ponds; they don't avoid them. You matched the wording without checking what it said.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
Notes:
- Ruth Adeyemi is a labor economist.
- Before her best-known study, she spent six years as a union contract negotiator.
- In 2009, she began tracking pay at 300 warehouses in Ohio.
- The warehouse study found that pay rose fastest where workers could easily switch employers.
- In 2021, she was appointed to a state wage board.

Goal: describe Adeyemi's work before her warehouse study.
items.stem: Which sentence gives exactly the detail named in the goal?
choices: After her warehouse study, Adeyemi was appointed to a state wage board in 2021.
Adeyemi's warehouse study, begun in 2009, tracked pay at 300 Ohio warehouses.
Before her warehouse study, Adeyemi served six years on a state wage board.
Before her warehouse study, Adeyemi spent six years negotiating union contracts.
items.explanation: The goal has a time limit: work done before the warehouse study. Only one note fits that window, her six years as a union contract negotiator, and D states it accurately. When a goal says 'before,' 'after,' or names a year, that restriction rules out every note outside it. Spotting this is what you need for the 'accomplishments before event X' version of Rhetorical Synthesis questions.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. It is about the right person, but the wrong time: it describes what came after the study. You missed the word 'before' in the goal.

B.why: This describes the warehouse study itself, which is the marker the goal uses for timing, not the period it asks about.

C.why: This puts the wage board in the wrong place. She joined it in 2021, after the study, and her earlier six years were spent as a union negotiator. You combined details from two different notes.

Notes:
- Agronomists in Kenya tested three varieties of sorghum, a grain crop.
- The variety Gadam ripens in about 75 days.
- The variety Seredo has a waxy coating on its leaves that slows water loss.
- The variety Macia produces the largest grain heads of the three.

Macia has a waxy coating on its leaves that slows the loss of water from the plant.
items.explanation: The goal names one member of the group (Seredo) and one feature of it (what helps it in dry weather). items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ecologist Priya Raman studied dragonflies in Montana's Bitterroot Valley.
• She asked whether ponds created by beaver dams support more dragonfly species than nearby stream reaches without dams.
• Over two summers, her team netted adult dragonflies along 40 transects, half at beaver ponds and half along undammed stretches of stream.
• Beaver-pond transects averaged 14 dragonfly species; undammed transects averaged 8.
• Raman concluded that beavers indirectly boost insect diversity by creating still water.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the method Raman used in her study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Comparing transects at beaver ponds and undammed stretches, Raman found an average of 14 dragonfly species at the ponds versus 8 elsewhere.
Over two summers, Raman's team netted adult dragonflies along 40 transects, half at beaver ponds and half along undammed stretches of stream.
Raman asked whether ponds created by beaver dams support more dragonfly species than do nearby stream reaches that lack dams.
Raman concluded that by creating still water, beavers indirectly increase the diversity of the dragonflies living in the valley.
items.explanation: The goal asks for the study's method, meaning how the data were collected. Choice B's main clause gives exactly that: the team netted adult dragonflies along 40 transects over two summers, split between beaver ponds and undammed streams. It is the only choice whose main point is the procedure.

A.why: You saw the method words in the opening phrase ("comparing transects") and stopped there. The main clause of this sentence reports the result, 14 species versus 8. The method is only tucked into a side phrase, and the goal needs it to be the main point.

C.why: This is the study's question, not its method. You may have taken the comparison it sets up for a description of the procedure, but nothing here tells how Raman collected her data.

D.why: This sentence is accurate to the notes, but it gives Raman's conclusion, which is the last stage of the study, not the method. It's true, but it doesn't do the job the goal asks for.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Kettle Ridge fossil bed in Oregon preserves plants from about 34 million years ago.
• Paleobotanists have described three new species from the site.
• Quercus prima, an oak, had leaves with deeply lobed margins.
• Alnus vetusta, an alder, had leaves with finely double-toothed edges; more than 600 specimens have been recovered, making it the site's most abundant species.
• Ginkgo kettlensis, named for the ridge, had fan-shaped leaves split by a single central notch.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the leaves of the most abundant plant species at the Kettle Ridge site. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Of the three new species found at Kettle Ridge, one had lobed leaves, one had toothed leaves, and one had fan-shaped leaves.
With more than 600 specimens recovered so far, Alnus vetusta is the most abundant plant species at the Kettle Ridge fossil bed.
Alnus vetusta, the most abundant species at the Kettle Ridge site, had leaves with fine edges that were double-toothed.
Ginkgo kettlensis, named for the ridge where it was found, had fan-shaped leaves that were split by a single central notch.
items.explanation: The goal has two steps. First, work out which species is most abundant (Alnus vetusta). Then describe its leaves. Choice C names Alnus vetusta, identifies it as the most abundant species, and uses its main clause to describe its finely double-toothed leaves.

A.why: This sentence covers the whole collection instead of zooming in on one member. It never says which leaf type belongs to the most abundant species, so a reader can't tell what that species' leaves looked like.

B.why: This is the subtype trap. It names the right species, but it describes how abundant the species is, not what its leaves looked like. The goal's restriction is the leaves.

D.why: This describes leaves, but they belong to the wrong species. Ginkgo kettlensis isn't the most abundant plant at the site. You matched the word "leaves" without first working out which species the goal points to.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Prairie Ember is a red winter wheat released in 2021 by Canada's Northfield Agricultural Station.
• Breeder Tomasz Wilk developed it over eleven years by crossing a drought-tolerant Turkish landrace with a high-yield Canadian line.
• Wilk named the variety for the deep copper glow its kernels take on as they ripen, which he likened to embers.
• In field trials, it yielded 12% more grain than standard varieties during dry seasons.
• Farmers in three provinces planted it on about 40,000 hectares in its first year.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how Prairie Ember got its name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Named by breeder Tomasz Wilk, Prairie Ember was produced by crossing a drought-tolerant Turkish landrace with a Canadian line.
Prairie Ember, a red winter wheat with copper-colored kernels, yielded 12% more grain than standard varieties in dry seasons.
In its first year, farmers in three Canadian provinces planted the new wheat Prairie Ember on about 40,000 hectares.
Prairie Ember takes its name from the copper glow of its ripening kernels, which reminded breeder Tomasz Wilk of embers.
items.explanation: The goal ends with "how it got its name," and only one note answers that. Choice D builds its main clause around that note: the variety is named for the copper glow of its ripening kernels, which Wilk likened to embers.

A.why: This is the subtype trap. The naming appears only in an opening phrase ("Named by breeder Tomasz Wilk"), and that phrase says who named it, not why. The main clause is about how the wheat was bred.

B.why: This mentions the copper-colored kernels that inspired the name, so it looks close. But it never links that color to the name, and its main clause is about yield.

C.why: This is accurate, but it describes how widely the wheat was planted in its first year. Nothing in it explains where the name came from.

The Tarrow Fault, a 90-kilometer fault on the South Island, has been studied through both trenching and satellite radar.

items.subtype_name: Zoom in on one named detail
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Vela Ridge Observatory in northern Chile houses three telescopes.
- The Harrow Telescope, built in 1998, has a 4.1-meter mirror and is used to study distant galaxies.
- The Linden Telescope, built in 2006, has a 2.3-meter mirror.
- The Linden Telescope is used mainly to track asteroids whose orbits bring them near Earth.
- The third telescope, the Oriel, is reserved for training graduate students.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the primary purpose of the Linden Telescope. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The Linden Telescope, which was built in 2006, has a mirror that measures 2.3 meters across.
The Linden Telescope at the Vela Ridge Observatory is used mainly to track near-Earth asteroids.
The Vela Ridge Observatory, home of the Linden Telescope, houses three telescopes in Chile.
Unlike the Linden Telescope, the Harrow Telescope is used to study galaxies that are very distant.
items.explanation: The goal names one telescope and one feature: the Linden Telescope's purpose. Choice B makes the Linden Telescope its subject and uses its main clause to state that purpose, tracking near-Earth asteroids.

A.why: You saw the right name and stopped checking. This choice describes the Linden Telescope's construction date and mirror size, not what the telescope is used for.

Seismologists have long cautioned that earthquakes cannot be predicted with any useful precision. Small tremors occur constantly, and only rarely does one turn out to be a foreshock to a major quake, so no one can say in advance when a large rupture will strike.

Text 2
Although the exact timing of large quakes remains beyond reach, warning is still possible. Sensors can detect the fast, weak first waves of a quake that has already begun and send alerts seconds before the slower, damaging waves arrive, time enough to halt trains.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It accepts Text 1's point about prediction but describes another kind of warning.
It claims that new sensors can now predict when large quakes will occur.
It gives an example of a small tremor that turned out to be a foreshock.
It rejects the alert sensors that the seismologists in Text 1 had recommended.
items.explanation: Text 2 opens with a concession ("Although the exact timing... remains beyond reach"), which agrees with Text 1 that quakes cannot be predicted. It then turns to a different kind of warning: detecting a quake that has already started and alerting people seconds before the damaging waves arrive.

B.why: You missed the concession. Text 2 says timing remains beyond reach. The sensors detect a quake that has already begun and do not predict one.

C.why: You fixed on a detail from Text 1. Foreshocks appear only in Text 1, and Text 2 gives no example of one.

D.why: You attributed something to Text 1 that it does not say. Text 1 never mentions or recommends alert sensors, and Text 2 supports them.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Folklorists studying modern urban legends have argued that such stories spread because they give voice to shared anxieties. Tales of contaminated fast food, for instance, circulated most widely as families began relying on meals prepared by unseen strangers.

Text 2
Nineteenth-century sailors' accounts of sea serpents fit a similar pattern. Reports of the creatures multiplied in decades when shipwrecks were frequent and crossings felt especially perilous, suggesting that the tales expressed fears crews could not otherwise name.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It disputes Text 1's claim that legends express widely shared anxieties.
It extends the explanation in Text 1 to stories from an earlier period.
It offers the general theory that the examples in Text 1 then illustrate.
It argues that sailors' reports of sea serpents were largely accurate.
items.explanation: Text 1 explains that legends spread because they express shared anxieties, and it gives a modern example. Text 2 says sailors' tales "fit a similar pattern" and applies the same explanation to stories from the 1800s. Text 2 extends Text 1's idea to an earlier era.

A.why: You missed the agreement signal. "Fit a similar pattern" tells you Text 2 accepts Text 1's explanation and uses it.

C.why: You reversed which text does what. Text 1 states the general theory, and Text 2 supplies another case of it.

D.why: You read in a claim Text 2 never makes. It treats the sightings as expressions of fear and never says the serpents were real.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Divers surveying Caribbean reefs counted far more parrotfish inside no-fishing zones than in nearby fished waters. Because parrotfish graze the algae that smother young coral, the researchers concluded that banning fishing is enough to bring a damaged reef back.

Text 2
While no-fishing zones clearly hold more parrotfish, grazing cannot protect coral from heat. During an unusually warm summer, reefs inside the zones bleached just as badly as reefs outside them.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Banning fishing is enough by itself to restore a damaged reef.
No-fishing zones tend to contain more parrotfish than fished waters.
Water temperature matters more to reefs than fishing does.
Parrotfish are the most important animals living on a reef.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins by granting Text 1's finding: 'While no-fishing zones clearly hold more parrotfish.' Text 1 reports that finding directly, so both authors accept it. Text 2 then disputes only Text 1's conclusion that a fishing ban is enough. This is groundwork for questions that ask how Text 2 relates to Text 1. Before you can say that Text 2 qualifies Text 1, you need to find the part it concedes, and that part is usually in the 'While...' clause.

A.why: You got Text 1's role right but missed Text 2's. This is Text 1's final conclusion, and it's exactly the claim Text 2 was written to challenge with the bleaching example.

C.why: Text 2 only says heat can damage reefs that a fishing ban protects. It never ranks temperature above fishing, and Text 1 doesn't mention temperature at all.

D.why: Both texts discuss parrotfish, but neither compares them to other reef animals. You turned a shared topic into a claim that neither author makes.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
At a coastal settlement, archaeologists uncovered several thin layers of charcoal mixed with burned seeds. The team concluded that the inhabitants regularly set fires to clear land for planting crops.

Text 2
No one disputes that the site contains layers of burned material. However, a wildfire sparked by lightning could have left the same charcoal, and nothing found so far makes it possible to exclude that explanation.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The inhabitants grew crops on land they had cleared by burning.
Lightning was the most likely cause of the fires at the site.
The seeds at the site came from plants that grew in the wild.
The settlement contains layers of material that had been burned.
items.explanation: Text 2 says outright that 'no one disputes' the burned layers, and Text 1 is the source of that observation. The two authors agree on what was found and disagree about what caused it. This is the 'same observation, different explanation' pattern. Being able to separate the shared observation from the disputed explanation is what lets you choose 'offers an alternative explanation' on a real relationship question.

A.why: This is Text 1's explanation, the claim that Text 2 is questioning. You correctly identified Text 1's position but assumed that Text 2 accepts it.

B.why: Text 2 says only that lightning 'could have' caused the fires and can't be ruled out. It never says lightning is the most likely cause, and Text 1 would reject the idea.

C.why: Neither author says where the seeds came from. You latched on to a detail that appears in Text 1, the seeds, and attached a claim that neither text makes.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Pavement and buildings absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly, so cities are usually warmer than the countryside around them. Meteorologists call this pattern the urban heat island.

Text 2
Although most cities are indeed warmer than their surroundings, some desert cities break the pattern during the day. There, irrigated parks and shade trees cool the streets, leaving the city cooler at noon than the bare desert outside it.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Most cities are warmer than the countryside that surrounds them.
Every city stays warmer than its surroundings at all hours.
Desert cities are cooler than their surroundings at noon.
Shade trees are the best way to cool down a crowded city.
items.explanation: Text 2 opens with 'Although most cities are indeed warmer than their surroundings,' which concedes Text 1's main point. It then names one group of cities and one time of day where the pattern breaks down. That narrows Text 1's claim without rejecting it. When a relationship question asks what Text 2 does, the answer here would be that it limits Text 1's claim, not that it disagrees with Text 1.

B.why: Text 1 says cities are 'usually' warmer. It doesn't say every city at all hours. Text 2 is responding to a stronger claim than the one Text 1 makes.

C.why: This is Text 2's own point, and it's limited to 'some' desert cities. Text 1 never mentions deserts, so you can't treat this as something the two authors share.

D.why: Text 2 says shade trees help cool some desert cities. It never calls them the best method, and Text 1 doesn't discuss ways to cool a city.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In warm climates, many trees have leaves with smooth edges, while in cool climates, more trees have toothed edges. By counting smooth-edged fossil leaves at an ancient site, paleobotanists estimated its past temperature and concluded the site was once tropical.

Text 2
Leaf edges are certainly a useful clue to past climate. Yet plants growing beside streams often have toothed leaves no matter how warm the air is, so fossils from old riverbanks may make a site seem cooler than it was.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The ancient site described in Text 1 was once a tropical place.
Fossils from riverbanks should not be used to study past climate.
The shape of leaf edges can give information about past climate.
Trees with toothed leaves grow only in places with cool climates.
items.explanation: Text 1 relies on leaf edges to estimate temperature, and Text 2 begins by calling leaf edges 'certainly a useful clue to past climate.' Both authors accept the method. Text 2 then adds a warning about one kind of site. Identifying this shared ground is the first step in recognizing that Text 2 qualifies Text 1 rather than rejecting it.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion. Text 2 never confirms it, and its warning about riverbank fossils raises doubts about this kind of estimate. You applied Text 1's view to both authors.

B.why: Text 2 says riverbank fossils may make a site 'seem cooler.' That is a caution, not a ban. Text 1 doesn't mention riverbanks at all.

D.why: Text 1 says only that toothed edges are more common in cool climates. Text 2 directly contradicts this choice by saying toothed leaves appear beside streams 'no matter how warm the air is.'

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Woolen cloth fragments found at a fourteenth-century Baltic trading post contain red dye from a variety of madder that grew only far to the south. Historian Ilse Varga concludes that the post therefore imported its finished cloth from southern workshops rather than weaving its own.

Text 2
The dye evidence is sound, but dyestuffs were trade goods in their own right: light, durable, and valuable. Bundles of dried madder root could have reached the post as easily as bolts of cloth, and local weavers could simply have dyed their own wool with it. The loom weights recovered at the site make that possibility difficult to exclude.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 presents new chemical evidence that the dye discussed in Text 1 came from a plant grown locally.
Text 2 rejects the dye evidence in Text 1 as unreliable and concludes the post imported no cloth at all.
Text 2 accepts the evidence that Text 1 relies on but suggests another process that could have produced it.
Text 2 offers further evidence for Text 1's view that the post obtained finished cloth from southern workshops.
items.explanation: Text 1 uses the southern madder in the fragments to conclude that the cloth was imported finished. Text 2 opens by granting that the dye evidence is sound, then offers a second route: the post could have imported the raw dye and done the weaving and dyeing itself. Same observation, different explanation, so Text 2 accepts the evidence and proposes another process behind it.

A.why: You credited Text 2 with disputing where the dye came from. Text 2 accepts that the madder was southern and calls the dye evidence sound. It disputes only what Varga infers from that evidence.

B.why: You took a hedged alternative and turned it into flat disagreement. Text 2 calls the evidence sound and says only that local dyeing 'could have' happened. It never says the post imported no cloth.

D.why: This is the trap of getting one text's role right and the other's wrong. Text 1's view is described correctly, but Text 2 does not support it. The loom weights point toward local weaving, which works against Varga's conclusion.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In listening studies with Western concert audiences, participants consistently rate passages in a minor key as sadder than the same passages in a major key. Musicologist Paulo Brandt argues that the link between minor mode and sadness is therefore a universal feature of human music perception.

Text 2
Researchers played the same passages to listeners in a remote highland community with little exposure to Western recordings. These listeners rated the minor and major versions as equally sad, although they readily judged fast passages as happier than slow ones.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 describes listeners for whom a pattern that Text 1 treats as universal did not appear.
Text 2 argues that tempo rather than mode conveys sadness to all listeners, including those in Text 1.
Text 2 questions whether the concert audiences in Text 1 really rated minor-key passages as sadder.
Text 2 supports Text 1's conclusion by showing that highland listeners also hear emotion in music.
items.explanation: Text 1 moves from one population, Western concert audiences, to a claim about all humans. Text 2 presents a group of listeners for whom the minor-means-sad pattern did not hold. That case limits the scope of Text 1's universal claim. Text 2 does not dispute the original finding.

B.why: You generalized Text 2's side observation about tempo into a claim about every listener. Text 2 reports only how the highland listeners judged tempo and says nothing about tempo for Western audiences.

C.why: You had Text 2 attack the wrong part of Text 1. Text 2 leaves the concert-audience finding alone and challenges only the leap from that finding to 'universal'.

D.why: You fixed on the fact that the highland listeners heard some emotion in music. That isn't the point. On the specific link Brandt calls universal, minor mode and sadness, they did not show the pattern, so Text 2 works against his conclusion.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Self-healing concrete contains dormant bacterial spores that, when a crack lets in water, become active and produce limestone that seals the gap. In laboratory trials, cracks up to 0.8 millimeters wide closed within four weeks, and engineer Rosa Achterberg argues the material could sharply reduce maintenance costs for bridges and tunnels.

Text 2
Although the laboratory results are impressive, the spores in those trials were tested within months of mixing. Bridges and tunnels are built to last for decades, and no one yet knows whether the spores remain viable that long inside hardened concrete. Until long-term data exist, the cost savings remain a projection.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 provides evidence that the bacteria in Text 1 stop working after several years inside concrete.
Text 2 disputes the laboratory results in Text 1, arguing that the trials were too brief to be trusted.
Text 2 explains the chemical process by which the bacteria described in Text 1 produce limestone.
Text 2 accepts the trial results in Text 1 but notes an untested condition on which its projection depends.
items.explanation: Text 2 begins with a concession ('Although the laboratory results are impressive'), then turns. Achterberg's predicted savings depend on the spores staying viable for decades, and that has not been tested. Text 2 accepts the results and points out the untested condition the projection relies on.

A.why: You read uncertainty as a negative finding. Text 2 says 'no one yet knows' whether the spores survive. It gives no evidence that they fail.

B.why: You got Text 2's role half right. It does raise the short testing period, but to question the long-term projection, not the lab results, which it calls 'impressive'.

C.why: You picked a detail from Text 1. Text 1, not Text 2, describes how the bacteria make limestone, and this choice says nothing about how the two texts relate.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
In the ten days before a magnitude 6.1 earthquake in 2019, seismometers near the fault recorded a sharp rise in small tremors. Seismologist Kenji Arima concluded that such swarms are foreshocks marking a fault's final weakening and thus could serve as warnings of large earthquakes.

Text 2
Tremor swarms like the one Arima describes are common, yet most are followed by no large earthquake at all. A pattern identified only after a major quake is hard to use as a forecast, because the many swarms that came to nothing are rarely studied with the same care.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 denies that the increase in small tremors described in Text 1 occurred before the 2019 earthquake.
Text 2 raises a problem for Text 1's conclusion that such tremor swarms could serve as warnings.
Text 2 proposes a different physical mechanism to explain why tremor swarms precede large earthquakes.
Text 2 argues that large earthquakes cannot be forecast by any method, including the one in Text 1.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends on its conclusion: swarms 'thus could serve as warnings.' That is the sentence Text 2 answers. Text 2 does not deny the 2019 swarm. It points out that most swarms are followed by no large quake, which makes swarms unreliable as warnings.

A.why: You had Text 2 reject the observation. Text 2 refers to 'the one Arima describes' as a real swarm and accepts that it happened.

C.why: This is the near-miss. 'Alternative explanation' is a common way two texts relate, but Text 2 offers no mechanism. Its objection is about how useful the pattern is as a forecast, not about why the tremors happen.

D.why: You stretched a narrow objection into a sweeping one. Text 2 criticizes only the swarm-based forecast and says nothing about other prediction methods.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
After a city required restaurants to post calorie counts on their menus, a study of sales receipts found that the average purchase contained about 4 percent fewer calories. Health economist Dana Whitcombe argues that menu labeling is therefore an effective way to reduce calorie intake across the population.

Text 2
A follow-up analysis of the same receipts sorted purchases by customer. Nearly all of the decline came from customers who were already buying lower-calorie meals; among the customers who bought the most calories, totals barely changed.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 shows that the 4 percent decline reported in Text 1 resulted from an error in calculation.
Text 2 tests whether the result in Text 1 holds in a different city and finds that it does not.
Text 2 reexamines the data behind Text 1's claim and finds the effect largely confined to some customers.
Text 2 uses the same receipts to show that menu labeling had no effect on what customers purchased.
items.explanation: Text 1 claims an effect 'across the population.' Text 2 goes back to the same receipts and finds the decline concentrated among customers who were already buying lighter meals. The heaviest buyers barely changed. Text 2 keeps the overall finding but narrows who it applies to.

A.why: You treated a breakdown of the data as a correction of it. Text 2 never says the 4 percent figure is wrong. It explains where the decline came from.

B.why: You got Text 2's method wrong. It analyzes 'the same receipts,' not data from a second city.

D.why: You picked flat disagreement when Text 2 only qualifies. Text 2 says the decline came 'nearly all' from one group, so labeling clearly affected some customers.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Many songbirds sing more at dawn than at any other time of day. One long-standing explanation holds that cool, still morning air carries sound farther, so a song delivered at dawn reaches more rivals and potential mates. Researchers who favor this explanation acknowledge that it is unlikely to be the only factor involved.

Text 2
Ecologist Mariana Duque broadcast recorded songs at different hours in a tropical forest and measured how far away they could be detected. Songs played at dawn were detectable roughly 20 percent farther than identical songs played at midday.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 shows that the explanation discussed in Text 1 does not apply to birds living in tropical forests.
Text 2 establishes that sound transmission is the sole cause of the dawn singing pattern in Text 1.
Text 2 describes a bird species whose singing schedule is an exception to the pattern in Text 1.
Text 2 reports a measurement that is consistent with an explanation described in Text 1.
items.explanation: Text 1 presents the acoustic explanation, that dawn air carries song farther, as one factor among possibly several. Text 2 measures sound travel and finds dawn songs carry about 20 percent farther. That result fits the explanation in Text 1.

A.why: You reversed what Text 2 found. In the tropical forest, songs carried farther at dawn, which supports the explanation there.

B.why: This is the Hard-tier trap: Text 2 is made to answer a stronger claim than Text 1 makes. Text 1 says the acoustic factor is 'unlikely to be the only factor,' and one distance measurement cannot show it is the sole cause.

C.why: You assumed Text 2 must be an exception because it is set somewhere new. Text 2 used recorded songs and reports no species' singing schedule. It tests sound travel, not when birds sing.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Marine reserves are often judged by counting the fish inside their boundaries. But much of a reserve's value may lie beyond its borders. If protected adults release larvae that drift into fished waters, a reserve can replenish nearby fisheries in ways that a count taken inside it would never register.

Text 2
Off a temperate rocky coast, researchers used genetic parentage tests on young rockfish caught in heavily fished waters. Although the nearby reserve covered only about a tenth of the local reef, adults living inside it had produced roughly 30 percent of the young fish sampled outside it.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: Text 2 documents a specific case of the kind of benefit that Text 1 says counts inside reserves would miss.
Text 2 argues that counting fish inside reserves, a method Text 1 recommends, overstates their benefits.
Text 2 states a general principle about reserves that Text 1 then illustrates with a single coastal case.
Text 2 shows that reserves help fisheries more than any other management approach that has been tried.
items.explanation: Text 1 makes a general point: a reserve's benefits can come from larvae drifting into fished waters, which inside counts miss. items.stimulus:
Text 1
Permeable paving lets rainwater soak into the ground instead of rushing into storm drains. In a pilot neighborhood, storm runoff fell by about 60 percent during the first two years after installation, leading urban planner Teodor Lund to call permeable paving a durable solution to urban flooding.

Text 2 accepts the early results in Text 1 but questions whether they show the benefit is lasting.
Text 2 maintains that permeable paving fails to reduce runoff under any set of conditions.
Text 2 describes a maintenance practice that Text 1 credits for the pilot neighborhood's success.
items.explanation: Text 2 opens by granting the point ('Certainly those early figures are encouraging'), then turns to time. Without maintenance, performance drops sharply within seven years. Text 1

It argues that Text 1's conclusion may not hold in areas unlike those mostly studied.
It presents a finding about rural employers that Text 1 then attempts to explain.
It claims that the payroll records in Text 1 were gathered using flawed methods.
items.explanation: Text 1 ends with a broad conclusion: moderate increases don't reduce employment. items.stimulus:

It argues that professional observatories are less precise than Text 1 suggests.

It shifts attention from amateur observers to the size of objects striking Jupiter.

B.why: Neither text says anything about how precise professional instruments are. Text 1's point is about scheduling and attention, and Text 2 says only that no professional telescope was aimed at Jupiter.

C.why: You swapped the roles. Text 1 is the general claim and Text 2 is the particular case. This choice describes the relationship in reverse.

items.subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Seismologist Rafael Duarte examined 40 major earthquakes along the Kessar subduction zone and found that 28 were preceded, days or weeks earlier, by clusters of small tremors known as foreshock swarms. Duarte therefore suggests that monitoring such swarms could give coastal communities advance warning.

Text 2
Duarte's pattern is real, but it looks only backward from large earthquakes. Looking forward, the Kessar zone produced more than 300 swarms over the same period, and nearly all of them faded without a major quake. A warning system based on swarms would mostly sound false alarms.
items.stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
choices: It reports that the large earthquakes in Text 1 were rarely preceded by swarms.
It proposes a more reliable method of forecasting large earthquakes than swarms.
It accepts the pattern in Text 1 but disputes the practical use Text 1 proposes.
It presents a warning proposal that Text 1 goes on to test with earthquake records.
items.explanation: Text 1 builds from evidence (28 of 40 quakes had foreshock swarms) to a final proposal marked by "therefore": monitor swarms to warn communities. Text 2 grants the pattern ("is real, but") and then answers that final proposal: most swarms are never followed by a major quake, so a warning system would mostly sound false alarms. C captures both halves.

A.why: Text 2 accepts that 28 of the 40 quakes followed swarms. Its point runs the other way: most swarms aren't followed by quakes. It doesn't say most quakes lacked swarms.

B.why: Text 2 criticizes the swarm-based approach but never offers a replacement. Nothing in it describes another forecasting method.

D.why: You got the direction wrong. The warning proposal comes from Text 1, and Text 2 responds to it. Text 1 doesn't test anything that Text 2 proposes.

The following text is adapted from an imagined dialogue written to defend an early form of vaccination. Lysander, a worried father, questions Theron, a country physician.
LYSANDER: You would have me scratch my daughter's arm with matter from a cow's sore. Is it not madness to give a healthy child a disease?
THERON: And is it wisdom to leave her open to one that kills? The milkmaids of this parish took the cowpox and were well within a week; when smallpox swept through, not one of them sickened. If a mild illness can stand guard against a deadly one, then the madness lies in refusing it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Theron argues that a mild infection is worth accepting because it appears to shield against a deadly one.
Lysander objects that deliberately giving any disease to a healthy child is an irrational thing to do.
Theron admits that leaving a child unprotected may be wiser than taking the risk of inoculation.
Theron argues that the milkmaids of the parish are naturally immune to every illness that passes through.
items.explanation: Theron's claim sits in his closing conditional: if a mild illness can protect against a deadly one, then refusing it is the real madness. The milkmaids are his evidence. Choice A restates that argument.

B.why: This summarises Lysander's speech, which is the objection Theron answers. It isn't the point the passage builds toward.

C.why: You took Theron's rhetorical question literally. 'Is it wisdom to leave her open to one that kills?' means it is not wise. He is pushing for inoculation, not conceding.

D.why: Theron says only that the milkmaids didn't catch smallpox after having cowpox. He never says they resist every illness, or that their protection was natural rather than caused by the cowpox.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Two excavators, Corbett and Ines, are examining a buried hearth at a site that published accounts describe as a brief seasonal camp.
CORBETT: A single hearth. Hunters stopped here one autumn, cooked, and moved on. The textbooks say as much.
INES: Then tell me why the clay floor beneath it has been replastered seven times. Travelers passing through don't mend a floor they will never see again. Whoever cooked here came back, year upon year, or never left at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Corbett maintains that the hearth shows hunters used the site only briefly, just as published accounts claim.
Ines asks Corbett to explain the replastering because she cannot account for the repairs herself.
Ines argues that the replastering proves the site's occupants had built permanent stone houses nearby.
Ines argues that the repeated replastering shows the site was used over a long period rather than once.
items.explanation: The introduction sets up the accepted view, and Ines's reply overturns it. The seven layers of plaster point to people who returned or stayed, because short-term visitors don't repair a floor. Choice D captures that challenge.

A.why: This is Corbett's position, the textbook view Ines argues against. Choosing it means you matched the wrong speaker.

B.why: You took 'tell me why' literally. Ines isn't stuck. She is making a point and already gives the answer: the people came back or never left.

C.why: Ines talks only about the replastered floor and repeated use. Nothing in the text mentions stone houses, so this claims more than the evidence supports.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set at a coastal weather station in the 1870s. Abel, the station keeper, is reassuring his assistant, Ruth, who has been watching the barometer all afternoon.
ABEL: Sky's clear as glass, and the wind's dropped to nothing. We'll have a fine night of it.
RUTH: A fine night, says he, and the glass fallen a full inch since noon. Ere morning that calm will have teeth. When did still air ever hold off a falling barometer? Bring in the boats.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Abel argues that the clear sky and the still wind show that the coming night will be calm.
Ruth warns that the falling barometer signals a coming storm despite the calm conditions.
Ruth wonders whether still air has ever stopped a barometer from continuing to fall.
Ruth warns that the barometer has failed and can no longer be trusted to predict weather.
items.explanation: Put Ruth's lines into plain English: the barometer has dropped sharply, so the calm will turn violent before morning, and the boats should come in. Choice B states her warning.

A.why: This is Abel's reassurance, which Ruth mocks ('A fine night, says he'). You matched the character who is being corrected.

C.why: Ruth's question is rhetorical. She means calm air has never held off a storm that a falling barometer predicts. She isn't genuinely wondering.

D.why: This reverses Ruth's position. She trusts the barometer and acts on it. It's the clear sky she distrusts.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Three weeks before a championship, Coach Delaney wants his runners training hard every day. The team physiologist, Dr. Osei, responds.
DELANEY: Every day they rest is a day the other teams gain on us.
OSEI: Gain what? A muscle isn't built during the run. It is torn a little, and it rebuilds in the hours afterward. Take those hours away and you are only tearing. If you want them fastest on race day, then the easy days are part of the training, not a holiday from it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Delaney argues that rest days let rival teams pull ahead of his runners before the final.
Osei argues that hard runs damage muscles and should be dropped in the weeks before a race.
Osei argues that recovery days are essential because muscles strengthen while rebuilding.
Osei argues that muscles grow mainly during runs, so the team should keep training daily.
items.explanation: Osei's claim sits in his final conditional: if you want the runners fastest, the easy days count as training. His reasoning is that muscle rebuilds after effort, not during it. Choice C states both parts.

A.why: This restates Delaney's worry, which Osei is answering. It's the other character's line, not the point the text makes.

B.why: Osei says hard runs tear muscle a little, but he never says to stop them. He wants them balanced with recovery days. This half-right choice names his topic and then attaches a claim he doesn't make.

D.why: Osei says the opposite: 'A muscle isn't built during the run.' You may have lifted words from the passage without checking what they say.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in a seventeenth-century woodcut workshop. The apprentice Tobias has complained that the master's blocks print faintly; the master, Hendrick, replies.
TOBIAS: The lines come out pale and broken. Cut deeper, master, and the ink will hold.
HENDRICK: Deeper? Cut deeper and thou dost but carve away wood that never touched the paper. 'Tis the raised face that prints, boy, not the hollow. Thy fault lies in thy dabber: ink thinly and evenly, press firm, and the paleness goes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tobias proposes that cutting the block more deeply would allow its lines to hold more ink.
Hendrick argues that the block must be recut because its printing surface has worn too smooth.
Hendrick asks whether deeper cuts are wise and leaves that decision to his apprentice.
Hendrick argues that the faint prints come from poor inking, not from how deeply the block is cut.
items.explanation: In plain English, Hendrick says that cutting deeper only removes wood that never prints, because the raised surface does the printing, and that Tobias's uneven inking is the real problem. Choice D states that diagnosis.

A.why: This is Tobias's suggestion, the one Hendrick rejects. You chose the other character's speech.

B.why: Hendrick never says the block is worn or needs recutting. He blames the apprentice's dabber, meaning how the ink is applied.

C.why: 'Deeper?' is a scornful rhetorical question, not a real one. Hendrick rejects the idea immediately and doesn't hand the decision to Tobias.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play. After a month of small tremors, the town's mayor, Fenwick, speaks with a visiting geologist, Dr. Asante.
FENWICK: Forty little shakes, and not one cracked a cup. Surely the ground is letting off its pressure gently, a bit at a time.
ASANTE: I wish it worked so. But a fault that slips by inches has not paid down a debt of yards. Swarms like this have come before large earthquakes about as often as they have simply faded. They may mean nothing, but they are no reason to stop inspecting the school.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Asante argues that the small tremors offer no assurance of safety, so precautions should continue.
Fenwick suggests that the frequent small tremors are harmlessly releasing the fault's pressure.
Asante argues that the small tremors show a large earthquake will certainly strike the town soon.
Asante argues that the small tremors have already released most of the strain stored in the fault.
items.explanation: Asante's 'But' rejects Fenwick's comforting idea. Small slips don't relieve much of the stored strain, and swarms like this one are as likely to come before a large earthquake as to fade away. Her hedge, 'They may mean nothing,' leads into her real point: keep the precautions going. Choice A fits both her doubt and her caution.

B.why: This is Fenwick's hope, which Asante rejects ('I wish it worked so'). You matched the wrong speaker.

C.why: You ignored Asante's hedge. She says swarms come before large earthquakes about as often as they fade, and that they 'may mean nothing.' That rules out 'certainly.'

D.why: Asante says the opposite: inches of slip haven't 'paid down a debt of yards,' so most of the strain is still there.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set aboard a whaling ship in the 1840s. The cook, Pell, is defending the crew's diet to the ship's surgeon, Haddon.
PELL: Salt pork fills a man's belly, and a full belly never yet went sick. Give them enough of it and they'll want for nothing.
HADDON: Enough of it? They've had their fill every day since we left port, and still their gums bleed. A belly may be full and the body starve all the same. 'Tis not how much they eat but what. Put the limes back on the table.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Pell maintains that a crew given plenty of salt pork will stay healthy throughout a voyage.
Haddon argues that the crew's illness stems from what their diet lacks, not how much they eat.
Haddon argues that the crew has been underfed and needs larger daily portions of salt pork.
Haddon argues that salt pork is itself poisonous and is the direct cause of the bleeding gums.
items.explanation: Haddon's key sentence is 'Tis not how much they eat but what.' The crew have eaten their fill and are still sick, so something is missing from their food, and the limes should come back. Choice B states that point.

A.why: This summarises Pell's speech, the view Haddon is answering. You picked the other character's claim.

C.why: Haddon says the crew have 'had their fill every day.' Quantity isn't the problem, so more pork isn't his fix.

D.why: Haddon blames what the diet is missing, not anything harmful in the pork. Calling it poisonous claims more than he says.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 1904 play. Mr. Pell, an amateur bird collector, has just shown his niece Agnes a drawer of mounted warblers.
PELL: There, every one labeled. Thou canst not know a bird till thou hast it in hand.
AGNES: And what hast thou learned of it, Uncle, save the colour of its coat? This one sang at dawn from the alder, I'd wager, and fed its young on midges. If the drawer holds only feathers, then all the bird's life went out of it with its breath. Ere you take another, sit an hour by the marsh and watch.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Agnes argues that a mounted specimen shows how a bird looked but reveals little about how it lived.
Agnes comes to accept that a bird must be collected and labeled before it can be properly studied.
Agnes asks her uncle to explain what the warblers' feathers have taught him about their coloring.
Agnes argues that collecting warblers should be forbidden because it threatens the marsh's birds.
items.explanation: Put Agnes's lines into plain English: a drawer of skins tells you only the bird's color, while its singing, feeding and raising of young are lost when it dies. Her conditional ('If the drawer holds only feathers, then...') and her advice to watch living birds both make one point: specimens show appearance, not behavior. That claim covers everything she says.

B.why: This is Pell's position, not Agnes's. You matched the other character's line, and Agnes rejects that view instead of accepting it.

C.why: You read 'what hast thou learned of it' as a real question. It is rhetorical: Agnes means he has learned almost nothing, so she is not actually asking for an explanation.

D.why: Agnes asks her uncle to watch before he collects again. She never calls for a ban or says the marsh's birds are under threat, so this choice claims more than the text supports.
