items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set in an English weaving village in 1822. Mr. Cartwell, a mill owner, has told the hand weaver Hannah Doyle that his new power looms will free weavers from their toil.
HANNAH: Free us, sir? Aye, free us of our bread. If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me for the other six days? You call it relief. But a weaver relieved of her loom is only a woman with empty hands and a hungry family.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hannah argues that power looms will strip hand weavers of their income instead of easing their labor.
Hannah agrees that power looms will spare hand weavers the long hours their work currently demands.
Hannah asks Cartwell to explain how he plans to pay weavers for the days the new looms stand idle.
Hannah argues that power looms will ruin the mill because machine-woven cloth is poorer than hers.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Hannah is answering Cartwell's claim that the looms will free weavers. Her conditional ('If your engine weaves in a day what I weave in a week, then who will pay me...') and the 'But' sentence turn that claim around: the looms will take away weavers' livelihood rather than bring them relief.

B.why: This summarizes Cartwell's claim, which the introduction reports. Hannah mocks 'Free us, sir?' and rejects it, so this choice gets her position backward.

C.why: You took 'who will pay me for the other six days?' literally. Her point is that nobody will pay her. She is not asking about a payment plan, and the looms would not be the ones standing idle.

D.why: Hannah says nothing about the quality of machine-made cloth or about the mill failing. You added an argument the text never makes.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from an English translation of a nineteenth-century dialogue. A professor has just told his student Lena that regional dialects are corruptions of the standard language.
LENA: Corruptions, sir? Then was the standard never itself a dialect? Yet the speech of the capital was once a village tongue like any other, and it rose only because the court happened to sit there. If a dialect may become "correct" by the accident of where kings live, then correctness is a matter of power, not of grammar.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lena argues that the standard language owes its status to political circumstance, not superior grammar.
Lena agrees that regional dialects are flawed versions of a standard language that is more correct.
Lena asks the professor whether the language of the capital was ever regarded as a regional dialect.
Lena argues that schools should teach regional dialects in place of the standard form of the language.
items.explanation: Lena's conditional holds her claim: if a dialect becomes 'correct' because the court happened to sit in its region, then correctness comes from power rather than grammar. Her history of the capital's 'village tongue' supports that conclusion, so the choice that says the standard's status is political states her point.

B.why: This is the professor's view, given in the introduction. Lena's whole reply argues against it.

C.why: 'Then was the standard never itself a dialect?' is rhetorical. Lena answers it herself in the next sentence, so she is not really asking the professor anything.

D.why: Lena questions where 'correctness' comes from, but she never proposes changing what schools teach. This choice goes beyond what she says.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set aboard a trawler in 1958. The captain, Ewan Muir, has dismissed a young biologist's worry about his catch by remarking that the sea is too big to empty.
DR. SORENSEN: So said the men who fished the old cod banks, Captain. The sea is wide, I grant you, but a shoal is not. Your nets go where the fish gather to spawn. If you take them before they breed, then it matters little how many miles of water lie beyond your boat.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Sorensen argues that the ocean's size cannot protect a fish population that is caught before it breeds.
Sorensen accepts that the ocean is too vast for fishing to seriously reduce the number of its fish.
Sorensen recounts how fishermen on the old cod banks once boasted about the size of their catches.
Sorensen argues that commercial fishing should be stopped until all of the cod banks have recovered.
items.explanation: Sorensen grants a small concession ('The sea is wide, I grant you') and then moves to her real point with 'but a shoal is not.' Her conditional finishes the argument: if fish are caught before they spawn, the size of the ocean makes no difference. The ocean's size does not protect a population fished at its spawning grounds.

B.why: This is the captain's remark from the introduction. Sorensen grants only that the sea is wide, then rejects his conclusion. You treated her concession as her claim.

C.why: The cod-bank fishermen come up in one clause, as a warning example that they once said what Muir says now. The text never mentions them boasting about catches, and the example is not her main point.

D.why: Sorensen warns about catching fish before they breed but never proposes stopping commercial fishing. This choice is a stronger claim than she makes.

items.subtype_name: The point a character makes in dialogue or drama
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play set on a merchant ship in 1912. Captain Rourke has insisted that his crew is well fed, since the men have all the salted beef and ship's biscuit they want and none ever goes hungry.
DR. ABARA: Hunger is not the measure, Captain. A man may eat his fill each day and still sicken, if what he eats lacks what the body needs. Look at Hollis: his belly is full, yet his gums bleed and his old scars have opened. The body is starving long before the stomach complains.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Dr. Abara argues that eating enough food does not ensure a person is getting the nourishment the body needs.
Dr. Abara agrees that the crew is healthy because the men have as much beef and biscuit as they want.
Dr. Abara argues that the salted beef itself is to blame for causing the illness that Hollis is suffering.
Dr. Abara notes that bleeding gums and reopened scars are the earliest signs that a sailor feels hungry.
items.explanation: The introduction gives you the captain's measure: nobody is hungry. Dr. Abara rejects that measure ('Hunger is not the measure'), and her conditional says a man can eat his fill and still get sick if his food lacks what the body needs. Hollis is her single example, and her last sentence sums up the argument: a full stomach is not proof of good nourishment.

B.why: This is Captain Rourke's position, taken from the introduction. Dr. Abara disputes it in her first sentence.

C.why: Dr. Abara says the diet lacks something the body needs, not that the beef actively causes harm. Blaming the beef goes further than her words support.

D.why: You focused on the Hollis detail and got it wrong. Dr. Abara says these symptoms appear even though he is not hungry, so they are not signs of hunger. She uses them to show his body is starving while his stomach is full.

items.subtype_name: Read one value from a table or graph
items.stimulus:
Share of Varnhold Speakers Producing the Vowel Merger

| Age group | 2004 | 2024 |
|---|---|---|
| 18–30 | 41% | 78% |
| 31–50 | 33% | 59% |
| 51–70 | 22% | 36% |
| 71 and older | 15% | 19% |

Linguist Teodora Vasić studies a vowel merger in the coastal town of Varnhold, where word pairs such as ‘pail’ and ‘pell’ have begun to sound identical. She interviewed residents in 2004 and again in 2024, recording the share of speakers in each age group who pronounced the pairs the same way. The merger spread fastest among younger residents, but it also advanced among middle-aged speakers: in 2024, the share of speakers aged 31–50 who produced the merger was ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
items.explanation: The statement names two things: the 31–50 row and the 2024 column. Where they cross, the table shows 59%, so that is the value that completes the statement.

items.explanation: First get $x^2$ by itself: divide both sides by 4 to get $x^2 = 25$. Then take the square root of both sides: $x = 5$ or $x = -5$. The positive solution is $5$. You can check it: $4(5)^2 = 4(25) = 100$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
While fitting a model to the dive path of an osprey, an ornithologist arrives at the equation below.

$x^2 - 3x - 28 = 0$
items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Look for two numbers that multiply to $-28$ and add to $-3$. Those are $-7$ and $4$, so the equation factors as $(x - 7)(x + 4) = 0$. The solutions are $x = 7$ and $x = -4$, and only $7$ is among the choices. Check: $49 - 21 - 28 = 0$.

A.why: You flipped the sign when turning the factor $(x - 7)$ into a solution. Setting $x - 7 = 0$ gives $x = 7$, not $-7$. The value $-7$ solves $x^2 + 3x - 28 = 0$, which has the sign of the middle term reversed.

B.why: You flipped the sign of the other root. The factor $(x + 4)$ gives $x = -4$, not $4$. Substituting $4$ gives $16 - 12 - 28 = -24$, not 0.

D.why: 28 is the constant term in the equation, not a root. The constant is the product of the factor numbers, so it doesn't tell you a value of $x$ directly.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stem: What values of $x$ satisfy $x^2 = 36$?
items.explanation: $x^2$ is already by itself, so take the square root of both sides and keep both signs: $x = 6$ or $x = -6$. Both work, because $6^2 = 36$ and $(-6)^2 = 36$. This is the last step of every SAT question that asks you to solve a bare quadratic. Once $x^2$ is by itself, there are two roots.

A.why: You took the positive square root and stopped. $(-6)^2$ is also $36$, so $-6$ is a solution too. Missing the negative root is the trap this question type is built to catch.

C.why: You divided $36$ by $2$, which halves it. Taking a square root is not halving. You need the number whose square is $36$, and that is $6$.

D.why: You put a ± in front of $36$ but never took the square root. $36$ is the value of $x^2$, not the value of $x$.

items.stem: What is the positive solution to $x^2 + 9 = 25$?

items.stimulus:
An agricultural scientist calibrating an irrigation schedule reduces the problem to the following equation.

items.stem: What is the positive solution to the equation?
items.explanation: The zero-product property only works when one side is 0, so you can't set each factor equal to 20. Distribute and move everything to one side: $6x^2 + 7x - 20 = 0$. This factors as $(3x - 4)(2x + 5) = 0$, so $x = \frac{4}{3}$ or $x = -\frac{5}{2}$. The positive solution is $\frac{4}{3}$. You can also use the quadratic formula: the discriminant is $49 + 480 = 529 = 23^2$, so $x = \frac{-7 \pm 23}{12}$, which gives $\frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3}$. items.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Distribute the 4 to get $4x^2 - 20 = x^2 + 7$. Then $3x^2 = 27$, so $x^2 = 9$ and $x = \pm 3$. The positive root, 3, isn't among the choices, but $-3$ is. Check it: $4(9-5) = 16$ and $9+7 = 16$.

A.why: You multiplied only $x^2$ by 4 and left $-5$ unchanged, so you got $4x^2 - 5 = x^2 + 7$. That leads to $x^2 = 4$.

C.why: You reached $3x^2 = 27$ but never divided by 3. You took the square root of 27 when you should have taken the square root of 9.

D.why: 9 is the value of $x^2$. You stopped before taking the square root to find $x$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a bare quadratic
items.stimulus:
An astronomy student calibrating the spacing of marks on a star-tracking scale writes the equation below.

$(x-4)(x+2) = 2x + 7$
items.stem: What is the positive solution to the given equation?
items.explanation: Expand the left side to get $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 2x + 7$, which becomes $x^2 - 4x - 15 = 0$. The quadratic formula gives $x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16+60}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{19}$. Only $2+\sqrt{19}$ is positive.

A.why: You expanded the middle term as $+2x$ when it should be $-2x$. The $x$ terms then cancelled and you were left with $x^2 = 15$.

B.why: You added 7 when you moved it to the left side, so you solved $x^2 - 4x - 1 = 0$. The correct step subtracts 7, which gives $-15$.

D.why: You divided only the radical in $\frac{4 \pm \sqrt{76}}{2}$ by 2. The 4 has to be divided by 2 as well, which gives 2.

items.stimulus:

$x^2 + 6x + c = 2x - 5$
items.stem: In the given equation, $c$ is an integer constant. The equation has no real solutions. What is the least possible value of $c$?

D.why: You never subtracted $2x$ from both sides and kept $b = 6$. That gives $36 < 4(c + 5)$, or $c > 4$, and $5$ is the least integer in that range. With the correct $b = 4$, smaller values also work.

items.subtype_name: Effect of changing data, and comparing centers across sets
items.stimulus: An ecologist counted the nesting pairs of a shorebird species at 7 coastal sites. The counts were 12, 15, 18, 18, 18, 22, and 24. The ecologist then surveyed an eighth site, a protected island, and counted 96 nesting pairs.
items.stem: If the count from the eighth site is included with the counts from the original 7 sites, which of the following best describes how the mean and the median change?
choices: The mean increases, and the median stays the same.
The mean increases, and the median increases.
The mean stays the same, and the median increases.
The mean decreases, and the median stays the same.
items.explanation: The value 96 is far larger than every other count, so it pulls the mean up sharply, from $\frac{127}{7} \approx 18.1$ to $\frac{223}{8} \approx 27.9$. Now check the middle. In order, the 8 values are 12, 15, 18, 18, 18, 22, 24, 96. The two middle values are 18 and 18, so the median is $\frac{18+18}{2} = 18$, which is the same as the original median. The mean increases and the median stays the same.

B.why: You assumed that a large value added to the data moves the median as well as the mean. Adding one value shifts the middle by at most half a position. Here both middle values are 18, so the median doesn't change.

C.why: You swapped the two measures. The mean is the one that reacts to an extreme value. The median is protected by the repeated 18s in the middle.

D.why: You had the direction of the mean wrong. A value far above the others pulls the mean up, not down.

items.stimulus: A folklorist counted the number of distinct versions of a trickster tale recorded in each of 11 villages. The 11 counts have a mean of 16 and a median of 14. The folklorist then adds a twelfth village, where 60 versions of the tale were recorded.
items.stem:
Which of the following must be true?

I. The mean of the 12 counts is greater than 16.
II. The median of the 12 counts is greater than 14.
III. The median of the 12 counts is not less than 14.
items.explanation: The original total is $11 \times 16 = 176$. Adding 60 gives 236, and $236 \div 12 \approx 19.7$, which is greater than 16. So statement I must be true. Before the twelfth village, the median, 14, was the 6th of 11 sorted values. The new value goes at the top of the list, so the new median is the average of 14 and the old 7th value. That 7th value is at least 14, so the median can't drop below 14 (III must be true). However, the 7th value could equal 14, which would leave the median at exactly 14, so II need not be true.

A.why: You treated the median as completely unknown after the change. The new value sits above every old value, so the new median is the average of 14 and a value that is at least 14. It can't fall below 14.

C.why: You assumed the median must rise because the mean does. That's possible, but if the 7th sorted value is also 14, the median stays at 14. 'Must be true' rules out claims that are only possible.

D.why: You swapped the roles of the two measures and treated the mean as the resistant one. A value of 60, far above the mean of 16, must pull the mean up.

In 2016, a team led by archaeologist Samir Haddad excavated a grinding stone at Tell Qaran, a site in present-day Jordan.
The grinding stone excavated at Tell Qaran carries residue of wild barley starch that dates to about 12,000 years ago.
The grinding stone from Tell Qaran proves that people in the region began farming barley about 12,000 years ago.
items.explanation: The last note explains why the find matters: the residue is about 1,500 years older than the earliest known barley farming in the region. Choice A states that comparison directly, so it makes clear why the stone is significant.

C.why: You chose the bare date. '12,000 years ago' only becomes significant when it's compared with when barley farming began, and this choice leaves that comparison out.

D.why: The starch came from wild barley, and the notes say farming came about 1,500 years later. Claiming that the stone proves farming began 12,000 years ago goes beyond the evidence.

items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Velmora Bridge spans a 410-meter river gorge in northern Chile.
• Engineer Lucía Ferrán designed the bridge in 1931.
• It is built from a series of reinforced concrete arches.
• The region has had four major earthquakes since the bridge opened.
• Of the region's bridges from the 1930s, the Velmora Bridge is the only one to have survived all four undamaged.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the achievement of Ferrán's bridge design. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Ferrán's Velmora Bridge is built from a series of reinforced concrete arches and spans a gorge in northern Chile.
Designed by engineer Lucía Ferrán in 1931, the Velmora Bridge spans a 410-meter river gorge in northern Chile.
Ferrán's Velmora Bridge is the only 1930s bridge in the region to have come through four major earthquakes undamaged.
Like the region's other bridges from the 1930s, Ferrán's Velmora Bridge has survived four major earthquakes undamaged.
items.explanation: An achievement needs to be measured against something. Choice C says the Velmora Bridge is the only bridge of its era in the region that survived all four earthquakes undamaged, and being the only one is what makes the design an achievement.

A.why: You picked a description of what the bridge is made of and where it is. That says what the bridge looks like, not what it accomplished.

B.why: This choice says who designed the bridge, when, and how long a gorge it crosses. None of that shows why the design was an achievement.

D.why: The notes say the Velmora Bridge was the only 1930s bridge to survive undamaged. Saying it did 'like' the others reverses that and erases the very thing that makes it an achievement.

items.stimulus:
Notes:
• Ecologist Maya Ortiz surveyed a restored wetland in northern Ohio in 2019.
• During the survey, she recorded a pair of black terns building a nest.
• Before that pair, no black terns had nested anywhere in Ohio for more than 30 years.
items.stem: Goal: emphasize the significance of what Ortiz recorded. Which sentence does this?
choices: In 2019, ecologist Maya Ortiz surveyed a restored wetland in northern Ohio.
The terns Ortiz recorded showed that black terns now nest across all of Ohio.
The terns Ortiz recorded were the first to nest in Ohio in more than 30 years.
During a 2019 survey, Ortiz recorded black terns building a nest in a wetland.
items.explanation: The goal asks why the nest matters, so you need the note that gives the reason: no black terns had nested in Ohio for over 30 years. Choice C keeps that comparison with the past, and the comparison is what makes the nest significant. This is the one step behind every 'emphasize the significance' synthesis question: before you look at the choices, find the note that says why the thing matters.

A.why: You chose a sentence that says who did the survey, where, and when. All of it is accurate, but it never says why the finding matters. Saying who and when is not the same as saying why it matters.

B.why: You went past the notes. One pair nested in one wetland, and nothing in the notes says the terns now nest all over the state.

D.why: You chose the event without the comparison. Building a nest only matters because it hadn't happened in Ohio for 30 years, and this sentence leaves that part out.

items.stem: Goal: emphasize the achievement of the library's blood-pressure station. Which sentence does this?

In one year, the library station found more undiagnosed cases than both clinics combined.
In one year, the library station ended undiagnosed high blood pressure in Ferrisburg.
In one year, the library station identified many cases of undiagnosed high blood pressure.
items.explanation: An achievement is a result measured against something. The last note supplies the measure: the station found more cases than both clinics put together. A.why: You chose the sentence that says what started and when. That is background information, and it gives no result, so there is no achievement in it.

C.why: You claimed more than the notes support. Finding more cases than the clinics is not the same as ending undiagnosed high blood pressure in the whole town.

D.why: You kept the result but dropped the comparison. 'Many cases' could mean anything. The achievement is that the station beat both clinics combined, and this sentence leaves that out.

Notes:

items.stem: Goal: emphasize the significance of Reyna's recording. Which sentence does this?
choices: Reyna's recording showed that "The Salt Bride" still survived as a spoken tale, not only in print.
Reyna recorded "The Salt Bride" in 1972 as told by an 80-year-old weaver in a mountain village.
Earlier collectors had assumed that "The Salt Bride" survived only in the pages of printed books.
Reyna's recording proved that every printed tale in Portugal was still being told aloud in 1972.
items.explanation: The last note sets the recording against an earlier belief: collectors thought the tale lived only in books. The recording proved them wrong, and that is why it matters. Choice A joins the recording to the belief it overturned. This is the move to make when a significance question's notes end with a background claim: the significance comes from the recording contradicting that claim.

B.why: You chose who, when, and from whom. The details are accurate and vivid, but the sentence never says why the recording mattered.

C.why: You chose the background claim alone. This sentence says what people believed but leaves out the recording that proved them wrong, so it says nothing about why Reyna's work matters.

D.why: You stretched one tale into a claim about every tale. The notes tell you about "The Salt Bride" only, not about every printed tale in Portugal.

items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the late 1700s, weavers in the town of Kessmer produced patterned linen for export.
• Weaver Ilse Vartenau designed a loom attachment that used notched wooden slats to raise warp threads in a set sequence.
• With the attachment, one weaver could produce a repeating damask pattern without the second worker earlier patterned looms required.
• Vartenau's attachment was patented in 1784.
• Joseph-Marie Jacquard's better-known punched-card loom, which also automated the lifting of warp threads, was introduced in 1804.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the historical significance of Vartenau's attachment relative to later developments in loom automation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Vartenau's attachment, which used notched wooden slats to raise warp threads in a set sequence, was patented in 1784.
Patented in 1784, Vartenau's attachment automated the lifting of warp threads two decades before Jacquard introduced his punched-card loom.
With Vartenau's attachment, a single weaver could produce a repeating damask pattern that had previously required a second worker.
Vartenau's attachment was the first device ever to automate pattern weaving, and Jacquard later copied its slat design.
items.explanation: The goal asks for significance relative to later developments, so you need the comparison that makes the 1784 date matter. Choice B sets Vartenau's attachment against Jacquard's 1804 loom and states the relationship outright: it did the same job two decades earlier.

A.why: You picked an accurate description of how the attachment worked and when it was patented. On its own, though, the bare date of 1784 says nothing about why it matters. Without Jacquard's 1804 loom beside it, nothing shows the attachment came earlier.

C.why: This choice does give a real benefit of the attachment, which is why it is tempting. But it compares the attachment with earlier looms, not later developments, so it misses the goal's specific comparison.

D.why: The notes never say the attachment was the first device of its kind or that Jacquard copied it. You went with a choice that claims more significance than the notes support.

items.subtype_name: Emphasize significance / achievement
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Many economists have assumed that raising the minimum wage leads employers to cut teenage workers' hours.
• Economist Tomasz Reyl studied 140 grocery stores along a county line; in 2019, one of the two counties raised its wage floor by 12%.
• He compared scheduled hours at stores in the two counties over the next 24 months.
• Teen workers' hours in the higher-wage county fell by less than 1%.
• Reyl drew hours from stores' scheduling software rather than from worker surveys.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Reyl's finding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Reyl found that over 24 months, teen workers' hours at grocery stores in the higher-wage county fell by less than 1%.
Reyl's study, which drew on stores' scheduling software rather than worker surveys, compared hours in two neighboring counties.
Reyl's study proved that raising the minimum wage never reduces teen workers' hours, overturning a long-held assumption.
Contrary to the common assumption that a higher minimum wage cuts teen workers' hours, Reyl found their hours fell by less than 1%.
items.explanation: A finding is significant here because it challenges a background belief. Choice D places the result (hours fell by less than 1%) against the assumption that higher wages cut teen hours. It marks that relationship with "Contrary to."

A.why: This choice states the finding accurately but leaves out the assumption it contradicts. Without that background, a drop of less than 1% is just a number, and the reader can't see why it matters.

B.why: You focused on the study's method. The goal asks about the significance of the finding, and this choice never says what Reyl found.

C.why: One study of grocery stores in two counties can't show that minimum-wage increases "never" reduce hours. Hours did fall slightly, too. This choice turns a limited result into a universal claim.

items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of the kiln's age. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

The glass residue in the Kerevan Höyük kiln chemically matches glass beads found at a site some 300 kilometers away.
Dated to around 1850 BCE, the Kerevan Höyük kiln is the oldest glassmaking site in the world, showing that glass was first made there.

B.why: This choice gives the date and how it was obtained, but 1850 BCE on its own carries no significance. You needed the comparison with the region's later workshops to show why the age matters.

C.why: The chemical match points to a different kind of significance, possibly trade, but it says nothing about the kiln's age. That is the specific thing the goal names.

items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Tilde-4's performance in field trials. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

In field trials during a season with 290 millimeters of rain, the sorghum variety Tilde-4 lost 9% of its yield.
In field trials, Tilde-4 proved fully resistant to drought, meaning it will end crop losses for sorghum growers in dry regions.
items.explanation: A 9% loss is significant only next to what usually happens. Choice B sets Tilde-4's loss against the more than 40% that most varieties lose below 350 millimeters of rain. It joins the two with "whereas," so the reader sees why the result matters.

A.why: This choice tells you who released Tilde-4 and what its grains look like, but nothing about how it performed in the trials. That performance is what the goal asks you to emphasize.

• Most songbirds that breed in northern Europe migrate south each autumn along a single, consistent route.

• Solvang found that individual warblers used different routes in different years, sometimes shifting by more than 400 kilometers.

items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $f(x)$. Function $f$ is linear. Which equation defines $f$?
items.explanation: From $x = 0$ to $x = 2$, the output goes from 14 to 20, so the slope is $\frac{20 - 14}{2 - 0} = 3$ millimeters per week. The row where $x = 0$ gives the intercept, 14. So $f(x) = 3x + 14$. Check the last row: $3(5) + 14 = 29$. It matches.

C.why: You swapped the slope and the intercept. The fragment starts at 14 mm, so 14 is $b$. It grows 3 mm per week, so 3 is $m$.

D.why: You used the change from 14 to 20 as the slope without dividing by the 2 weeks it took. This equation fits the first row, but at $x = 2$ it gives 26, not 20.

items.subtype_name: Build the line from two points, a table, or slope plus a point
items.stimulus: A textile historian rebuilds an eighteenth-century hand loom and records how much cloth it produces after a new warp is set. Line $\ell$ models the total length $y$, in meters, of cloth woven $x$ days after the warp was set.
items.stem: In the xy-plane, line $\ell$ has a slope of 4 and passes through the point $(3, 21)$. Which equation defines line $\ell$?
items.explanation: Substitute the point into $y = 4x + b$: $21 = 4(3) + b$, so $21 = 12 + b$ and $b = 9$. The line is $y = 4x + 9$.

A.why: You used the point's y-coordinate, 21, as the intercept. That only works when the point's x-coordinate is 0. Here $x = 3$, so substituting gives $4(3) + 21 = 33$, not 21.

C.why: You added 12 to 21 when solving $21 = 12 + b$. To isolate $b$ you have to subtract: $b = 21 - 12 = 9$.

D.why: You found the correct intercept, 9, but then put it in the slope's place. The slope is given as 4, so it multiplies $x$. Also, $9(3) + 4 = 31$, so this line misses $(3, 21)$.

items.stimulus: In an agricultural science trial, researchers model the mean height of sorghum seedlings, in centimeters, as a linear function of the number of days after planting. According to the model, the mean height is 13 centimeters on day 4 and 28 centimeters on day 10.
items.stem: According to the model, on what day after planting will the seedlings' mean height be 53 centimeters?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{28 - 13}{10 - 4} = \frac{15}{6} = 2.5$ cm per day. From $13 = 2.5(4) + b$, you get $b = 3$, so $h = 2.5d + 3$. Setting $2.5d + 3 = 53$ gives $2.5d = 50$ and $d = 20$.

A.why: You worked out how many more days it takes to grow from 28 cm to 53 cm, which is 10 days. That count starts at day 10. The question asks for the day after planting, which is $10 + 10 = 20$.

B.why: You treated 13 cm as the height at planting and solved $2.5d + 13 = 53$. The 13 cm was measured on day 4, not day 0.

D.why: You found the slope as days over centimeters, $\frac{6}{15} = 0.4$. That leads to $b = 11.4$ and $d = 104$. The growth rate is change in height over change in days.

items.subtype_name: Build the line from two points, a table, or slope plus a point
items.stimulus:
A marine biologist studying where reef fish feed records the water temperature at several depths. She models the temperature $f(x)$, in degrees Celsius, at a depth of $x$ meters below the surface with a linear function $f$.

Water Temperature by Depth
$x$ (meters) | $f(x)$ (°C)
6 | 19
14 | 15
22 | 11
items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $f(x)$. Function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $ab$?
items.explanation: Find the slope from any two rows: going from $x = 6$ to $x = 14$, the output changes by $15 - 19 = -4$ while the input changes by $14 - 6 = 8$. So $a = \frac{-4}{8} = -\frac{1}{2}$. The temperature falls as depth increases, so a negative slope fits the story. Next, substitute $(6, 19)$: $19 = -\frac{1}{2}(6) + b$, so $19 = -3 + b$ and $b = 22$. The row $(22, 11)$ checks out: $-\frac{1}{2}(22) + 22 = 11$. The question asks for the product, so $ab = -\frac{1}{2} \cdot 22 = -11$.

A.why: You worked out the slope as change in $x$ over change in $y$, $\frac{8}{-4} = -2$. That gave $b = 19 + 12 = 31$ and $ab = -62$. Slope is change in output over change in input. You can also catch this by checking the third row, since $-2(22) + 31 = -13$, not $11$.

C.why: You mixed up the subtraction order, taking $19 - 15$ over $14 - 6$, and got a positive slope of $\frac{1}{2}$. Then $b = 19 - 3 = 16$ and $ab = 8$. The temperature goes down as depth goes up, so the slope has to be negative.

D.why: You found the intercept correctly, $b = 22$, but stopped there. The question asks for the product $ab$, so you still need to multiply by $a = -\frac{1}{2}$.

items.stimulus: At an excavation site, an archaeologist models the age $A$, in years, of a sediment layer as a linear function of its depth $d$, in centimeters, below the surface. The model gives an age of 1,150 years at a depth of 20 centimeters and an age of 2,050 years at a depth of 50 centimeters.
items.stem: According to the model, what is the age, in years, of sediment at a depth of 72 centimeters?
items.explanation: Treat the two facts as the points $(20, 1150)$ and $(50, 2050)$. The slope is $\frac{2050 - 1150}{50 - 20} = \frac{900}{30} = 30$ years per centimeter. Substitute one point into $A = 30d + b$: $1150 = 30(20) + b$, so $b = 550$. The model is $A = 30d + 550$. At $d = 72$, $A = 30(72) + 550 = 2160 + 550 = 2710$.

items.stimulus:
In a treadmill trial, a sports scientist found that a runner's steady-state heart rate, in beats per minute, is a linear function $f$ of running speed $x$, in kilometers per hour.

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
|---|---|
| 2 | 110 |
| 4 | 126 |
| 6 | 142 |
items.stem: The table shows three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $f(x)$, where $f$ is a linear function. Which equation defines $f$?
items.explanation: When $x$ goes up by 2, $f(x)$ goes up by 16, so the slope is $\frac{16}{2} = 8$. Substitute the first row: $110 = 8(2) + b$, so $b = 94$. That gives $f(x) = 8x + 94$, and it checks against all three rows.

A.why: You used the 16-beat jump as the slope without dividing by the 2-unit change in $x$. This equation fits the first row, since $16(2) + 78 = 110$, but it fails the other two, because $16(4) + 78 = 142$, not 126.

C.why: You worked out the slope as change in $x$ over change in $f(x)$, $\frac{2}{16}$, so the rate is upside down. Slope is always the change in output divided by the change in input.

D.why: You took 110 as the y-intercept, but 110 is the value when $x = 2$, not when $x = 0$. To get the intercept, go back one step of 2 from the first row: $110 - 16 = 94$.

items.stimulus: A civil engineer models the elevation of a drainage culvert's floor, in centimeters above a fixed reference mark, with the linear function $g$, where $x$ is the distance in meters along the culvert from its inlet.
items.stem: The graph of the linear function $g$ in the xy-plane passes through the points $(4, 23)$ and $(10, 8)$. Which equation defines $g$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{8 - 23}{10 - 4} = \frac{-15}{6} = -\frac{5}{2}$. Substitute $(4, 23)$: $23 = -\frac{5}{2}(4) + b = -10 + b$, so $b = 33$. That gives $g(x) = -\frac{5}{2}x + 33$. The elevation drops along the culvert, so a negative slope makes sense.

A.why: You mismatched the subtraction order, taking $8 - 23$ over $4 - 10$ in effect, and got a positive slope. The output falls from 23 to 8 as $x$ rises, so the slope has to be negative.

B.why: You used the y-coordinate of $(4, 23)$ as the y-intercept. The intercept is the value when $x = 0$, and this point has $x = 4$.

D.why: You found the slope as change in $x$ over change in $y$, $\frac{6}{-15}$, and then solved for $b$ from one point. The line goes through $(4, 23)$ but misses $(10, 8)$.

items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The graph of $y = f(x)$ in the xy-plane has a slope of 6 and passes through the point $(5, 47)$. What is the value of $a + b$?

D.why: You added 30 to 47 when solving for $b$ instead of subtracting it, which gave $b = 77$ and $a + b = 83$. From $47 = 30 + b$, you get $b = 17$.

D.why: You treated 412 as the elevation at $x = 0$ and calculated $412 + 18(7)$. But 412 is the elevation at $x = 1$.

items.explanation: Substitute the point into $p(x) = -3x + b$: $40 = -3(12) + b = -36 + b$, so $b = 76$. That gives $p(x) = -3x + 76$.

A.why: This line goes through $(12, 40)$, but its slope is $+3$, not $-3$. You dropped the negative sign, so your model has the starch increasing when it should be decreasing.

C.why: You used 40 as the y-intercept. But 40 is the value when $x = 12$, not when $x = 0$.

D.why: You subtracted 36 from 40 instead of adding it. From $40 = -36 + b$, you get $b = 76$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker models the total time, in minutes, needed to pull $x$ prints from an inked linocut block with the linear function $f$. The time includes a fixed setup period.
items.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The graph of $y = f(x)$ in the xy-plane passes through the points $(3, 17)$ and $(7, 29)$. What is the value of $ab$?
items.explanation: The slope is $\frac{29 - 17}{7 - 3} = \frac{12}{4} = 3$, so $a = 3$. Substitute $(3, 17)$: $17 = 9 + b$, so $b = 8$. The question asks for the product, so $ab = 3 \times 8 = 24$.

A.why: You computed the slope as change in $x$ over change in $y$, $\frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$. That gives $b = 16$ and $ab = \frac{16}{3}$. Slope is the change in output divided by the change in input.

B.why: 8 is $b$, the setup time. The question asks for $ab$, so you still have to multiply by the slope, 3.

C.why: 11 is $a + b$. You found both constants correctly, but the question asks for their product, not their sum.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus:
A weather balloon records the air temperature $T$, in degrees Celsius, at several altitudes $h$, in kilometers, above a launch site. Over this range of altitudes, the relationship between $h$ and $T$ is linear.

Weather Balloon Readings
Altitude, $h$ (km) | Temperature, $T$ (°C)
1 | 9
3 | -4
5 | -17
items.stem: The relationship between $h$ and $T$ shown in the table can be represented by the equation $13h + kT = c$, where $k$ and $c$ are constants. What is the value of $c$?

items.stimulus: A cartographer represents the straight edge of a surveyed property boundary on a coordinate grid with the equation $3x - 4y = 24$, where $x$ and $y$ are grid coordinates, in kilometers, measured from a fixed benchmark.
items.stem: Which table gives three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$ for the given equation?
items.explanation: Substitute each x-value into $3x - 4y = 24$. When $x = 0$, $-4y = 24$, so $y = -6$. When $x = 4$, $12 - 4y = 24$, so $y = -3$. When $x = 8$, $24 - 4y = 24$, so $y = 0$. Only this table works for all three rows.

B.why: This table gets the signs of the y-intercept and the slope wrong. It does share the x-intercept $(8, 0)$, so it looks right if you check only that row. At $x = 0$, though, $3(0) - 4(6) = -24$, not 24.

C.why: You divided 24 by 3 instead of by 4 when you found the y-intercept, which gave $-8$. The slope of $\frac{3}{4}$ is right, but $3(0) - 4(-8) = 32$, not 24.

D.why: The first two rows fit the equation, but at $x = 8$ you get $24 - 4(-1) = 28$, not 24. You have to check every row before you choose a table.

items.subtype_name: Match the equation to a table or graph
items.stimulus: On a coordinate grid laid over a survey map, a cartographer draws a straight boundary line for a protected wetland. Every point $(x, y)$ on the boundary satisfies the equation $2x + 3y = 36$, where $x$ and $y$ are measured in grid units.
items.stem: Which table gives three values of $x$ and their corresponding values of $y$ for the given equation?
items.explanation: Substitute each value of $x$. When $x = 0$, $3y = 36$, so $y = 12$. When $x = 3$, $6 + 3y = 36$, so $y = 10$. When $x = 6$, $12 + 3y = 36$, so $y = 8$. Only this table has all three pairs.

A.why: These $y$-values go up as $x$ goes up, so the slope is positive. Rearranging gives $y = -\frac{2}{3}x + 12$, so $y$ has to go down.

B.why: To find $y$ at $x = 0$, you divided 36 by 2 (the coefficient of $x$) when you should have divided by 3 (the coefficient of $y$). Every row is 6 too high as a result.

C.why: $(0, 12)$ is on the line, but $(3, 9)$ is not: $2(3) + 3(9) = 33$, not 36. A table has to work for every row, not only the first.

items.stem: Which equation represents the relationship between $x$ and $y$?
items.explanation: The line crosses the $y$-axis at $(0, 60)$, so the stipend is \$60 and $b = 60$. From $(0, 60)$ to $(5, 160)$, pay goes up by \$100 over 5 hours, so the slope is $\frac{100}{5} = 20$. The equation is $y = 20x + 60$.

The function $T$ is defined by $T(x) = \frac{x}{6} + 4$, where $T(x)$ is the time, in seconds, after the earthquake begins and $x$ is the station's distance from the earthquake, in kilometers.
items.stem: What is the value of $T(39)$?
items.explanation: Put 39 in for $x$: $T(39) = \frac{39}{6} + 4$. Only the 39 is divided by 6, so $\frac{39}{6} = \frac{13}{2}$. Then $\frac{13}{2} + 4 = \frac{13}{2} + \frac{8}{2} = \frac{21}{2}$ seconds.

A.why: You added before dividing and computed $\frac{39 + 4}{6}$. In the function, only $x$ is divided by 6, and the 4 is added afterward.

C.why: You solved $T(x) = 39$ and got $x = 210$. That is the distance that gives a 39-second time. The question asks for the output when the input is 39.

D.why: You multiplied 39 by 6 instead of dividing it by 6 and got $234 + 4 = 238$.

items.stimulus: A nutrition scientist tests changes to a granola recipe. The function $c$ is defined by $c(x) = 9x + 120$, where $c(x)$ is the number of calories in one serving and $x$ is the number of grams of fat per serving added to the standard recipe. A negative value of $x$ means fat is removed.
items.stem: What is the value of $c(-6)$?
items.explanation: Put $-6$ in for $x$: $c(-6) = 9(-6) + 120 = -54 + 120 = 66$. Taking out 6 grams of fat lowers the calories, so an answer below 120 makes sense.

A.why: You solved $c(x) = -6$ and got $x = -14$. The question asks for the output $c(-6)$, not for the input that gives $-6$.

C.why: This is $c(0)$, the calories in the standard recipe. It is the starting value, not the output at $x = -6$.

D.why: You dropped the negative sign on the input and computed $9(6) + 120$. Removing fat should lower the calorie count, not raise it.

The function $r$ is defined by $r(x) = -\frac{2}{3}(x - 9) + 14$, where $r(x)$ is the predicted average pause between phrases, in hundredths of a second, and $x$ is the speaker's rate minus their usual rate, in percentage points.
items.stem: What is the value of $r(-3)$?
items.explanation: Put $-3$ in for $x$ and work inside the parentheses first: $-3 - 9 = -12$. Then $-\frac{2}{3}(-12) = 8$, and $8 + 14 = 22$.

A.why: You distributed incorrectly and wrote $-\frac{2}{3}x - 9 + 14$, which applies $-\frac{2}{3}$ to $x$ but not to $-9$. That gives $2 - 9 + 14 = 7$.

B.why: You correctly found $-\frac{2}{3}(-12) = 8$ but stopped before adding 14.

C.why: You dropped the negative sign on the input and evaluated $r(3) = -\frac{2}{3}(-6) + 14 = 18$.

items.stem: A sports science model uses the function $p(x) = -x^2 + 23$. What is the value of $p(-2)$?
items.explanation: Substitute $-2$ for x. The exponent comes before the negative sign out front, so $x^2 = (-2)^2 = 4$, and then $-x^2 = -4$. That gives $-4 + 23 = 19$. Exam questions on quadratics that open downward, such as a height or a maximum value, depend on getting this sign right.

A.why: You solved $-x^2 + 23 = -2$ and got $x = 5$, which finds the input for an output of $-2$. The question gave $-2$ as the input.

C.why: You didn't square and computed $-(-2) + 23 = 25$. You have to square the input before you apply the negative sign.

D.why: You squared the negative sign along with the input and treated $-x^2$ as $(-x)^2 = 4$. The negative sign is outside the square, so $-x^2 = -4$.

items.stem: If $f(k) = 14$ and $k > 0$, what is the value of $f(k + 2)$?

items.stimulus: An immunologist models the concentration of a certain antibody in a patient's blood after the concentration peaks. The function $C$ is defined by $C(t) = 640\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5}$, where $C(t)$ is the concentration, in units per milliliter, $t$ days after the peak.
items.stem: For what value of $t$ does $C(t) = 40$?
items.explanation: You are given the output, so set $640\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5} = 40$. Divide both sides by 640 to get $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5} = \frac{1}{16} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4$. So $\frac{t}{5} = 4$, which gives $t = 20$. Check: $C(20) = 640 \cdot \frac{1}{16} = 40$.

A.why: You worked out $C(40)$, the concentration when the input is 40, instead of finding the input that makes the concentration 40. That mixes up the value of $C$ at 40 with the value of $t$ where $C$ equals 40.

B.why: You correctly found that the exponent $\frac{t}{5}$ equals 4, but you stopped there. You still need to multiply by 5 to get $t$.

C.why: 16 is the ratio $\frac{640}{40}$, which is the number of times the concentration halves in total, not the number of days. You need to turn it into a power of 2 and then solve for $t$.

items.stem: For what value of $x$, where $x < 12$, does $h(x) = 10$?
items.explanation: Set $18 - \frac{1}{8}(x - 12)^2 = 10$. Subtract 18 to get $-\frac{1}{8}(x - 12)^2 = -8$, then multiply by $-8$ to get $(x - 12)^2 = 64$. So $x - 12 = 8$ or $x - 12 = -8$, which means $x = 20$ or $x = 4$. Only $x = 4$ meets the condition $x < 12$.

C.why: You found $h(10)$, the height at a distance of 10 meters, instead of the distance at which the height is 10 meters. You swapped the input and the output.

D.why: 20 does solve $h(x) = 10$, but it fails the condition $x < 12$. You took only the positive square root and missed the solution from the negative root.

items.stem: For what value of $h$ does $Q(h) = 81$?

items.stem: For what value of $t$ does $g(t) = 9$?
items.explanation: Set $4\sqrt[3]{t - 3} + 1 = 9$ and undo the operations in reverse order. Subtract 1: $4\sqrt[3]{t - 3} = 8$. Divide by 4: $\sqrt[3]{t - 3} = 2$. Cube both sides: $t - 3 = 8$. Add 3: $t = 11$. Check: $g(11) = 4(2) + 1 = 9$.

D.why: You cubed 8 before dividing by the coefficient 4. When you work backward, divide by 4 first so that the cube root is on its own, and only then cube.

items.stimulus: A marine biologist tracks the growth of a single giant kelp frond in a coastal research tank. The function $L(w) = \frac{1}{2}(w + 4)^2 + 10$ models the length $L(w)$, in centimeters, of the frond $w$ weeks after the biologist began measuring it, where $0 \le w \le 12$.
items.stem: According to the model, what was the length, in centimeters, of the kelp frond 4 weeks before it reached a length of 60 centimeters?
items.explanation: You are given an output (60 cm), so first work backwards to find the week. Set $\frac{1}{2}(w + 4)^2 + 10 = 60$. Subtract 10 to get $\frac{1}{2}(w + 4)^2 = 50$, then multiply by 2 to get $(w + 4)^2 = 100$, so $w + 4 = 10$ or $w + 4 = -10$. That gives $w = 6$ or $w = -14$, and only $w = 6$ is in the domain $0 \le w \le 12$. Four weeks earlier is $w = 2$, so substitute it: $L(2) = \frac{1}{2}(6)^2 + 10 = 18 + 10 = 28$ centimeters.

A.why: You found the week when the frond reached 60 cm, which is an input, $w = 6$. The question asks for a length, which is an output. You still needed to step back 4 weeks to $w = 2$ and evaluate $L(2)$.

B.why: You correctly substituted $w = 2$ and got $\frac{1}{2}(6)^2 = 18$, but then you dropped the $+10$ at the end of the function. Every output of $L$ includes that constant, so the length is $18 + 10 = 28$.

D.why: You took the negative square root, $w + 4 = -10$, which gives $w = -14$. You then evaluated $L(-18) = \frac{1}{2}(196) + 10 = 108$. A negative number of weeks is outside the domain $0 \le w \le 12$, so that root has to be rejected.

items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: For decades, many track coaches held that a long session of static stretching just before a race would help sprinters run faster. When exercise physiologists timed 40 trained sprinters over 60 meters, however, the athletes who had stretched beforehand ran slightly slower on average than those who had not. These results ______ the coaches' long-standing belief.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The coaches believed stretching makes sprinters faster, but after the word "however" the study found that sprinters who stretched ran slower. That evidence goes against the belief, so the results "challenge" it.

B.why: You picked a neutral word that sounds like research. The results don't "reveal" the coaches' belief, because the passage already stated it. The blank needs a word that says whether the evidence agrees or disagrees with the belief, and "reveal" says neither.

C.why: You missed the "however." To "repeat" the belief, the results would have to say the same thing the coaches said. Instead they show the opposite: sprinters who stretched were slower.

D.why: "Celebrate" is approving, as if the study praised the coaches' view. The slower times work against that view, so the sentence calls for disagreement, not praise.

items.stimulus: Because it contains so few stars, a faint dwarf galaxy near the Milky Way was assumed by many astronomers to hold almost no dark matter. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The astronomers assumed there was almost no dark matter. The word "however" and the finding of stars moving faster than visible matter can explain both point to hidden mass, which goes against the assumption. The measurements "undermined" it.

A.why: You were drawn to a word that sounds like astronomy. Astronomers observe stars, but measurements don't "observe" an assumption. The word also doesn't say whether the new data agreed or disagreed with the assumption.

B.why: You missed the "however." Stars moving too fast for the visible matter suggest extra unseen mass. That weakens the assumption of little dark matter. It doesn't reinforce it.

D.why: To "anticipate" an assumption would mean the measurements expected it or came before it. The measurements came later and conflict with the assumption, so this word reverses the relationship.

items.stimulus: Vegetable growers in the region had long ______ that planting beans in a field one season leads to a bigger corn harvest there the next season. items.stem: Who is doing the action in the blank, and do they agree with the view? Choose the word that fits.

The trial 'supports their view,' so the growers believed beans help corn before anyone proved it. 'Suspected' means believed something without proof, which fits. items.stimulus: When a city replaced the steel cables on an old footbridge with a lighter synthetic material, some engineers worried that the new cables would stretch in freezing weather and let the deck sag. items.stimulus: For decades, hydrologists simply ______ that the Lirvan Basin's aquifer was refilled chiefly by spring snowmelt; the idea was so widely shared that no one had thought to test it. items.stimulus: Some linguists have proposed that speakers of the Varese coastal dialect began dropping word-final consonants only in the 1980s, a change they attribute to the influence of national television. items.subtype_name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
items.stimulus: Many track coaches require sprinters to stretch statically before races, reasoning that the routine prevents hamstring strains. items.stimulus: When frogs began disappearing from the Arden Marsh, ecologists suspected chytrid, a fungal pathogen that had devastated amphibian populations in nearby wetlands. D.why: You chose a word that sounds scientific. The suspicion came from the disease's past record, not from measuring anything at the marsh. The only measurements in the text are the swabs, and those came after the suspicion and went against it.

items.stimulus: Seismologist Rafael Okonjo ______ the accepted view that the Tessaly Fault had been dormant for 10,000 years long before he had the data to test it: as early as 2009, he remarked in a conference talk that the terraces along the fault looked oddly fresh. items.stimulus: For decades, hydrologists modeled the Saltillo Basin aquifer as if it were refilled mainly by snowmelt draining from the surrounding peaks. When geochemist Ines Varga analyzed oxygen isotopes in water drawn from 60 wells, however, she found that most samples carried the signature of late-summer monsoon rain rather than winter snow. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The text sets up an earlier belief, that snowmelt refills the aquifer. Then "however" brings in isotope data pointing to monsoon rain instead. A.why: You mixed up who did what. The hydrologists who built the model presumed snowmelt was the source. Varga's results are what tested that assumption, so they didn't presume anything.

B.why: You picked a neutral, research-sounding verb. "Document" says nothing about whether the findings agree or disagree with the model, and "however" plus "therefore" require you to name that relationship.

D.why: You reversed the relationship. Rain signatures "rather than" snow go against the snowmelt model, so the results can't corroborate it.

However, in a three-year field trial, agronomist Priya Venkataraman found that tomato plants grown alongside marigolds carried just as many whiteflies as tomato plants grown with no marigolds nearby. Her results cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: whiteflies prefer to feed on marigolds rather than on tomatoes.
marigolds planted among tomatoes help protect them from whiteflies.
whitefly numbers on tomatoes do not change when marigolds are nearby.
tomatoes grown without marigolds yield more fruit than other tomatoes.
items.explanation: The old view is that marigolds keep whiteflies off tomatoes. Venkataraman found the same number of whiteflies with or without marigolds, so her trial attacks exactly that belief. The blank comes after "cast doubt on the idea that," so it has to restate the old view.

A.why: The trial counted whiteflies on tomato plants only. It never tested whether whiteflies like marigolds better, so you added a claim the passage doesn't contain.

C.why: This is what the new trial supports, not what it casts doubt on. You attached the choice to the wrong side of the "however."

D.why: The trial measured whiteflies, not fruit yield. This choice shifts to a topic the passage never discusses.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Some astronomers have interpreted the reddish color of Orla, a small icy body beyond Neptune, as a sign that its surface is coated with frozen methane, which darkens and reddens when exposed to sunlight over long periods. But new infrared observations of Orla show none of the light-absorption patterns that methane ice reliably produces, casting doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Orla's surface is covered with a layer of frozen methane.
Orla's reddish color is caused by a material besides methane.
Orla does not actually appear reddish when it is observed.
all reddish bodies beyond Neptune lack methane on their surfaces.
items.explanation: The old interpretation is that Orla's red color comes from frozen methane on its surface. The new observations find no sign of methane ice, so they undercut that exact claim. The blank restates the view that is being doubted.

B.why: If the red color isn't from methane, it must come from something else, so the new evidence points toward this idea rather than against it. You picked the side of the "but" that the data supports.

C.why: The passage treats Orla's reddish color as a given. The new data question what causes the color, not whether the color is there.

D.why: The observations covered only Orla. Stretching one object's result to "all" reddish bodies is strength creep.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Many dietitians have advised against drinking water with meals, reasoning that the extra liquid dilutes stomach acid and therefore slows digestion. However, when nutrition researchers measured stomach acidity and digestion time in volunteers who drank water with a meal and in volunteers who did not, they found no meaningful difference between the two groups, casting doubt on the claim that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: water consumed during a meal passes through the stomach quickly.
drinking water with a meal interferes with the process of digestion.
people should avoid drinking large amounts of water at any time.
stomach acidity stays the same whether or not water is consumed.
items.explanation: The dietitians' view is that water with meals slows digestion by diluting stomach acid. The study found no difference in acidity or digestion time, which knocks out that reasoning. So the blank restates the old claim.

A.why: The study measured acidity and total digestion time. It didn't track how fast the water itself moves through the stomach, so this choice is about a detail nobody tested.

C.why: The passage is only about water with meals. A rule about avoiding water "at any time" goes far beyond both the old advice and the new study.

D.why: This is what the study found, so it can't be the idea the study casts doubt on. You landed on the wrong side of the "however."

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Because its outline of the coast closely matches older Portuguese charts, historians long assumed that a 1583 map by cartographer Tomás Reyna was simply copied from those earlier works. Recent analysis, however, shows that Reyna's map records water depths and several small inlets that appear on no earlier chart of the region, casting doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Reyna's map was merely copied from older Portuguese charts.
Reyna personally surveyed every inlet shown on his 1583 map.
Reyna's map includes details missing from the earlier charts.
older Portuguese charts depicted that coastline with accuracy.
items.explanation: The historians' view rested on the match in coastlines: Reyna must have copied. Details found on no earlier chart could not have been copied, so the new analysis undercuts that view. The blank restates it.

B.why: New details suggest Reyna had some source beyond the old charts. They don't prove he surveyed every inlet himself, which is the extra step this choice requires.

C.why: This is the new finding itself, so it can't be the idea being doubted. You picked the evidence instead of the old view it overturns.

D.why: The analysis is about where Reyna's map came from, not whether the older charts were accurate. Nothing in the passage questions them.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Forecasters have long believed that the summer afternoon thunderstorms in Colter Valley are triggered by moist air drifting up from nearby Lake Annis. But weather-balloon records from several summers when drought had left the lake nearly empty show that storms formed over the valley just as often as in wetter years, casting doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Lake Annis has been nearly empty for most recent summers.
moisture from Lake Annis is what sets off the valley's storms.
the valley's storms are set off by a different moisture source.
thunderstorms rarely form over the valley in drought summers.
items.explanation: The forecasters' view is that the lake's moisture triggers the storms. If storms formed just as often while the lake was nearly empty, the lake can't be what sets them off. The blank restates that old belief.

A.why: The passage mentions only "several summers" of drought. It never says the lake was low in most recent summers, so this inflates the evidence.

C.why: The balloon data rule out the lake but never identify another moisture source. This is a new claim the study didn't test, not the old view being doubted.

D.why: The records show storms formed in drought summers just as often as in wet ones. This choice reverses what the passage says.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Seismologists long thought that frequent small earthquakes along a fault release built-up stress, making a large earthquake on that fault less likely. However, a 2024 study of 300 faults found that large earthquakes were just as common on faults with many small quakes as on faults with few, casting doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the study casts doubt on?
choices: small earthquakes lower the chance of a large earthquake on the same fault.
large earthquakes occur equally often on faults with many or few small quakes.
small earthquakes are what trigger large earthquakes on the same fault.
seismologists have now gathered data on roughly 300 faults worldwide.
items.explanation: The blank comes right after 'casting doubt on the idea that,' so it has to restate the old view: the one before 'However.' Seismologists thought small quakes release stress and make big ones less likely. The study's result (big quakes are just as common either way) attacks that exact reasoning, so A is the idea being doubted. This is the first step of every 'new evidence undercuts a prior view' inference question: find the old view and put it in the blank.

B.why: This is what the new study found, which puts it on the wrong side of 'However.' Evidence can't cast doubt on itself. You picked the finding when the blank asked for the belief the finding overturns.

C.why: The study showed that small quakes don't make large ones less likely. It never tested whether small quakes cause large ones. You flipped the old view into its opposite and treated that as something the passage discusses.

D.why: This is about the study's sample size, a background detail. It isn't a view that anyone held or that the evidence could undercut.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Many hydrologists have assumed that the amount of water a mountain stream carries in summer depends mainly on how much rain falls that summer. But measurements from 40 mountain streams showed that summer flow tracked the depth of the previous winter's snowpack far more closely than it tracked summer rain, challenging the assumption that ______
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the measurements cast doubt on?
choices: winter snowpack is the main source of a mountain stream's summer flow.
summer rainfall mainly determines how much water a stream carries in summer.
summer rainfall has no effect on a stream's flow in any season of the year.
hydrologists measure mountain streams more often than they measure lowland rivers.
items.explanation: 'Challenging the assumption that' tells you the blank holds the old assumption, which is the sentence before 'But.' Hydrologists assumed summer rain mainly drives summer flow. The measurements point to snowpack instead, and that attacks this assumption directly. Spotting which side of the contrast the blank belongs to is the skill that 'challenging the assumption' inference questions rest on.

A.why: This is what the new measurements suggest, so it sits after 'But.' You picked the evidence's conclusion when the blank wanted the assumption being challenged.

C.why: The data show that rain matters less than snowpack, not that it doesn't matter at all. 'No effect' and 'any season' are far stronger than anything the passage establishes.

D.why: The passage never compares how often different rivers are measured. This choice is about method, not the view the data undercut.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Astronomers once believed that a planet orbiting very close to its star could not hold on to an atmosphere, because the star's intense heat would strip any gas away. However, telescope observations of a scorching close-orbiting planet revealed a thick layer of gas surrounding it, casting doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the observation casts doubt on?
choices: a planet very close to its star can still keep a thick layer of gas.
every planet orbiting close to its star has a thick atmosphere of gas.
a planet very close to its star is unable to hold on to an atmosphere.
telescopes can now measure the surface temperature of distant stars.
items.explanation: The old view comes before 'However': astronomers believed close-orbiting planets couldn't keep an atmosphere. One close planet with a thick layer of gas is a direct counterexample to that belief, so C is the idea being doubted. In this subtype, you don't need to know any astronomy. beaver dams improve conditions for every fish species in every stream.
ecologists have surveyed trout populations in about 25 different streams.
beaver dams harm trout populations by keeping the fish from moving freely.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Because slow slip events release built-up strain gradually, over days or weeks and without violent shaking, many seismologists long regarded them as a kind of safety valve for faults. Geophysicist Tomasz Rydel's analysis of two decades of GPS data from a Pacific subduction zone, however, found that four of the region's six largest earthquakes struck within months of a slow slip event on a neighboring stretch of the fault. Each of those slip events appeared to have shifted strain onto the segment that later ruptured. Rydel's findings therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: slow slip events lower the likelihood of a major earthquake on a fault.
slow slip events can move strain from one section of a fault to another.
most major subduction earthquakes are triggered by earlier slow slip events.
GPS measurements can detect fault slip that produces no violent shaking.
items.explanation: The old view is the 'safety valve' idea: by releasing strain quietly, slow slip events make large earthquakes less likely. Rydel found that most of the biggest quakes came soon after slow slip events that loaded strain onto the segment that then ruptured. That attacks the safety-valve reasoning directly, so the doubted idea is that slow slip lowers the chance of a major earthquake.

B.why: You picked what Rydel's data support, not what they undercut. The strain shifting between segments is the new finding, on the far side of the 'however'. It is not the old view being doubted.

C.why: You made the study's claim bigger than it is. Four quakes in one subduction zone can't show that most subduction earthquakes everywhere are triggered this way, and nothing here is doubted in any case.

D.why: You latched onto a detail of the method. Rydel's study depends on GPS picking up quiet slip, so it takes that ability for granted and doesn't question it.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Transportation agencies have long set weight limits on aging bridges on the premise that the repeated stress of heavy trucks is what chiefly wears down concrete decks. But when civil engineer Priya Nandakumar compared 212 bridges in a northern state, she found that decks carrying only light local traffic had deteriorated at nearly the same rate as decks on busy freight routes. In both groups, the damage tracked closely with the number of winters in which the deck had been treated with de-icing salt. Nandakumar's results challenge the assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: de-icing salt harms concrete decks more than freezing temperatures do.
decks treated with de-icing salt tend to show greater deterioration.
heavy truck traffic is the main cause of wear on concrete decks.
bridges in northern states deteriorate faster than bridges elsewhere.
items.explanation: The old assumption behind weight limits is that heavy trucks are the main thing wearing decks down. If lightly used decks deteriorate about as fast as decks on freight routes, traffic load can't be the chief cause. So the challenged assumption is that heavy truck traffic is the main source of wear.

A.why: You claimed a comparison the study never made. Nandakumar linked damage to salt treatment but never measured salt against freezing temperatures on their own.

B.why: You chose the new finding instead of the old belief. The salt pattern is what Nandakumar's data support, so it can't be the assumption her results challenge.

D.why: You stretched the sample beyond where it came from. All 212 bridges were in one northern state, so the study says nothing about how they compare with bridges elsewhere.

items.stimulus: In classic planetarium experiments, caged migratory songbirds hopped toward the correct seasonal direction when shown a projected night sky, and ornithologists concluded that such birds rely primarily on the stars to steer. Recently, however, a team led by Ines Varga fitted 40 wild Swainson's thrushes with miniature radio tags. The researchers found that birds flying beneath complete cloud cover held their headings just as accurately as birds flying on clear nights. The team's results cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: thrushes rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field to steer at night.
night-migrating thrushes depend chiefly on the stars to steer.
thrushes can hold a steady heading without seeing the night sky.
caged songbirds orient correctly under projected star patterns.
items.explanation: The old conclusion was that these birds steer mainly by the stars. Thrushes that can't see any stars under full cloud cover still navigate as accurately as on clear nights, which undercuts the claim that stars are their main guide. The doubted idea is therefore that the thrushes depend chiefly on the stars.

D.why: You restated the old experiment's result, not the conclusion drawn from it. Varga's study doesn't dispute that caged birds oriented under a projected sky. It disputes the idea that stars are their main guide.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Flood models used by regional planners typically represent a restored wetland as a sponge with a fixed storage volume, which is why restoration is often promoted as a dependable way to lower downstream flood peaks. Hydrologist Kofi Mensah-Boateng's stream-gauge records from the Kessler Creek basin tell a more complicated story. While restored wetlands there did reduce peak flows during isolated storms, during a run of back-to-back storms the already saturated wetlands released runoff almost as quickly as the surrounding cropland. These records call into question the assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: restored wetlands fail to lower peak flows during isolated storms.
saturated wetlands release runoff more quickly than dry ones do.
restored wetlands worsen flooding compared with nearby cropland.
a restored wetland can hold the same volume of water in every storm.
items.explanation: The models treat a wetland as a sponge with a fixed storage volume. The gauge records show that storage shrinks once the wetland is saturated from earlier storms. What they call into question is the fixed-capacity assumption: that a wetland holds the same amount of water in every storm.

A.why: You reversed the half of the finding that held steady. The passage says the wetlands did reduce peak flows during isolated storms.

B.why: You picked what the new records suggest, not the assumption they challenge. Saturation cutting a wetland's capacity is the new finding, not the old model's premise.

C.why: You pushed 'almost as quickly as' up to 'worse than'. At their weakest, saturated wetlands roughly matched cropland. They never did worse.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Surveys have repeatedly found that athletes who stretch before exercising report fewer injuries than those who do not, a pattern that has made the pre-workout stretch nearly universal advice. Surveys cannot show, though, whether stretching itself is responsible. When sports scientist Lena Okafor randomly assigned 1,400 recreational runners either to stretch before every run or to skip stretching for a season, injury rates in the two groups were nearly identical, although the stretchers said they felt looser on their runs. Okafor's trial therefore undermines the belief that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: stretching before a run raises a runner's risk of being injured.
runners who stretch are more cautious in their training overall.
stretching before a run lowers a runner's risk of being injured.
stretching before a run leaves runners feeling less stiff overall.
items.explanation: The widely held belief, built on survey data, is that stretching prevents injuries. Okafor randomly assigned runners to groups, which rules out the problem the surveys had, and found nearly identical injury rates. That undermines the belief that stretching before a run lowers injury risk.

D.why: You added the two polynomials instead of subtracting the second from the first, so you found the sum, not the difference.

A.why: You applied the minus sign to $3xy$ but not to $-4x$, so you subtracted $4x$ instead of adding it.

C.why: You added the two expressions instead of subtracting the second from the first, so you found their sum.

D.why: You subtracted in the wrong order for the $xy$-terms and computed $3xy - 5xy$ instead of $5xy - 3xy$.

items.subtype_name: Expand, distribute, combine like terms
items.stimulus: A hydrologist models the combined inflow, in thousands of cubic meters, from two streams feeding a reservoir, where $x$ is the number of days after a storm.
items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(x^2 - 3x + 8) + 2(x^2 + 4x - 1)$?
items.explanation: Multiply every term in the second bracket by 2: $2x^2 + 8x - 2$. Then add like terms: $x^2 + 2x^2 = 3x^2$, $-3x + 8x = 5x$ and $8 - 2 = 6$. That gives $3x^2 + 5x + 6$.

A.why: You multiplied only $x^2$ by 2 and left $4x$ and $-1$ undoubled, so you got $x$ and $7$ where you should have $5x$ and $6$.

B.why: You doubled $x^2$ and $4x$ but not the constant $-1$, so you got $+7$ instead of $+6$.

C.why: You treated $-3x$ as $+3x$ and added it to $8x$, getting $11x$ instead of $5x$.

items.subtype_name: Expand, distribute, combine like terms
items.stimulus: A seismologist uses two polynomials to model readings from two monitoring stations, where $x$ is the number of seconds after a tremor begins. The functions are $P(x) = 4x^2 + 3x - 5$ and $Q(x) = x^2 - 6x + 2$.
items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $P(x) - Q(x)$?
items.explanation: Put each definition in parentheses: $(4x^2 + 3x - 5) - (x^2 - 6x + 2)$. Apply the minus sign to every term in the second bracket to get $4x^2 + 3x - 5 - x^2 + 6x - 2$. Then combine like terms: $4x^2 - x^2 = 3x^2$, $3x + 6x = 9x$, and $-5 - 2 = -7$. The result is $3x^2 + 9x - 7$.

A.why: You applied the minus sign only to $x^2$, the first term in the second bracket, and then added $-6x$ and $+2$ as they were written. That gives $3x - 6x = -3x$ and $-5 + 2 = -3$. The minus sign has to reach every term in $Q(x)$.

C.why: You found $P(x) + Q(x)$ instead of $P(x) - Q(x)$. Adding the two polynomials gives $5x^2 - 3x - 3$, but the question asks for the difference.

D.why: You correctly changed $-6x$ to $+6x$, but you did not change the sign of the constant. You computed $-5 + 2 = -3$ when it should be $-5 - 2 = -7$.

items.subtype_name: Expand, distribute, combine like terms
items.stimulus: An archaeologist uses the expression $3(2x^2 - x + 4) + 4x^2 - 5x$ to estimate the number of pottery fragments catalogued at a dig site, where $x$ is the number of excavation days.
items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $3(2x^2 - x + 4) + 4x^2 - 5x$?
items.explanation: Multiply each term inside the parentheses by 3 to get $6x^2 - 3x + 12$. Then add the remaining terms: $6x^2 - 3x + 12 + 4x^2 - 5x$. Combine like terms: $6x^2 + 4x^2 = 10x^2$, $-3x - 5x = -8x$, and the constant is $12$. The result is $10x^2 - 8x + 12$.

A.why: You multiplied only the first term, $2x^2$, by 3 and left $-x + 4$ unchanged. The factor of 3 has to multiply every term inside the parentheses.

B.why: You multiplied $-x$ and $4$ by 3 but skipped $2x^2$, so you added $2x^2 + 4x^2$ and got $6x^2$. Every term inside the parentheses has to be multiplied by 3.

D.why: You treated $-5x$ as $+5x$ when you combined the $x$-terms, so you got $-3x + 5x = 2x$ with the wrong sign. Both terms are negative, so they add to $-8x$.
