items.subtype_name: 2D area or perimeter: plug in and combine
items.stimulus: A folklore studies exhibit displays a festival banner made of a square panel with an equilateral triangle panel sewn along its top edge. The triangle's base and the top side of the square are the same seam. Each side of the square and each side of the triangle has a length of $(2x + 3)$ inches. A ribbon is sewn around the outer edge of the whole banner but not along the inside seam.
items.stem: Which expression represents the perimeter, in inches, of the banner?
items.explanation: The outer edge has 3 sides from the square and 2 sides from the triangle. The shared seam is inside the banner, so it is not counted. That makes 5 sides of $(2x + 3)$ inches each: $5(2x + 3) = 10x + 15$.

A.why: You counted the 5 outer sides correctly but multiplied only the $2x$ by 5 when you distributed. You need $5 \cdot 3 = 15$, not 3.

B.why: You added the full perimeter of the square (4 sides) to the full perimeter of the triangle (3 sides), giving $7(2x + 3)$. The shared seam is inside the banner and has to be left out of the outer edge.

D.why: You gave the equilateral triangle 4 sides as if it were a square and added it to the square's 4 sides, giving $8(2x + 3)$. A triangle has 3 sides, and the shared one is not part of the outer edge.

items.subtype_name: 2D area or perimeter: plug in and combine
items.stimulus: A cartography student prints a rectangular map sheet that is 1.2 meters long and 80 centimeters wide. A rectangular legend box that is 20 centimeters long and 15 centimeters wide is printed in one corner of the sheet.
items.stem: What is the area, in square centimeters, of the map sheet that is not covered by the legend box?
items.explanation: First convert to the same units: 1.2 meters = 120 centimeters. The sheet has area $120 \times 80 = 9{,}600$ square centimeters, and the legend box has area $20 \times 15 = 300$ square centimeters. The uncovered area is $9{,}600 - 300 = 9{,}300$ square centimeters.

D.why: 9,600 is the area of the whole sheet. You didn't subtract the part the legend box covers.

items.subtype_name: Generalization vs. specific example
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Cleaner fish are species that feed by removing parasites and dead skin from other fish.
• Larger reef fish often line up at "cleaning stations," fixed spots on a reef where cleaner fish gather.
• The bluestreak cleaner wrasse, a small striped fish of Indo-Pacific reefs, eats parasites off the bodies of other fish.
• One bluestreak cleaner wrasse may inspect more than 2,000 visiting fish in a single day.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an example of a cleaner fish. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Cleaner fish are species that feed by picking parasites and dead skin off the bodies of other fish.
The bluestreak cleaner wrasse is a cleaner fish: it eats parasites off the bodies of other reef fish.
Larger reef fish often line up at cleaning stations, fixed reef spots where cleaner fish gather.
Every reef fish in the Indo-Pacific is a cleaner fish that removes parasites from other fish.
items.explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named instance tied to the category. Choice B names a specific fish, the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, and links it to the category by saying it eats parasites off other fish.

A.why: You picked a general statement about cleaner fish as a group. It defines the category but never names a specific fish, so it gives no example. This is the wrong-level trap.

C.why: You went for a vivid detail about cleaning stations. It describes where cleaner fish gather but doesn't name any particular cleaner fish.

D.why: The notes never say every Indo-Pacific reef fish is a cleaner fish. The larger fish that line up at cleaning stations are the ones getting cleaned. This choice also makes a sweeping claim when the goal asked for one example.

items.subtype_name: Generalization vs. specific example
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Body waves are seismic waves that travel through Earth's interior rather than along its surface.
• Primary (P) waves are body waves that squeeze and stretch rock as they pass through it.
• Secondary (S) waves are body waves that shake rock from side to side.
• After an earthquake, body waves generally reach distant seismometers before surface waves do.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about body waves. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: P waves squeeze and stretch rock as they pass, while S waves shake rock from side to side.
P waves are body waves that squeeze and stretch rock as they pass through Earth's interior.
Body waves, which travel through Earth's interior, generally reach seismometers before surface waves.
Surface waves, which travel along Earth's exterior, generally reach seismometers before body waves.
items.explanation: A generalization makes a claim about the whole category, with no single instance as its subject. Choice C makes body waves as a group its subject and states something true of them in general: they usually arrive before surface waves.

A.why: You picked a choice that compares two specific kinds of body wave. Contrasting P waves with S waves stays at the level of instances, so it isn't a claim about body waves as a whole. This is the subtype's main trap.

B.why: This choice is about one specific type, P waves, rather than body waves in general. It's an example, and the goal asked for a generalization.

D.why: This reverses the notes. Body waves reach seismometers before surface waves, not after.

items.subtype_name: Generalization vs. specific example

• Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins produced by immune cells called B cells.

items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about antibodies. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

IgA is an antibody that is found mainly in saliva, tears, and mucus rather than in the blood.
Antibodies, including IgG, are found mainly in saliva, tears, and mucus rather than in blood.

items.subtype_name: Generalization vs. specific example
items.stimulus:
Notes:
• A creole language forms when speakers of different languages build a shared language that children then learn as their first language.
• Most creole languages take much of their vocabulary from a single source language.
• Haitian Creole draws most of its vocabulary from French.
• Tok Pisin, spoken in Papua New Guinea, draws most of its vocabulary from English.
items.stem: Which sentence makes a generalization about the vocabulary of creole languages?
choices: Haitian Creole, a creole language, draws most of its vocabulary from French.
Most creole languages take much of their vocabulary from one source language.
Haitian Creole draws on French, while Tok Pisin draws on English instead.
All creole languages take their vocabulary from either French or English.
items.explanation: A generalization is a claim about the whole category, and no single language is its subject. Choice B is about "most creole languages" and names none of them, so it works at the category level. This is the first step in any Rhetorical Synthesis question whose goal says "make a generalization": before you look at anything else, decide whether a choice is about the category or about one member of it.

A.why: You chose a specific instance. Calling Haitian Creole "a creole language" connects it to the category, but the sentence is still about one language. That makes it an example, not a generalization.

C.why: You chose a comparison of two instances. Naming two creoles and setting them side by side is still talking about individual languages, not making a claim about creoles as a group.

D.why: You picked a choice that sounds broad, but it says more than the notes do. The notes give French and English as sources for two languages only. They never say that every creole draws on one of those two.

items.subtype_name: Generalization vs. specific example

Notes:
• Tapering means reducing training volume in the days before a competition.
• Studies of swimmers, runners, and cyclists have found that most athletes perform better after a taper of one to three weeks.

items.stem: Which sentence makes a generalization about tapering?
choices: Twelve college swimmers cut their 100-meter times by about 2 percent after tapering.

Any athlete who tapers for two weeks will improve performance by at least 2 percent.
items.explanation: Choice C is about "most athletes" across several sports, and no single study or group is its subject. That makes it a claim about tapering in general. In real Rhetorical Synthesis questions, the generalization is often the note that the specific studies support, so look for the sentence that sits above the individual cases.

A.why: You chose one specific study. A result from twelve swimmers is an instance that supports the generalization, but it is not the generalization itself.

B.why: You chose a comparison between two studies. Comparing cyclists to swimmers keeps the sentence at the level of individual cases, not tapering in general.

D.why: This sounds general, but it turns "most athletes" into "any athlete" and turns one study's 2 percent into a guaranteed minimum. The notes support neither change.

A.why: You chose the category statement. It defines attenuated vaccines but never names one, and an example has to name an instance.

items.subtype_name: Write a function for a geometric quantity
items.stimulus: A rectangular solar panel on a small research satellite has a length that is 4 meters greater than its width. The length of the panel is $x$ meters.
items.stem: Which function $A$ gives the area of the panel, in square meters, in terms of $x$?
items.explanation: The length is $x$, and the width is 4 meters less than the length, so the width is $x - 4$. The area is length times width: $x(x - 4) = x^2 - 4x$.

B.why: You wrote the width as $x + 4$, as if $x$ were the width. Here $x$ is the length, so the width is the smaller dimension, $x - 4$, and the sign of the offset flips.

C.why: You added the two dimensions, $x + (x - 4)$, when you should have multiplied them to get the area.

D.why: You multiplied $x$ by $x$ but did not multiply $x$ by $-4$. Distributing fully gives $x^2 - 4x$.

The area is $A(x) = x \cdot \frac{x - 10}{2} = \frac{1}{2}x^2 - 5x$. Check with $x = 30$: the width is 10, so the area is 300 square meters, and $\frac{1}{2}(900) - 5(30) = 300$.

A.why: You wrote the width as $2x + 10$, which applies the relationship to the wrong side. It is the length that equals twice the width plus 10, not the other way around.

B.why: You divided by 2 correctly but added 10 when you should have subtracted it. Solving $x = 2w + 10$ for $w$ gives $w = \frac{x - 10}{2}$.

C.why: You subtracted 10 but never divided by 2, so you used $x - 10$ as the width. That value is twice the width, not the width.

items.subtype_name: Write a function for a geometric quantity
items.stimulus: At an excavation site, archaeologists uncover an ancient grain-storage pit shaped like a right circular cylinder. The depth of the pit is 4 feet more than its radius.
items.stem: Which function $V$ gives the volume, in cubic feet, of the pit in terms of its depth $h$, in feet?
items.explanation: The variable is the depth, $h$. The depth is 4 more than the radius, so the radius is $h - 4$. A cylinder's volume is $\pi r^2 h$, so $V(h) = \pi (h - 4)^2 h = \pi h(h - 4)^2$. Check with $h = 6$: the radius is 2, so the volume is $\pi(4)(6) = 24\pi$, and $\pi(6)(2)^2 = 24\pi$.

A.why: You squared the depth instead of the radius. In $\pi r^2 h$, only the radius, $h - 4$, is squared.

C.why: You wrote the radius as $h + 4$, which flips the sign of the offset. The depth is the larger value, so the radius is 4 less than $h$.

D.why: This is $2\pi r h$, the area of the pit's curved wall. It is not the volume, which is $\pi r^2 h$.

items.stem: The graph of a system of linear equations is shown. What is the solution $(x, y)$ to the system?

items.stem: Which equation represents the line shown in the graph?
items.explanation: The line crosses the vertical axis at $(0, 8)$, so the y-intercept is $8$. From $(0, 8)$ to $(1, 6)$ the line drops $2$ for every $1$ it moves right, so the slope is $-2$. That gives $y = -2x + 8$. This is the reading you need when a question shows two graphed lines and asks which pair of equations they could be: you do this for each line, then keep only the choice that matches both.

A.why: You read the steepness correctly but missed the direction. The line goes down from left to right, so its slope is negative. Mixing up whether a line rises or falls is the most common mistake when matching graphed lines to equations.

C.why: You used where the line meets the horizontal axis, at $x = 4$, as $b$. In $y = mx + b$, $b$ is where the line crosses the vertical axis, which is $8$.

D.why: You found the slope as run over rise. Slope is rise over run: the line falls $2$ for every $1$ to the right, so the slope is $-2$, not $-\frac{1}{2}$.

items.stimulus: A folklore studies student graphed a system of two linear equations in the $xy$-plane while comparing how quickly two collections of folktales grew. The first line slants up from left to right and passes through the points $(0, 1)$, $(3, 2)$, and $(6, 3)$. items.stem: If $(x, y)$ is the solution to the system, what is the value of $y$?
items.explanation: The solution is the one point that lies on both lines. That point is not a lattice point, so you need each line's equation first. The first line rises 1 for every 3 to the right and crosses the y-axis at 1, so $y = \frac{1}{3}x + 1$. The second line falls 1 for every 1 to the right and crosses the y-axis at 6, so $y = -x + 6$. Set the two equal: $\frac{1}{3}x + 1 = -x + 6$, so $\frac{4}{3}x = 5$ and $x = \frac{15}{4}$. Then $y = -\frac{15}{4} + 6 = \frac{9}{4}$. The question asks for $y$, so the answer is $\frac{9}{4}$, or 2.25.

items.stem: One of the two graphed equations is $3x + ky = 12$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: First work out which line $3x + ky = 12$ can be. Solving for $y$ gives $y = -\frac{3}{k}x + \frac{12}{k}$. For the rising line you would need $-\frac{3}{k} = \frac{3}{2}$, so $k = -2$, and also $\frac{12}{k} = -2$, so $k = -6$. Those two values disagree, so the equation has to be the falling line. That line passes through $(0, 2)$. Substitute: $3(0) + k(2) = 12$, so $k = 6$. Check it with the slope: $-\frac{3}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}$. That matches the falling line, which drops 2 over a run of 4, from $(0, 2)$ to $(4, 0)$.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: A textile historian made a calibration line to convert thread-count readings from a damaged loom record. The graph of $y = f(x)$ is shown.
items.stem: The graph of the linear function $f$ is shown, for $4 \le x \le 12$. If the graph of $y = f(x)$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(0, b)$, what is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: The window starts at x = 4, so you can't read the y-intercept straight off the picture. Find two points that sit exactly on gridlines, (4, 14) and (8, 20). The slope is $\frac{20 - 14}{8 - 4} = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$. Then use $b = y - mx$ with (4, 14): $b = 14 - \frac{3}{2}(4) = 14 - 6 = 8$. Another way: step back 4 units from x = 4 to x = 0, and y drops by $\frac{3}{2}\cdot 4 = 6$, from 14 to 8.

common_errors.why: Took the y-value at the left edge of the window (x = 4) as if it were the y-intercept, without noticing that the window does not include x = 0.
Found the x-intercept by solving $0 = \frac{3}{2}x + 8$ ($x = -\frac{16}{3}$) instead of the y-intercept.
Flipped rise over run and used slope $\frac{2}{3}$, so $b = 14 - \frac{2}{3}(4) = \frac{34}{3}$.
Made a sign slip in $b = y - mx$ and added: $14 + \frac{3}{2}(4) = 20$.
Gave the slope $m$ instead of the intercept $b$.

items.explanation: The $y$-intercept is where the line crosses the $y$-axis, so $x = 0$ there. Substituting $x = 0$ gives $2y = 40$, so $y = 20$. The point is $(0, 20)$.

B.why: You set $y = 0$ and solved $5x = 40$. That gives the x-intercept, which is where the line crosses the x-axis. The question asked where it crosses the y-axis.

C.why: You found the right value, 20, but swapped the coordinates. A point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0, so the 20 belongs in the second position.

D.why: You set $x = 0$ but then read $y$ as 40 without dividing by the coefficient 2. From $2y = 40$, $y$ is 20.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: A linguist modeling a trend in a word-frequency study uses the linear function $f$. Part of the graph of $y = f(x)$ is shown.
items.stem: What is the $y$-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?
items.explanation: The segment does not reach the y-axis, so you have to extend it. From $(2, 13)$ to $(4, 12)$, $y$ drops 1 while $x$ rises 2, so the slope is $-\tfrac{1}{2}$. Step 2 units left from $(2, 13)$ to $x = 0$ and $y$ goes up 1, to 14. The y-intercept is $(0, 14)$.

A.why: You took the first point drawn, where $y = 13$, as the intercept. That point is at $x = 2$, not $x = 0$, so you still need to extend the line back to the y-axis.

C.why: You found the correct value, 14, but reversed the coordinates. The y-intercept has an x-coordinate of 0.

D.why: You solved $14 - \tfrac{1}{2}x = 0$ and got $x = 28$. That is where the line would cross the x-axis, which is the x-intercept, not the y-intercept.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist uses the equation $y = \frac{3}{4}x - 6$ as a linear calibration line when dating fossil pollen layers.
items.stem: What is the $x$-intercept of the graph of $y = \frac{3}{4}x - 6$ in the $xy$-plane?
items.explanation: The x-intercept is where the line crosses the x-axis, so $y = 0$ there. Setting $0 = \tfrac{3}{4}x - 6$ gives $\tfrac{3}{4}x = 6$, so $x = 8$. The point is $(8, 0)$.

A.why: You read the constant $-6$ off the equation. That gives the y-intercept, but the question asked for the x-intercept.

B.why: When you moved the $-6$ across the equals sign, you didn't change its sign. That gave $\tfrac{3}{4}x = -6$, but it should be $\tfrac{3}{4}x = 6$.

D.why: You found $x = 8$ correctly but put it in the wrong position. A point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0, so it is $(8, 0)$, not $(0, 8)$.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: A meteorologist plots a linear model on a coordinate grid as part of a forecasting exercise. The graph of the model is shown.
items.stem: Which equation defines the line shown?
items.explanation: The line crosses the y-axis at $(0, 6)$, so $b = 6$. Going from $(0, 6)$ to $(3, 4)$, $y$ falls 2 while $x$ rises 3, so the slope is $-\tfrac{2}{3}$. The equation is $y = -\tfrac{2}{3}x + 6$.

A.why: The y-intercept is right, but the slope has the wrong sign. The line goes down from left to right, so its slope must be negative.

B.why: You divided the run by the rise, $3 \div 2$, instead of the rise by the run. Slope is the change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$, which is $-\tfrac{2}{3}$.

D.why: You used 9 as $b$, but 9 is where the line crosses the x-axis. In $y = mx + b$, $b$ is the y-intercept, which is 6.

items.subtype_name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
items.stimulus: In a nutrition science course, students graph the linear function $f$, defined by $f(x) = 4(x - 3) + 5$.
items.stem: What is the $y$-intercept of the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the $xy$-plane?
items.explanation: The y-intercept is where $x = 0$, so evaluate $f(0) = 4(0 - 3) + 5 = -12 + 5 = -7$. The y-intercept is $(0, -7)$.

A.why: You took the 5 at the end as $b$. The function isn't in $y = mx + b$ form yet. Once you distribute the 4, the constant is $-12 + 5 = -7$.

B.why: You lost the negative sign when you distributed. $4(0 - 3)$ is $-12$, not $12$, so $f(0) = -7$, not 17.

C.why: You solved $4x - 7 = 0$ and got $x = \tfrac{7}{4}$. That is the x-intercept. The question asked where the graph crosses the y-axis.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: Marine biologists surveying a coral reef found that the number of parrotfish on the reef increased by $30\%$ from 2020 to 2024. In 2020, the biologists counted $p$ parrotfish on the reef.
items.stem: Which expression represents the number of parrotfish counted on the reef in 2024?
items.explanation: An increase of $30\%$ means you keep all of the original amount, $1p$, and add $30\%$ of it, $0.30p$. So the 2024 count is $p + 0.30p = 1.30p$. The multiplier for a $30\%$ increase is $1 + \frac{30}{100} = 1.30$.

A.why: $0.30p$ is only the number of parrotfish added to the population. You wrote the rate as the multiplier and forgot to add the increase to the original $p$ fish.

B.why: $0.70p$ is what you get after a $30\%$ decrease. The population went up, so you need $1 + 0.30$, not $1 - 0.30$.

D.why: You used the percent as a whole number. $30\%$ is $\frac{30}{100} = 0.30$, not $30$. Multiplying by $30$ would make the population 30 times as large.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: After a 12-week endurance training program, a cyclist's resting heart rate was $15\%$ lower than it was before the program. The cyclist's resting heart rate after the program was $k$ times the resting heart rate before the program.
items.stem: What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: A decrease of $15\%$ leaves $100\% - 15\% = 85\%$ of the original rate. As a multiplier, that is $1 - \frac{15}{100} = 0.85$, so $k = 0.85$.

A.why: $0.15$ is how much the heart rate dropped, written as a decimal. It is not what is left. You needed to subtract it from 1.

C.why: $1.15$ is the multiplier for a $15\%$ increase. The heart rate went down, so you subtract the rate from 1 instead of adding it.

D.why: You wrote the percent as a whole number. $15\%$ is $0.15$, and even then you would still need to subtract it from 1 to get a multiplier for a decrease.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A food company changed the recipe for one of its breakfast cereals. Nutrition scientists found that one serving of the new cereal contains $50\%$ more dietary fiber than one serving of the original cereal. One serving of the original cereal contains $f$ grams of dietary fiber.
items.stem: Which expression represents the number of grams of dietary fiber in one serving of the new cereal?
items.explanation: Fifty percent more means the original amount plus half of it: $f + 0.5f = 1.5f$. The multiplier for a $50\%$ increase is $1 + \frac{50}{100} = 1.5$.

A.why: You converted $50\%$ to $0.05$ instead of $0.5$. You also left out the original $f$ grams. $0.05f$ would be only a small part of the fiber that was added.

B.why: $0.5f$ is only the extra fiber the new recipe adds. You used the rate as the multiplier and did not add it to the original $f$ grams.

C.why: You added 1 correctly but converted $50\%$ to $0.05$ instead of $0.5$. $1.05f$ is a $5\%$ increase, not a $50\%$ increase.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: Seismologists tested a model building on a shake table. When the model was fitted with base isolators, its peak floor acceleration was $60\%$ less than the peak floor acceleration of the same model without isolators. The peak floor acceleration without isolators was $a$ meters per second squared.
items.stem: Which expression represents the peak floor acceleration, in meters per second squared, of the model building with base isolators?
items.explanation: Sixty percent less means $60\%$ of the acceleration is removed and $100\% - 60\% = 40\%$ remains. The multiplier is $1 - \frac{60}{100} = 0.40$, so the acceleration with isolators is $0.40a$.

B.why: $0.60a$ is how much the acceleration went down, not what is left. You needed to subtract the rate from 1.

C.why: $1.60a$ is what you get after a $60\%$ increase. The isolators reduced the acceleration, so the multiplier is $1 - 0.60$, not $1 + 0.60$.

D.why: You used the percent as a whole number. $60\%$ is $0.60$, and you would still need to subtract it from 1. Multiplying by $60$ makes the acceleration much larger.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A county health department reported that the number of residents who got a seasonal flu vaccine increased by $8\%$ from one year to the next. The number of residents vaccinated in the second year is equal to the product of $n$ and $r$, where $n$ is the number of residents vaccinated in the first year and $r$ is a constant.
items.stem: What is the value of $r$?
items.explanation: An $8\%$ increase means the second-year count is the first-year count plus $8\%$ of it: $n + 0.08n = 1.08n$. Since this equals $nr$, $r = 1 + \frac{8}{100} = 1.08$.

A.why: $0.08$ is only the rate of increase. $0.08n$ is the number of new vaccinated residents, not the total for the second year. You needed to add 1.

B.why: $0.92$ is the multiplier for an $8\%$ decrease. Vaccinations went up, so you add $0.08$ to 1 instead of subtracting it.

D.why: You converted $8\%$ to $0.8$ instead of $0.08$. $1.8$ is the multiplier for an $80\%$ increase.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stem: The tempo of a piece of music is $t$ beats per minute. The tempo is increased by $25\%$. Which expression gives the new tempo, in beats per minute?
items.explanation: An increase of $25\%$ means you keep all of the original tempo, $1t$, and add $25\%$ of it, $0.25t$. Together that is $(1 + 0.25)t = 1.25t$. You will use this step in every SAT question that asks which expression shows a quantity after a percent increase: write $1 + \frac{p}{100}$ and look for that number in the choices.

A.why: $0.25t$ is only the amount the tempo goes up by. You found the increase but did not add it back to the original $t$. The new tempo is $t + 0.25t$.

B.why: You multiplied by $25$, using the percent as a whole number. $25\%$ means $\frac{25}{100} = 0.25$, so $25t$ would make the tempo twenty-five times faster.

D.why: $0.75t$ is what you get from a $25\%$ decrease, $(1 - 0.25)t$. The question says the tempo is increased, so you add the rate to 1 instead of subtracting it.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stem: The water level in a reservoir is $h$ meters. The level decreases by $40\%$, so the new level is $kh$ meters. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: A decrease of $40\%$ leaves $100\% - 40\% = 60\%$ of the original level. As a decimal, $60\%$ is $0.6$, so the new level is $0.6h$ and $k = 0.6$. This is the step behind SAT questions that say 'the new value is $k$ times the old value' after a percent decrease: the multiplier is $1 - \frac{p}{100}$.

A.why: $0.4$ is the fraction of the water level that was lost, not the fraction that is left. After losing $40\%$, the reservoir still has $60\%$ of its level.

C.why: $1.4$ is the multiplier for a $40\%$ increase. The level went down, so you subtract $0.4$ from 1 rather than adding it.

D.why: You used the percent as a whole number. Multiplying by $40$ would make the level forty times higher. A percent has to be divided by $100$ before you can use it as a multiplier.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stem: A serving of a food contains $p$ grams of protein. A new recipe increases the protein in a serving by $8\%$. The new amount is $p$ multiplied by what number?
items.explanation: $8\%$ as a decimal is $\frac{8}{100} = 0.08$. An increase keeps the original amount and adds the rate on top, so the multiplier is $1 + 0.08 = 1.08$. You will use this whenever an SAT question says a value 'is the product of the original and $r$' after a percent increase. Be careful with single-digit percents: $8\%$ is $0.08$, not $0.8$.

B.why: You wrote $8\%$ as $0.8$ instead of $0.08$. $0.8$ is $80\%$, so $1.8$ would be an $80\%$ increase. Divide by $100$ to get $0.08$.

C.why: $0.08$ is the bare rate. Multiplying by it gives only the extra protein, not the new total. Add it to 1 so the original amount is kept.

D.why: $0.92$ is $1 - 0.08$, which is the multiplier for an $8\%$ decrease. The protein went up, so the multiplier has to be greater than 1.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stem: A field produces $y$ bushels of wheat. Next season the yield decreases by $15\%$. Which expression gives the new yield, in bushels?
items.explanation: A $15\%$ decrease leaves $100\% - 15\% = 85\%$ of the yield. So the new yield is $(1 - 0.15)y = 0.85y$. This is the step behind SAT questions that ask which expression shows a quantity after a percent decrease: the answer is always $1 - \frac{p}{100}$ times the quantity.

A.why: $0.15y$ is the number of bushels lost, not the number left. The yield that remains is $y - 0.15y$, which is $0.85y$.

B.why: $1.15y$ is the yield after a $15\%$ increase. The question says the yield decreases, so subtract the rate from 1 instead of adding it.

C.why: You subtracted $0.15$ from $y$, which takes away $0.15$ of a bushel instead of $15\%$ of the yield. The amount taken away depends on $y$: it is $0.15y$, not $0.15$.

items.subtype_name: Turn a percent change into a multiplier
items.stimulus: A linguist tracking a regional dialect found that its number of fluent speakers fell by 15% from 2000 to 2010. From 2010 to 2020, the number of fluent speakers rose by 20%.
items.stem: The number of speakers in 2020 was $k$ times the number of speakers in 2000. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Turn each percent change into a multiplier. A 15% decrease means multiplying by $1 - 0.15 = 0.85$. A 20% increase means multiplying by $1 + 0.20 = 1.2$. When changes happen one after another, you multiply them: $k = (0.85)(1.2) = 1.02$. Don't add the percents. The 20% increase is taken of the smaller 2010 count, not the 2000 count, so the net change is +2%, not +5%.

common_errors.why: Added the percents (−15% + 20% = +5%) instead of multiplying the multipliers.
Found the net change as a bare rate (2%) and entered 0.02 instead of the multiplier 1 + 0.02.
Used 0.8 for the 20% increase, as if it were a decrease: (0.85)(0.8) = 0.68.
Used 1.15 for the 15% decrease, as if it were an increase: (1.15)(1.2) = 1.38.
Used only the 2010–2020 change and ignored the first decade.

items.subtype_name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
items.stimulus: In eighteenth-century Kashmir, a single luxury shawl could pass through the hands of two weavers for more than a year. Working from a coded pattern, they interlocked hundreds of small bobbins of dyed wool one thread at a time, joining each patch of color to the next so that no seam was visible on either face of the cloth. This ______ technique left no room for error, since a single misplaced thread would show in the finished design.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The passage describes slow, thread-by-thread work in which one misplaced thread would ruin the design. "This ______ technique" refers back to that description, so the blank has to mean demanding great precision and care. "Exacting" means exactly that.

A.why: "Perfunctory" means done quickly and with little care. That is the opposite of a technique that takes more than a year and allows no errors.

C.why: You matched the topic (luxury shawls) instead of what the blank has to do. "Ostentatious" means showy, and it would describe how the finished shawl looks. The blank describes how hard the technique is to carry out.

every bird species in the city has raised the pitch of its song.
city birds sing more at night, when the traffic is quietest.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: At most Bronze Age settlements in the Harrow Basin, the proportion of sheep bones to cattle bones rises during droughts, since sheep need far less water and forage than cattle do. At the settlement of Tell Omran, however, pollen records show a severe drought around 1900 BCE, yet cattle bones from that period outnumber those from wetter centuries. Sediment cores reveal that a spring-fed marsh beside Tell Omran stayed wet throughout the drought. The researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the marsh let Tell Omran keep cattle at a time when drought made them hard to keep elsewhere.
the drought around 1900 BCE was far less severe in the basin than the pollen records indicate.
sheep in the Harrow Basin needed more water and forage than researchers have usually assumed.
Tell Omran's residents hunted wild cattle more often than residents of other settlements did.
items.explanation: Normally drought shifts herds toward sheep, because cattle need more water and forage. Tell Omran went the other way. The one thing that sets it apart is a marsh that stayed wet through the drought. A reliable source of water and grazing explains why cattle could still be kept there, and even thrive, while the rest of the basin lost them.

B.why: The passage states that the pollen records show a severe drought. Doubting that evidence ignores the detail that makes Tell Omran unusual, the marsh that stayed wet. This is the trap of an explanation that sounds scientific but skips the setting.

C.why: The passage states that sheep need far less water and forage than cattle, and that the sheep-heavy pattern holds at most sites. This choice goes against that premise and still doesn't explain why Tell Omran differs.

D.why: Nothing in the passage mentions hunting or wild animals. You invented a new factor and ignored the marsh, which is the one local difference the passage points out.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In most corn-growing regions, planting a winter rye cover crop raises the yield of the corn that follows, largely because rye residue holds moisture in the soil through early summer. Agronomists studying the Lowmoor district, where spring rains are unusually heavy, expected this benefit to reverse there: the extra moisture held by rye residue, they reasoned, would keep already saturated fields waterlogged and force farmers to delay planting. They therefore anticipated that in Lowmoor, corn planted after rye would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: yield more than corn planted in Lowmoor fields where no rye cover crop had been grown.
grow in soil that dried out faster than the soil of Lowmoor fields left bare over winter.
yield less than corn planted in Lowmoor fields where no rye cover crop had been grown.
yield less than corn planted without rye in every region, regardless of spring rainfall.
items.explanation: The passage tells you the usual benefit will reverse in Lowmoor. Usually, corn after rye yields more than corn without rye. Flipped, corn after rye in Lowmoor yields less than corn without rye in Lowmoor. The reasoning given (waterlogged fields and delayed planting) supports a lower yield, and the comparison stays within Lowmoor.

A.why: This is the usual effect, not the reversed one. The agronomists expected the benefit to reverse in Lowmoor, and you kept the original direction.

B.why: The agronomists' reasoning is that rye residue holds extra moisture, so soil after rye should stay wetter, not dry out faster. This choice reverses the mechanism the passage relies on.

D.why: The reversal is predicted only for Lowmoor, because of its heavy spring rains. The passage says rye raises yields in most regions, so 'every region, regardless of spring rainfall' goes far beyond what was expected. Watch for words like 'every' and 'regardless.'

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Inspectors of the Carrow Viaduct found that the steel expansion joints at its north end had rusted through in half the time expected, while identical joints at the south end, installed the same year and carrying the same traffic, showed little rust. The viaduct's north end sits in the shadow of a cliff for most of the day, so snow and slush treated with deicing salt linger there for days after storms, whereas the sunlit south end clears within hours. The inspectors hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the cold at the shaded north end made its steel joints brittle and prone to cracking.
prolonged contact with salty meltwater caused the north joints to corrode more quickly.
the north joints were made from a lower grade of steel than the joints at the south end.
direct sunlight at the south end slowly damaged its joints as well, though less visibly.
items.explanation: The joints are identical, were installed the same year and carry the same traffic, so none of those explains the difference. What differs is how long salty slush sits on each end: days on the north, hours on the south. The damage is rust, and longer contact with salt water is a direct cause of rust. This explanation fits both the setting and the kind of damage.

A.why: This fixes on the shade and the cold but misses what the shade does in the passage, which is keep salty slush in place. It also describes brittleness and cracking, while the damage the inspectors found was rust. The explanation sounds scientific but doesn't match the damage.

C.why: The passage calls the joints identical. You explained the difference with a variable the passage has already ruled out.

D.why: The passage gives no sign that sunlight harms steel, and the south joints are described as showing little rust. This choice invents hidden damage instead of explaining why the north end rusted.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: A team testing a new self-healing polymer found that cracks near the surface of a sample sealed within a day, while cracks deep inside the same sample were still open a week later. The healing agent had been distributed evenly throughout the polymer, and all samples were kept at a constant temperature. Because the agent is known to react with water, and the surface is the only part of the material in contact with humid air, the team hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the interior cracks were larger than the surface cracks and so required more healing agent.
the healing agent had settled toward the surface of the sample before the polymer hardened.
water vapor in the air slows the healing reaction, so cracks near the surface should close last.
moisture from the surrounding air drives the healing reaction that seals the surface cracks.
items.explanation: Two possible causes are ruled out: the agent was spread evenly, and the temperature was held constant. The one remaining difference between surface and interior is contact with humid air, and the agent is known to react with water. If moisture from the air drives the reaction, surface cracks should heal quickly and deep cracks slowly, which is what the team saw.

A.why: The passage gives no information about crack size. You made up a difference and skipped the one the passage points to: water and humid air.

B.why: The passage says the healing agent was distributed evenly throughout the polymer. This choice depends on the agent being concentrated at the surface, which the setup rules out.

C.why: This gets the effect backward. The surface cracks, the only ones exposed to humid air, sealed fastest. A hypothesis that has them closing last contradicts the result it's supposed to explain.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Thick leaf cuticles, waxy coatings that limit water loss, are usually read as a sign that a plant grew in a dry climate. Fossils of the extinct shrub Salicornites, however, have unusually thick cuticles yet were found rooted in growth position in coastal swamp deposits. Other plants preserved in the same deposits, which grew farther from the shoreline, have thin cuticles, and chemical analysis shows that the water around Salicornites was highly salty. Plant roots struggle to draw water from salty soil. Paleobotanists therefore hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the regional climate was dry when Salicornites lived, even though the shrub grew in a swamp.
Salicornites leaves were carried into the swamp from drier upland areas after they had fallen.
thick cuticles helped Salicornites hold on to water that its roots could take up only poorly.
all plants that grew in salty coastal swamps developed thick cuticles like those of Salicornites.
items.explanation: The key detail is the comparison group. Plants in the same deposits have thin cuticles, so the climate as a whole wasn't dry. What set Salicornites apart was salty water, and the passage says roots struggle to draw water from salty soil. A plant that can't take up water easily would benefit from losing less of it, which explains the thick cuticles without needing a dry climate.

A.why: This is the usual reading that the passage undercuts. Plants in the same deposits have thin cuticles, which wouldn't fit a dry regional climate. You applied the rule of thumb and ignored the comparison group.

B.why: The fossils were found rooted in growth position, so Salicornites grew where it was preserved. It wasn't washed in from somewhere else.

D.why: The passage describes one shrub in one swamp. Stretching that to 'all plants' in every salty swamp is strength creep that the evidence can't support.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Roads usually lower the nesting success of forest songbirds, because the open edges they create draw nest predators such as crows. In the Elden Forest, however, wood thrush nests within 100 meters of a road fledge young more often than nests deeper in the forest. The forest's chief nest predator is not a crow but the eastern ratsnake, which basks on warm pavement and is frequently killed by vehicles. The researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: traffic keeps ratsnake numbers low near roads, leaving thrush nests there less exposed.
road edges in the Elden Forest draw ratsnakes, which then raid the thrush nests nearby.
thrushes nesting near roads find more insects for their young than thrushes elsewhere do.
roads raise the nesting success of every songbird species that breeds in the Elden Forest.
items.explanation: The surprise is that nests near roads do better, which is the opposite of the usual pattern. The passage explains why: the main predator here is a snake that basks on pavement and is often killed by cars. If traffic thins out the snakes near roads, fewer predators reach the nearby nests, and those nests fledge more young.

B.why: This is the usual pattern, roads drawing predators to nests, applied where the passage says it reverses. If roads drew raiding snakes, nests near roads would do worse, but they do better. You also skipped the detail that the snakes are frequently killed by vehicles.

C.why: The passage never mentions food. It builds its explanation around the predator. A made-up factor that ignores the ratsnake doesn't use the details you were given.

D.why: The finding is about wood thrush nests only. 'Every songbird species' stretches one species' result to a whole community, which is strength creep the passage can't support.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: For decades, historians blamed the errors in a 1740s chart of the Breton coast on careless copying from older charts. Copying mistakes, however, tend to fall at random. When cartographer Inès Morvan compared the chart with satellite imagery, she found that nearly every misplaced headland was shifted eastward. The size of the shift also grew steadily with the headland's distance from Brest, the port where the chart's maker was based. Morvan therefore hypothesizes that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the chart's maker worked from older charts that were themselves full of careless errors.
the headlands farthest from Brest have eroded eastward in the centuries since the chart was drawn.
a small, consistent error in the maker's measurements built up as positions were plotted outward from Brest.
the chart's maker deliberately misplaced the distant headlands in order to mislead rival navigators.
items.explanation: The surprise is that the errors are not random. They all point the same way (east), and they get bigger the farther a headland is from Brest. A small error that repeats in the same direction and adds up with each step away from the starting port accounts for both details. It also explains why Morvan rejects the copying explanation, since copying would scatter errors at random.

A.why: You picked the popular view the passage sets up only to knock down. Careless errors, whether the maker made them or copied them, would fall at random. Morvan found errors that all run east and grow with distance from Brest.

B.why: Erosion sounds scientific, but the passage never mentions it. It also can't explain the key detail: there is no reason erosion would increase with distance from the port where the chart's maker happened to work.

D.why: Nothing in the passage mentions rivals or any intent to deceive. You added a motive the text doesn't support. An error that grows smoothly with distance from the home port also points to how the maker measured, not to deliberate tampering.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In warm regions, street trees are known to extend the life of asphalt by keeping it cool enough to resist rutting. Engineers in a northern city were therefore surprised to find that heavily shaded streets there developed about 40 percent more potholes than sunny ones. Potholes in the city form mainly when water seeps into small cracks, freezes, and expands. Temperature sensors showed that on winter days, sunlit pavement usually stayed above freezing until dusk, whereas shaded pavement hovered near 0°C, crossing the freezing point several times. The engineers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: roots of the shading trees, rather than any temperature effect, are cracking the pavement from below.
water in shaded pavement freezes and thaws repeatedly, producing the additional potholes on those streets.
shade protects pavement against potholes in cold regions much as it protects against rutting in warm ones.
shaded streets in any climate will develop more potholes than comparable streets left in full sun.
items.explanation: The puzzle is that shade, which helps pavement in warm places, goes along with more damage here. The passage gives you everything you need to explain it. Potholes form when water in cracks freezes, and shaded pavement crosses the freezing point several times a day, while sunlit pavement stays above freezing until dusk. Repeated freezing and thawing in the shade explains the extra potholes using only those details.

A.why: Root damage sounds plausible, but the passage says nothing about roots. It also ignores the temperature data the engineers collected. You chose an explanation that leaves out the key detail the passage gives you.

C.why: This is the flipped-effect trap. In this city, shade goes along with more potholes, not fewer, so the warm-climate benefit has reversed. You carried over the original effect instead of flipping it.

D.why: Watch for strength creep: 'in any climate' claims far more than the passage supports. The passage itself says shade helps pavement in warm regions, and the extra potholes depend on freezing conditions that only some climates have.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: Agronomists often credit legume cover crops such as hairy vetch with improving soil structure, a benefit that should help any crop planted afterward. vetch benefited corn mainly by supplying nitrogen, which soybeans largely obtain on their own.
soybeans gain more than corn does from the improvements to soil structure that vetch provides.
corn yields after vetch would continue to rise if the trial were extended for several more years.

The passage gives you the detail that explains the split: vetch adds nitrogen, and soybeans already make much of their own. A hypothesis that vetch's benefit came mainly through nitrogen accounts for both the corn gain and the missing soybean gain, and it uses only facts the passage provides.

items.stimulus: In lowland populations of a certain meadow wildflower, plants secrete most of their nectar between late morning and midafternoon, when the bees that pollinate them forage most actively. Because producing nectar draws heavily on a plant's limited energy, ecologists anticipated that, compared with lowland plants, high-elevation plants would ______

secrete a greater total volume of nectar over a full day and night.
receive a larger share of their visits from daytime-foraging bees.
release most of their nectar during the hours after dark.

The plants should save their nectar for the hours when their actual pollinators are feeding, which means after dark.

items.subtype_name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
items.stimulus: In a survey of twelve villages in a rural district, childhood asthma rates generally rose with proximity to the district's only highway. The excess was concentrated among children under five, who spend most of the day at home, where, because the village has no gas supply, meals are cooked over indoor wood fires. Older children, who attend school in a neighboring town, had rates typical of remote villages. The researchers hypothesize that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: smoke from household cooking fires is responsible for much of the excess among young children.
exhaust from the highway reaches the village in concentrations high enough to harm young children.
the school in the neighboring town has features that protect older children from asthma.
distance from the highway has little relationship to childhood asthma rates in the district.
items.explanation: The surprise is a very high asthma rate in a village far from the highway. The excess shows up only in young children, who spend their days at home where meals are cooked over indoor wood fires, while older children who spend their days elsewhere have normal rates. Indoor smoke is the one explanation that fits the location, the age split, and the village's unusual cooking arrangement.

B.why: This sounds scientific but ignores the setting. The village is nearly 40 kilometers from the highway, and older children there have typical rates, which highway exhaust would not explain. You picked the usual cause and overlooked the detail that makes this village an exception.

C.why: This adds a step the passage never supports. Nothing is said about the school's features. Even if it protected older children, that would not explain why young children in this village have higher rates than young children in other villages.

most of the parish's traditional tales originated in the coastal villages its settlers left.
items.explanation: The puzzle is a coastal tale turning up far inland. Two details settle it. Lots of dark permeable asphalt formed less surface ice than lots of conventional asphalt of the same dark color during the same winters.

The impressions share identical outlines and details, showing that they were all printed from one block.
The woodcut's harbor scene closely resembles harbor scenes painted by artists working in the same city.
Records from the workshop show that it held a single large printing session for the woodcut in 1652.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: During the 1700s, weavers in one district of northern England largely abandoned wool in favor of linen. Linen required different spinning skills, but it could be woven on the same looms. choices: Weavers in the district were able to weave linen on the same looms they had previously used for wool.
Buyers throughout England increasingly preferred linen garments to woolen ones during the 1700s.
The district's sheep numbers fell by half just before the change, while local demand for wool held steady.
Disease reduced sheep populations in many parts of Europe during the century before the change.
items.explanation: Ashdown's claim has two parts: a local wool shortage caused the switch, and buyer demand did not. Choice C supports both. The district's flocks shrank right before the change, and demand for wool stayed the same, which rules out a shift in taste.

B.why: You supported the rival explanation. A change in buyer preference is exactly what Ashdown says was not the cause.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Astronomers have recorded repeated episodes in which a distant star dims for several weeks. Dust lying between a star and observers blocks blue light more strongly than infrared light, whereas a drop in a star's own energy output dims all wavelengths by roughly the same amount. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
choices: During the most recent episode, the star's total brightness dropped by roughly 20 percent.
During each episode, the star dimmed about three times as much in blue light as in infrared.
During each episode, the star dimmed by about the same amount in blue light as in infrared.
Several other stars in the same region of the sky have also been observed dimming for weeks.
items.explanation: The passage tells you how to test the claim: dust dims blue light more than infrared, and changes in the star itself dim both equally. Uneven dimming, stronger in blue, points to dust, so Choice B supports the team's conclusion.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Curb extensions widen the sidewalk at a street corner, shortening the distance pedestrians must walk to cross. After a city added curb extensions at forty intersections, its planners reviewed five years of injury reports. The planners claim that curb extensions reduce pedestrian injuries at intersections with heavy traffic, even if they do little at quiet intersections.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the planners' claim?
choices: At high-traffic intersections, injuries fell 40 percent after extensions were added but held steady at similar ones without them.
Across all of the city's intersections, pedestrian injuries fell by about 8 percent during the five years reviewed.
At quiet intersections, pedestrian injury counts were about the same before and after curb extensions were added.
At high-traffic intersections, injuries fell by similar amounts whether or not curb extensions had been added.
items.explanation: The scope words are 'at intersections with heavy traffic.' To support the claim, a finding has to show a drop at busy intersections that can be credited to the extensions. Choice A shows a large drop where extensions were added and none at comparable intersections without them.

C.why: You supported only the 'even if' concession. Showing that extensions did little at quiet corners doesn't show that they helped at busy ones, which is the actual claim.

D.why: You overlooked the comparison. If injuries fell just as much without extensions, something other than the extensions caused the drop, which undercuts the claim.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Younger speakers of a language spoken on several islands in the western Pacific have largely stopped using a set of honorific verb forms that their grandparents use routinely. The honorific verb forms are used mainly when a speaker is addressing a chief or an elder.
The young speakers who use English most at school are the least likely to use the honorific forms.
Where gatherings are still held often, young people use the forms as much as elders, despite equal English use.

items.subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
items.stimulus: Song sparrows living in cities tend to sing at higher pitches than rural song sparrows do, but cities differ from the countryside in many ways besides noise. The researchers hypothesize that low-frequency traffic noise itself causes young sparrows to develop higher-pitched songs.

choices: Song sparrows in large cities sing at higher pitches than song sparrows in nearby rural areas.
Birds raised in the two aviaries began producing recognizable songs at about the same age.
As adults, birds from the noisy aviary sang with noticeably higher pitches than birds from the quiet one.
As adults, birds from the two aviaries sang at nearly identical pitches regardless of the noise.
items.explanation: The aviaries differ in only one way: traffic noise. If the hypothesis is right, the birds from the noisy aviary should sing higher. Decide that direction first, and Choice C is the finding that matches it.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: For decades, relief printmakers have cleaned ink from their carved blocks with mineral spirits, a solvent that removes oil-based ink quickly. Printmaker Ana Ruiz, however, now tells students in her workshops to use vegetable oil followed by soap and water. She notes that fumes from mineral spirits can linger for hours in small studios with little ventilation. Ruiz's recommendation suggests that, in her view, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: vegetable oil leaves behind stronger and longer-lasting fumes than mineral spirits do.
mineral spirits have a drawback in some studios that the oil-and-soap method avoids.
mineral spirits should be banned from every printmaking studio regardless of its size.
students should give up relief printing in favor of techniques that use no ink at all.
items.explanation: Ruiz recommends a new cleaning method and gives one reason: mineral spirit fumes linger in small, poorly ventilated studios. To recommend the switch for that reason, she has to believe that mineral spirits have this drawback in some settings and that the oil-and-soap method avoids it. That is the smallest belief her advice depends on.

D.why: Ruiz's advice is about how to clean blocks, not whether to keep printing. Nothing in the text suggests she wants students to stop using ink.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Vaccination rates in Corley County have long been lowest in rural townships, many of which are more than an hour's drive from the nearest clinic. Last spring, the county health department began sending mobile vaccination vans to those townships on a weekly schedule rather than adding staff to its existing clinics. The department's decision suggests that it believed ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: residents near the clinics needed the vans more urgently than rural residents did.
the existing clinics should be closed and replaced entirely by mobile vans.
distance from clinics was keeping some rural residents from getting vaccinated.
vaccines given inside a vehicle work better than vaccines given in a clinic.
items.explanation: The department sent vans to the far-off townships with low vaccination rates instead of adding staff to the clinics. That only makes sense if it believed the distance to a clinic was part of the problem, and that bringing vaccines closer would reach people the clinics were missing.

B.why: Adding vans for distant areas doesn't mean the department thinks the clinics are useless. Nothing suggests it plans to close them, so this belief goes beyond anything the action requires.

D.why: The vans solve a problem of access, not effectiveness. The department's action doesn't depend on any belief about where vaccines work best.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?

formal interviews produce no data of any value to researchers studying dialects.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: For decades, a regional weather office has launched weather balloons twice a day to measure temperature and moisture high in the atmosphere. This year, its lead forecaster asked for four launches a day during storm season, when thunderstorms can build within a few hours. The request suggests that, in the forecaster's view, ______
items.stem: Which choice states the belief that the forecaster's request depends on?

four launches a day would be no more useful than two in storm season.
weather balloons are of no use at all for forecasting thunderstorms.
thunderstorms form far more often now than they did decades ago.
items.explanation: Ask why anyone would make this request. You only ask for more launches if you think the current two leave gaps, and the passage points to the gap: storms can build within a few hours, so they can form between launches. Choice A states that belief and nothing more. B.why: You reversed the comparison. The forecaster asked for more launches, which only makes sense if four would do better than two. This choice says the opposite of what the request depends on.

C.why: You pushed 'limited' all the way to 'useless.' The forecaster wants more balloon launches, so the forecaster clearly thinks balloons are useful. The belief is only that two a day is not enough.

D.why: You gave the forecaster a belief the request never needed. The passage says storms build quickly, not that they have become more common. The request makes sense even if storm frequency has not changed at all.

items.subtype_name: What must this person believe?
items.stimulus: Most orchestras perform Anna Lindqvist's Second Symphony from its printed first edition. When musicologist Pieter Haas prepared a new score, however, he checked every page of that edition against Lindqvist's handwritten draft, noting that music engravers of the period often quietly altered notes they judged to be mistakes. This approach suggests Haas thought that ______
items.stem: Which choice states the belief that the musicologist's approach depends on?
choices: the handwritten draft had itself been copied out from the printed edition.
the symphony is the most important work Lindqvist ever composed.
the printed edition might not match exactly what Lindqvist had written.
every note in the printed edition had been changed by its engravers.
items.explanation: Why check a printed score against the composer's own handwriting? Because you suspect the printed version may differ from it, and the passage gives the reason: engravers sometimes altered notes. unattended cameras tend to record fewer groupers on a reef than diver transects do.
damselfish populations have been overestimated in most past censuses of reef fish.
diver transects likely record fewer wary fish than are actually present on a reef.

items.stimulus: Manufacturers usually rate a new polymer adhesive by its strength immediately after curing. strength right after curing is an unreliable guide to how an adhesive will perform when damp.
humidity weakens every polymer adhesive by roughly half within the first six months of use.

bridges over rivers develop fatigue cracks faster than bridges built over dry land.

translations of prepared sentences always misrepresent the grammar of the variety being documented.
unscripted conversation is less likely than translation to reflect how speakers ordinarily talk.
speakers of the variety are generally unwilling to translate sentences prepared by outside researchers.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A musicologist compares two tuning schemes for a set of bell chimes. In the system below, $x$ is the number of chimes tuned by the first scheme and $y$ is the number tuned by the second.

$3x + 2y = 10$
$6x + 4y = k$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. If the system has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, the second equation must be a constant multiple of the first. The $x$-coefficient goes from $3$ to $6$ and the $y$-coefficient goes from $2$ to $4$, so every term is multiplied by $2$. The constant has to double as well: $k = 2(10) = 20$. That makes both equations describe the same line.

A.why: You saw that the factor is $2$ but divided $10$ by $2$ instead of multiplying. With $k = 5$ the lines are parallel, not the same line.

B.why: You matched the slopes and left the constant at $10$. The constant has to scale by $2$ too. With $k = 10$, the system $6x + 4y = 10$ is parallel to the first line, so it has no solution.

C.why: You added $3$ to the constant because $6 - 3 = 3$. Equivalent equations come from multiplying every term by the same number, not adding to it.

items.stimulus:
An urban planner models the projected length of a new bike lane network, $y$ kilometers, after $x$ years of construction with the equation below.

$y = 2x + 5$
items.stem: One of the two equations in a linear system is given. The system has infinitely many solutions. Which of the following could be the second equation in this system?
items.explanation: The second equation has to be the same line, so solve each choice for $y$. In $4x - 2y = -10$, subtract $4x$ from both sides to get $-2y = -4x - 10$, then divide by $-2$ to get $y = 2x + 5$. The slope and the intercept both match, so the two equations describe one line.

D.why: This choice rearranges to $y = -2x + 5$. The sign of the slope is wrong, so the lines cross at just one point.

items.stem: Which system of equations has infinitely many solutions?
items.explanation: In $2x + 4y = 8$, each term is twice the matching term in $x + 2y = 4$: $2 = 2 \times 1$, $4 = 2 \times 2$, $8 = 2 \times 4$. Both equations describe the same line, so every point on it is a solution. Checking whether all three ratios agree is the step that opens up SAT questions about infinitely many solutions.

D.why: The $x$-coefficient was multiplied by 4 and the $y$-coefficient by 1, so the terms got mixed up. The ratios don't agree, so these lines cross once.

C.why: You assumed the second equation must have the same constant as the first. The constants only need to be in the same ratio as the coefficients, so $r = 4t$ for any nonzero $t$, not necessarily $4$.

D.why: You treated infinitely many solutions as two lines crossing, so you expected different slopes and rejected I. Identical lines must have the same slope, which is exactly what statement I says.

items.stem: According to the equation, how many more acorns does one squirrel cache than one jay?

items.explanation: Move the rice term to the left side to get $9x + 3y = 216$. One serving of lentils has 9 grams of protein and one serving of rice has 3 grams. Lentils have $9 - 3 = 6$ more grams per serving.

items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of 7.9 in this context?

The equation $12b + 30f = 540$ represents this situation, where $b$ is the number of ballads and $f$ is the number of folktales in the collection.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of 30 in this context?
choices: The collection contains 30 folktales in all.
Each folktale fills 30 more pages than each ballad.
items.explanation: In $30f$, the 30 multiplies the number of folktales, so 30 is the number of pages for one folktale. The term $30f$ is the total number of pages taken up by folktales.

B.why: You treated the coefficient as the value of $f$. The 30 is pages per folktale. The number of folktales is $f$, which this equation doesn't fix.

C.why: You read a single coefficient as a difference. A folktale fills $30 - 12 = 18$ more pages than a ballad, and that number doesn't appear in the equation.

D.why: You matched 30 to the wrong variable. The 30 is attached to $f$ (folktales). Each ballad fills 12 pages.

items.subtype_name: What does the coefficient mean
items.stimulus: A dietitian is designing a plant-based meal plan that provides exactly 1,000 milligrams of calcium from two foods: cooked kale and fortified soy milk. The equation $80k + 250m = 1{,}000$ represents this situation, where $k$ is the number of servings of kale and $m$ is the number of cups of soy milk.
items.stem: Which of the following statements is true about the calcium provided by one serving of each food?
choices: One cup of soy milk provides 170 mg more calcium than one serving of kale.
One serving of kale provides 170 mg more calcium than one cup of soy milk.
One cup of soy milk provides 330 mg more calcium than one serving of kale.
One cup of soy milk provides 750 mg more calcium than one serving of kale.
items.explanation: One serving of kale gives 80 mg of calcium and one cup of soy milk gives 250 mg. Soy milk gives more, by $250 - 80 = 170$ mg.

B.why: You got the difference right but put it in the wrong direction. Kale has the smaller coefficient (80), so it provides less calcium, not more.

C.why: You added the coefficients ($250 + 80 = 330$) instead of subtracting them. A sum is the calcium in one serving of each food together, not a comparison.

D.why: You subtracted the soy milk coefficient from the total ($1{,}000 - 250 = 750$). The 1,000 is the plan's total calcium, not the amount in one serving of kale.

items.stimulus: A regional weather office collects upper-air data using weather-balloon launches and drone flights. Every balloon launch costs the same amount, and every drone flight costs the same amount. The office's monthly budget for these launches and flights is fully spent. The equation $1.8b + 0.6d = 24$ represents this situation, where $b$ is the number of balloon launches, $d$ is the number of drone flights, and all costs are in hundreds of dollars.
items.stem: How many more dollars does one balloon launch cost than one drone flight?
items.explanation: Costs are in hundreds of dollars, so one balloon launch costs $1.8 \times 100 = \$180$ and one drone flight costs $0.6 \times 100 = \$60$. A balloon launch costs $\$180 - \$60 = \$120$ more.

A.why: $60 is the cost of one drone flight. That's the cheaper item's cost, not how much more a balloon launch costs.

C.why: $180 is the cost of one balloon launch on its own. You converted one coefficient to dollars and didn't subtract the drone flight's cost.

D.why: You added the per-unit costs ($180 + $60 = $240) instead of subtracting them. That's the cost of one launch plus one flight, not the difference.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: An astronomy student selected 60 asteroids at random from a catalog of 1,500 main-belt asteroids and looked up the diameter of each one. Based on the sample, the student estimated that the mean diameter of the asteroids in the catalog is 14 kilometers, with an associated margin of error of 3 kilometers.
items.stem: Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: It is plausible that the mean diameter of all 1,500 asteroids in the catalog is between 11 and 17 kilometers.
It is plausible that every asteroid in the catalog has a diameter between 11 and 17 kilometers.
The mean diameter of all 1,500 asteroids in the catalog is exactly 14 kilometers.
The margin of error means the mean diameter of the 60 sampled asteroids could be anywhere from 11 to 17 kilometers.
items.explanation: You compute 14 − 3 = 11 and 14 + 3 = 17. The margin of error describes where the mean of the whole catalog plausibly falls, so a mean diameter between 11 and 17 kilometers for all 1,500 asteroids is the supported conclusion.

B.why: You applied the interval to individual asteroids. The margin of error is about the mean diameter, and single asteroids can be much larger or smaller than 11 to 17 kilometers.

C.why: You treated the estimate as exact. A margin of error of 3 kilometers means the true mean is uncertain, so 'exactly 14' claims more than the sample can show.

D.why: You applied the interval to the sample. The sample's mean is known: it is 14 kilometers. The interval estimates the mean of the whole catalog.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: Ecologists chose 200 trees at random in a forest reserve and checked each one for bark beetle damage. They found damage on 35% of the sampled trees. Based on the sample, they estimated that 35% of the trees in the reserve have beetle damage, with an associated margin of error of 4%.
items.stem: Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Exactly 35% of all trees in the reserve have bark beetle damage.
About 4% of the sampled trees were classified incorrectly as damaged or undamaged.
It is plausible that between 31% and 39% of all trees in the reserve have bark beetle damage.
It is plausible that between 31% and 39% of all trees in the state's forests have bark beetle damage.
items.explanation: You compute 35% − 4% = 31% and 35% + 4% = 39%. Because the trees were sampled only from the reserve, the supported conclusion is that between 31% and 39% of the reserve's trees plausibly have damage.

A.why: You treated the estimate as exact. The 4% margin of error says the true percent is uncertain, so 'exactly 35%' claims more than the data support.

B.why: You read the margin of error as the share of trees that were misclassified. It actually measures the uncertainty from using a sample to estimate the percent for the whole reserve.

D.why: You extended the result beyond the population that was sampled. Only trees in the reserve were sampled, so the conclusion can't cover every forest in the state.

items.stimulus: A random sample of warehouse workers in one city gives an estimated mean hourly wage of $\$20$, with a margin of error of $\$2$.
items.stem: Which statement does the estimate and its margin of error support?

items.stimulus: A random sample of tomato plants on one farm gives an estimated mean yield of $6$ kilograms (kg) per plant, with a margin of error of $1$ kg.
items.stem: Which statement does the estimate and its margin of error support?
choices: Most tomato plants on the farm yield between $5$ and $7$ kg of tomatoes.
It is not possible that the farm's mean yield per plant is below $5$ kg.
The mean yield per plant for the whole farm is plausibly between $4$ and $8$ kg.
The mean yield per plant for the whole farm is plausibly between $5$ and $7$ kg.
items.explanation: Subtract and add the margin: $6 - 1 = 5$ and $6 + 1 = 7$. The mean yield per plant across the whole farm is plausibly between $5$ and $7$ kg. You'll make the same calculation, then read the wording carefully, on SAT questions asking for the 'most plausible' conclusion from an estimate.

A.why: You applied the interval to individual plants. It describes the farm's MEAN yield. It doesn't say what most single plants produce, and many plants can yield well outside $5$ to $7$ kg.

B.why: You read the interval as a guarantee. 'Plausibly' isn't 'certainly', so a mean below $5$ kg is unlikely but not impossible. 'Not possible' is a certainty word.

C.why: You used double the margin, $6 \pm 2$. The interval is estimate $\pm$ margin, which is $6 \pm 1$.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: A textile museum owns 1,200 hand-stitched quilts made between 1850 and 1900. A conservator chose 80 of these quilts at random and measured the quilting stitches on each one. The 80 quilts had a mean of 9.4 stitches per inch, with an associated margin of error of 0.6 stitches per inch.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Every quilt in the museum's collection plausibly has between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean for all quilts made in the United States from 1850 to 1900 is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean for all 1,200 quilts in the museum's collection is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
The mean for the 80 quilts the conservator measured is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0 stitches per inch.
items.explanation: The interval is $9.4 - 0.6 = 8.8$ to $9.4 + 0.6 = 10.0$ stitches per inch. A margin of error describes where the population mean plausibly lies. The population here is the one the sample came from, which is the museum's 1,200 quilts. So the mean stitch density of the whole collection is plausibly between 8.8 and 10.0.

A.why: You applied the interval to individual quilts. It is a range for the collection's mean, and individual quilts can fall well outside it.

B.why: You generalized beyond the population that was sampled. The 80 quilts came only from this museum's collection, so the result can't speak for every American quilt from the period.

D.why: You applied the interval to the sample instead of the population. The conservator measured those 80 quilts directly, so their mean is known to be exactly 9.4. The margin of error describes uncertainty about the 1,200 quilts.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: A county health department surveyed 500 adults chosen at random from the county's residents. Of those surveyed, 38% reported getting a flu vaccine during the most recent season. The associated margin of error for this estimate is 4%.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: It is plausible that between 34% and 42% of the 500 surveyed adults got a flu vaccine last season.
It is plausible that between 34% and 42% of all adults in the county got a flu vaccine last season.
It is not possible that more than 42% of all adults in the county got a flu vaccine last season.
About 4% of the surveyed adults likely gave incorrect answers about getting a flu vaccine last season.
items.explanation: The interval is $38\% - 4\% = 34\%$ to $38\% + 4\% = 42\%$. It estimates the proportion for the population that was sampled, which is all adults in the county. So it is plausible that between 34% and 42% of the county's adults were vaccinated.

A.why: You applied the interval to the sample. The department knows that exactly 38% of the 500 respondents said yes. The uncertainty is about the whole county.

C.why: You treated the interval as a hard boundary. A margin of error gives a plausible range, so values outside it are unlikely but still possible. 'Not possible' claims too much certainty.

D.why: You read the margin of error as the share of respondents who answered wrongly. It measures sampling variability: how far the estimate could plausibly be from the true county proportion.
