items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: Biologists measured 60 green sea turtles chosen at random from those nesting on Isla Corva during one season. The mean carapace length of the 60 turtles was 98 centimeters, with an associated margin of error of 3 centimeters.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Most green sea turtles nesting on Isla Corva that season plausibly had carapace lengths between 95 and 101 centimeters.
The mean carapace length of all green sea turtles worldwide is plausibly between 95 and 101 centimeters.
It is not plausible that the mean carapace length of the turtles nesting on Isla Corva that season was above 98 centimeters.
The mean carapace length of all green sea turtles nesting on Isla Corva that season is plausibly between 95 and 101 centimeters.
items.explanation: The interval is $98 - 3 = 95$ to $98 + 3 = 101$ centimeters. The turtles were sampled from those nesting on Isla Corva that season, so the conclusion covers the mean carapace length of that population and nothing larger.

A.why: You applied the interval to individual turtles. It describes the population mean and says nothing about where most individual lengths fall. Individual lengths could vary far more than 3 centimeters.

B.why: You generalized beyond the population sampled. Turtles from one beach in one season can't represent green sea turtles worldwide.

C.why: You treated the estimate of 98 as if it were exact. Any value from 98 up to 101 is inside the plausible range, so a mean above 98 is entirely plausible.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: A city planning office surveyed 400 households chosen at random in Ward 3. The mean one-way commute time for these households was 34 minutes, with an associated margin of error of 5 minutes. A transit agency report claims that the mean one-way commute time for Ward 3 households is 40 minutes.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The claim is unlikely to be accurate, because 40 minutes is outside the plausible range for the Ward 3 mean.
The claim is plausible, because 40 minutes is within the margin of error of the survey's estimate of 34 minutes.
The claim is unlikely to be accurate, because no Ward 3 household has a commute longer than 39 minutes.
The claim is unlikely to be accurate, and the mean commute for the whole city is also less than 40 minutes.
items.explanation: The plausible range for the Ward 3 mean is $34 - 5 = 29$ to $34 + 5 = 39$ minutes. The value 40 is above that range, so the agency's claim about the Ward 3 mean is unlikely. Your conclusion has to stay about the mean and about Ward 3 only.

B.why: You made an arithmetic slip. The difference is $40 - 34 = 6$ minutes, which is more than the 5-minute margin of error, so 40 is outside the interval.

C.why: You applied the interval to individual households. The 29-to-39 range is for the Ward 3 mean, and plenty of individual households could commute longer than 39 minutes.

D.why: You extended the result to a population that was never sampled. Only Ward 3 households were surveyed, so the data say nothing about the citywide mean.

items.subtype_name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
items.stimulus: A museum conservator chose 40 coverlets at random from a collection of 600 hand-woven coverlets made in the 1800s. She counted the threads per inch in each one. items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Every coverlet in the collection has between 29 and 35 threads per inch.
The mean thread count for the collection is plausibly between 29 and 35 threads per inch.
The mean thread count for the collection is plausibly between 26 and 38 threads per inch.
The mean thread count for all American coverlets is plausibly between 29 and 35 threads per inch.
items.explanation: Subtract and add the margin of error: 32 − 3 = 29 and 32 + 3 = 35. The interval is a plausible range for the MEAN thread count of the population that was sampled, which is the museum's collection of 600 coverlets. Choice B says exactly that.

C.why: You used the margin of error twice on each side and got 32 ± 6. The interval is the estimate plus or minus the margin itself: 32 ± 3.

D.why: You stretched the result to a population nobody sampled. The coverlets came from one museum's collection, so the conclusion covers that collection only.

items.stimulus: A county health department surveyed 500 adults chosen at random from the county's 80,000 adults. Of those surveyed, 62% said they had received a flu vaccine this season. The estimate has an associated margin of error of 4 percentage points.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Plausibly between 46,400 and 52,800 adults in the county received a flu vaccine this season.
Plausibly between 290 and 330 adults in the county received a flu vaccine this season.
Exactly 49,600 adults in the county received a flu vaccine this season.
Plausibly between 49,600 and 52,800 adults in the county received a flu vaccine this season.
items.explanation: The plausible range for the county's percent is 62% − 4% = 58% to 62% + 4% = 66%. Apply that range to the population of 80,000 adults: 0.58 × 80,000 = 46,400 and 0.66 × 80,000 = 52,800.

C.why: You took 62% of 80,000 and treated it as exact. A margin of error means the true count is uncertain, so 'exactly' claims too much.

D.why: You added the margin of error but forgot to subtract it. The interval runs from 58% to 66%, so its lower end is 46,400, not 49,600.

items.subtype_name: What does this number or point mean in the story?
items.stimulus: A labour economist models the number of apprentices enrolled in a regional electricians' training program with the function $A(t) = 1{,}200(1.05)^t$, where $A(t)$ is the estimated number of apprentices $t$ years after 2020.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $1{,}200$ in this context?
choices: The estimated number of apprentices in the program 1 year after 2020
The estimated number of apprentices the program gains each year after 2020
The estimated number of apprentices in the program in 2020
The estimated number of years after 2020 for the program to gain 1,200 apprentices
items.explanation: In $A(t) = a \cdot b^t$, $a$ is the value when $t = 0$. Here $t = 0$ means 0 years after 2020, so $A(0) = 1{,}200(1.05)^0 = 1{,}200$. That is the estimated number of apprentices in 2020.

A.why: You treated the first year of the model as $t = 1$. One year after 2020 the model gives $A(1) = 1{,}200(1.05) = 1{,}260$, not 1,200. The starting value belongs to $t = 0$.

B.why: You read the exponential as a fixed amount added each year. The program grows by a constant percentage, 5% a year, so the number added changes from year to year. 1,200 is the starting count, not the yearly gain.

D.why: You swapped the input and output. 1,200 is an output, a number of apprentices. It is not a number of years, which is the input $t$.

items.stimulus: A cartographer drawing an elevation profile for a topographic map models the elevation of a mountain trail with the function $h(d) = -0.5(d - 20)^2 + 600$. Here $h(d)$ is the elevation, in meters, at a horizontal distance of $d$ kilometers from the trailhead, for $0 \le d \le 40$.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of the vertex of the graph of $y = h(d)$ in this context?
choices: The trail's lowest elevation, 600 meters, is reached 20 kilometers from the trailhead.
The trail's greatest elevation, 20 meters, is reached 600 kilometers from the trailhead.
The trail's elevation at the trailhead, 0 kilometers along, is 600 meters.
The trail's greatest elevation, 600 meters, is reached 20 kilometers from the trailhead.
items.explanation: In vertex form $a(x - h)^2 + k$, the vertex is $(h, k)$, so here it is $(20, 600)$. Because $a = -0.5$ is negative, the parabola opens downward and the vertex is a maximum. The trail's highest point is 600 meters, reached 20 kilometers from the trailhead.

A.why: You found the right numbers but called the vertex a minimum. The leading coefficient $-0.5$ is negative, so the parabola opens downward and the vertex is the highest point.

B.why: You swapped the coordinates. In $(20, 600)$, 20 is the input (distance in kilometers) and 600 is the output (elevation in meters).

C.why: You described the y-intercept instead of the vertex. At the trailhead, $d = 0$, and $h(0) = -0.5(400) + 600 = 400$ meters. The 600 is the peak elevation, not the elevation where the trail starts.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A printmaking studio uses the equation $C = 3p + 40$ to find the total cost $C$, in dollars, of pulling $p$ prints from a new linocut block. The total includes a one-time cost for carving the block.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $3$ in this context?
choices: The fixed cost, in dollars, of carving the linocut block
The cost, in dollars, of producing each additional print
The number of prints the studio produces for each dollar
The total cost, in dollars, of producing a single print
items.explanation: $3$ is the coefficient on $p$, so it is the rate: each extra print adds $3$ dollars to the total cost. The units are dollars per print, which are the units of $C$ divided by the units of $p$.

A.why: You gave the meaning of the constant. The one-time carving cost is the $40$, the value of $C$ when $p = 0$. The $3$ is the rate per print.

C.why: You flipped the units of the rate. The coefficient is dollars per print, not prints per dollar. Its units are the output's units divided by the input's units.

D.why: You forgot the fixed cost. Producing one print costs $C = 3(1) + 40 = 43$ dollars in total. The $3$ is only the added cost of each print.

items.stimulus: During a drought, the amount of water in a reservoir, $W$, in millions of gallons, $d$ days after the drought began is given by $W = 900 - 15d$.

items.stimulus: A cartographer is converting a hand-drawn survey map of a region into a digital format. The equation $2R + 70d = 1680$ models the area $R$, in square kilometers, of the survey map that still has not been digitized $d$ days after the cartographer began the project.

items.stimulus: During a drought, an ecologist recorded the water depth at the center of a seasonal pond. The graph shows a linear model of the depth $y$, in centimeters, $x$ weeks after the recording began.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A textile historian is studying the output records of a power loom from an 1840s cotton mill. The historian models the total length $L$, in yards, of cloth wound onto the loom's cloth beam $h$ hours after the start of a shift with the equation $L = 18(h - 2) + 50$.

items.stimulus:
A civil engineer monitors an expansion joint, a small gap between two sections of a steel bridge deck. The joint lets the deck lengthen as it warms. The width of the gap is a linear function of the deck temperature. The table shows three of the engineer's measurements.

Deck temperature (°C) | Gap width (mm)
10 | 38
25 | 29

items.stem: According to the model, what is the width, in millimeters, of the expansion joint gap when the deck temperature is $0^\circ\text{C}$?

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: During a drought, a town limits water use from its reservoir. The equation $V = 15(160 - t)$ models the volume of water $V$, in millions of gallons, left in the reservoir $t$ days after the limits began.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of 15 in this context?
choices: The reservoir held 15 million gallons of water when the limits began.
The reservoir's volume goes down by 15 million gallons each day.
The reservoir's volume goes up by 15 million gallons each day.
The reservoir will run out of water 15 days after the limits began.
items.explanation: Distribute to get $V = 2{,}400 - 15t$. The coefficient of $t$ is $-15$, so each extra day takes 15 million gallons out of the reservoir. The question asks what the 15 means, and it means the size of that daily drop: the volume falls by 15 million gallons per day.

D.why: You mixed up the two numbers inside the factored form. The reservoir is empty when $160 - t = 0$, so after 160 days, not 15.

The clinic's shipment of vaccine runs out 40 days after the campaign began.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A sports scientist records a runner's heart rate during the first 10 minutes of recovery after a hard interval session. The graph shows a linear model of the runner's heart rate, in beats per minute, against time since the session ended, in minutes.
items.stem: According to the graph, by how many beats per minute does the runner's heart rate decrease for each minute of recovery?
items.explanation: "For each minute" means the slope. Pick two points where the line crosses gridlines exactly, such as $(0, 180)$ and $(10, 130)$. The slope is $\frac{130 - 180}{10 - 0} = \frac{-50}{10} = -5$. The question asks how much the heart rate decreases, so give the size of the change: 5 beats per minute each minute. Watch the horizontal axis. Its gridlines are 2 minutes apart, so a drop of one gridline on the vertical axis covers 2 minutes, not 1.

figure.caption: Heart Rate During Recovery
figure.alt: A straight line falling from (0, 180) to (10, 130), passing through (2, 170), (4, 160), (6, 150), and (8, 140).

You read the y-intercept, the heart rate when recovery starts, instead of the rate of change.
You found the total drop over the 10 minutes and did not divide by the 10 minutes.
You saw a drop of 10 beats per minute from one gridline to the next and treated each gridline as 1 minute, but the horizontal gridlines are 2 minutes apart.
You calculated run over rise (10 ÷ 50) instead of rise over run.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A nutrition science student designs a basic smoothie recipe and adds hemp seed to it. The total protein in the smoothie, $P$, in grams, when $s$ tablespoons of hemp seed are added is modeled by the equation $P = 3(s + 6)$.
items.stem: According to the model, how many grams of protein are in the smoothie when no hemp seed is added?
items.explanation: "When no hemp seed is added" means $s = 0$, so you want the intercept. The equation is not in $y = mx + b$ form, so you cannot read the intercept straight off it. Either substitute $s = 0$, which gives $P = 3(0 + 6) = 18$, or distribute first, which gives $P = 3s + 18$. Both show the smoothie has 18 grams of protein before any hemp seed goes in. The 3 is the rate: each tablespoon of hemp seed adds 3 grams of protein.

You gave the coefficient, the protein added per tablespoon, when the question asked for the starting amount.
You added 3 and 6 instead of multiplying them when you expanded the expression.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A cartographer is making a topographic map of a straight mountain trail. Along the trail, the relationship between the elevation $E$, in meters, and the horizontal distance $d$, in kilometers, from the trailhead is modeled by the equation $3E + 90d = 4350$.
items.stem: According to the model, by how many meters does the elevation decrease for each kilometer of horizontal distance from the trailhead?
items.explanation: "For each kilometer" means the slope, but the equation is not solved for $E$, so you cannot read the slope straight off it. First isolate $E$: $3E = 4350 - 90d$, then divide every term by 3 to get $E = 1450 - 30d$. The coefficient on $d$ is $-30$, so the elevation drops 30 meters for each kilometer. The question asks how much it decreases, so the answer is 30. The 1450 is the elevation at the trailhead, not a rate.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: During a drought, a hydrologist models the depth of water in a reservoir with the equation $D = 42 - 0.6t$, where $D$ is the depth of the water, in meters, $t$ days after the drought began.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $0.6$ in this context?
choices: The depth of the water when the drought began, in meters
The decrease in the depth of the water each day, in meters
The increase in the depth of the water each day, in meters
The number of days it takes the depth to drop by 1 meter
items.explanation: The model has the form $D = b + mt$, with slope $m = -0.6$. The slope is a rate: each day $t$ goes up by 1, so $D$ changes by $-0.6$ meters. The sign tells you the depth goes down, so $0.6$ is the number of meters the water depth drops each day.

A.why: You gave the meaning of the constant term. The depth when the drought began is the value at $t = 0$, which is $42$, not $0.6$. You described the intercept when the question asked about the slope.

C.why: You read the size of the rate but dropped the minus sign in front of it. Because the term is $-0.6t$, the depth falls as time passes. It does not rise.

D.why: You flipped the rate. $0.6$ is meters per day, not days per meter. A drop of 1 meter would take $\frac{1}{0.6}$ days, which is a different quantity.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A county health clinic stocked flu vaccine doses before a vaccination drive and received no new shipments during the drive. The graph shows the number of doses remaining in stock, $y$, $x$ days after the drive began.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the line in this context?
choices: The clinic gives out 80 doses each day.
The clinic gives out 480 doses each day.
The clinic gives out 40 doses each day.
The clinic receives 40 doses each day.
items.explanation: Pick two clear grid points, such as $(0, 480)$ and $(2, 400)$. The slope is $\frac{400 - 480}{2 - 0} = -40$. The stock goes down by 40 doses per day, and since no shipments arrive, that drop is the number of doses given out. The clinic gives out 40 doses each day.

A.why: You found the 80-dose drop between two gridlines, but that drop happens over 2 days. You never divided by the run of 2 to get a per-day rate.

B.why: 480 is where the line meets the vertical axis. That is the starting stock, which is the y-intercept. It is not the slope.

D.why: You got the size of the slope right but not its direction. The line falls, so the slope is negative and the stock goes down. The clinic is not receiving doses.

figure.alt: A straight line graph of doses remaining against days after the drive began, falling from the vertical axis to the horizontal axis.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: After rats were removed from a small island in 2015, ecologists modeled the number of seabird nesting pairs on the island with the function $P(x) = 150 + 35x$, where $P(x)$ is the estimated number of nesting pairs $x$ years after 2015.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $150$ in this context?
choices: The estimated increase in nesting pairs each year
The estimated number of nesting pairs in 2016
The estimated greatest number of pairs the island can hold
The estimated number of nesting pairs in 2015
items.explanation: $150$ is the constant term, so it is the value of $P(x)$ when $x = 0$. Here $x$ counts years after 2015, so $x = 0$ means 2015 itself. The model estimates 150 nesting pairs in 2015.

A.why: You described the slope. The yearly increase is the coefficient of $x$, which is $35$. It is not the constant $150$.

B.why: You treated 2016 as the starting year. Since $x$ is the number of years after 2015, $x = 0$ is 2015. The 2016 estimate is $P(1) = 185$.

C.why: A linear model keeps growing and has no upper limit, so nothing in it describes the island's capacity. $150$ is where the model starts, not a ceiling.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: A field linguist estimates the time needed to transcribe recorded interviews in an endangered language with the equation $T = 4r + 30$, where $T$ is the total number of minutes of work and $r$ is the number of minutes of recorded audio.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $4$ in this context?
choices: Each additional minute of audio adds 4 minutes of work.
Each additional 4 minutes of audio adds 1 minute of work.
The linguist spends 4 minutes on setup before any audio.
Each additional minute of audio adds 34 minutes of work.
items.explanation: $4$ is the coefficient of $r$, so it is the rate of change of $T$ with respect to $r$. Each time $r$ goes up by 1 minute of audio, $T$ goes up by 4 minutes of work.

B.why: You flipped the rate. The slope is minutes of work per minute of audio. You divided output by input the wrong way around and got minutes of audio per minute of work.

C.why: You gave the coefficient the job of the constant. The fixed work done before any audio is the value at $r = 0$, which is $30$ minutes.

D.why: $34$ is $T$ when $r = 1$, which is the total work for a 1-minute recording, setup included. Each additional minute adds only the slope, $4$ minutes. The 30-minute setup is not repeated.

items.subtype_name: Say what the slope or intercept means
items.stimulus: At an excavation site, archaeologists estimate the age of material in a sediment layer with the equation $A = 2{,}500d + 400$, where $A$ is the estimated age of the material, in years, and $d$ is the depth of the layer below the surface, in meters.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $2{,}500$ in this context?
choices: Material at the surface is estimated to be 2,500 years old.
Each additional meter of depth adds 2,500 years of age.
Each additional centimeter of depth adds 2,500 years of age.
Each additional meter of depth removes 2,500 years of age.
items.explanation: $2{,}500$ is the coefficient of $d$, so it is the slope. It is measured in years per meter. The coefficient is positive, so every additional meter of depth raises the estimated age by 2,500 years.

A.why: The surface is depth $d = 0$, and there the age is the constant term, $400$ years. You gave the slope the meaning of the intercept.

C.why: You used the wrong unit for $d$. Depth is measured in meters, so the rate is 2,500 years per meter. One centimeter would add only 25 years.

D.why: The coefficient is positive, so age goes up as depth goes up: deeper layers are older. You reversed the direction of the relationship.

items.subtype_name: Introduce to an unfamiliar audience
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Orlenka Viaduct is a curved concrete railway bridge.
• It carries a freight line across the Tesna River valley.
• It was completed in 1974.
• Its longest span measures 212 meters.
• In 2019, engineers added sensors to its piers to monitor vibration.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the Orlenka Viaduct to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Completed in 1974, the Orlenka Viaduct had vibration sensors added to its piers in 2019.
The Orlenka Viaduct, a curved concrete railway bridge, carries freight trains across the Tesna River valley.
The Orlenka Viaduct's longest span, at 212 meters, was a remarkable length for a bridge built in 1974.
In 2019, engineers began monitoring vibration in the piers of the Orlenka Viaduct, which opened in 1974.
items.explanation: A reader who has never heard of the Orlenka Viaduct first needs to know what it is and what it does. Choice B gives it a category label in an appositive ("a curved concrete railway bridge") and then states its purpose (carrying freight trains across the Tesna River valley). After reading it, a newcomer knows what the viaduct is.

A.why: You picked a sentence built from two dates. It tells the reader when the viaduct was finished and when it got sensors, but it never says that the viaduct is a bridge. A reader new to the topic still doesn't know what the Orlenka Viaduct is.

C.why: The notes give the span length but never say it was remarkable for its time, so that judgment goes beyond the evidence. The sentence also skips what the viaduct is, which an unfamiliar audience needs first.

D.why: You went for a later development, the 2019 vibration monitoring. The sentence treats the viaduct as something the reader already knows and never says that it is a railway bridge or what it carries.

• Open Corners is a municipal initiative in the city of Bramhall.
• It converts unused corner parking spaces into small public seating areas.
• The program began in 2016 with four sites.
• By 2023, it had expanded to 61 sites.
• A spin-off program, Open Alleys, adds lighting and plantings to service alleys.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the Open Corners program to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

The Open Corners program in Bramhall grew from just four sites in 2016 to a total of 61 sites by 2023.
Open Corners is a Bramhall city initiative that converts unused corner parking spaces into public seating areas.
Since 2016, Open Corners has become the most popular public-space initiative in the history of Bramhall.
items.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to learn what Open Corners is and what it does. Choice C labels it ("a Bramhall city initiative") and states its purpose (turning unused corner parking spaces into public seating). That is the basic identifying information a newcomer needs.

• The glycemic index is a scale used in nutrition science.
• It ranks carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise blood sugar after eating.

items.subtype_name: Introduce to an unfamiliar audience
items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Beaufort scale is a system for estimating wind speed.
• It rates wind from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force).
• Ratings are based on effects an observer can see, such as waves or swaying trees, rather than on instruments.
• It was devised in 1805 by Francis Beaufort, an officer in Britain's Royal Navy.
• Some regions later added levels numbered 13 to 17.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the Beaufort scale to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: In 1805, Francis Beaufort, an officer in Britain's Royal Navy, devised the scale that now bears his name.
Some regions later added levels numbered 13 to 17 to the Beaufort scale's original top rating of 12.
The Beaufort scale is a system that measures wind speed exactly, using instruments placed on ships and towers.
The Beaufort scale is a system that estimates wind speed by rating visible effects, such as waves, from 0 to 12.
items.explanation: Your reader doesn't know what the Beaufort scale is, so the sentence has to say so. Choice D labels it as a system for estimating wind speed and briefly explains how it works. Naming the thing and giving its identifying description in one sentence is exactly what the 'introduce to an unfamiliar audience' version of Rhetorical Synthesis rewards.

A.why: You chose the origin story. The sentence tells the reader who made the scale and when, but it never says what the scale measures, so a newcomer still wouldn't know what it is.

B.why: You picked a later development, which is the subtype's trap. Talking about levels added to the scale only makes sense to someone who already knows what the scale is and what its ratings mean.

C.why: This choice labels the scale but gets its method backward. The notes say ratings come from effects an observer can see, not from instruments, and the scale estimates speed rather than measuring it exactly.

• A Harris matrix is a type of diagram used in archaeology.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

items.stem: The student wants to introduce the Calle Abierta program to an audience unfamiliar with it, emphasizing the program's purpose. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Since its launch in 2014, Calle Abierta has expanded from 6 to 41 kilometers of streets, and 68 percent of Marisel's residents have used it.
Calle Abierta, a program run by the city of Marisel, Chile, was designed chiefly to encourage residents to commute to work by bicycle.
items.explanation: The reader needs to learn what Calle Abierta is and why it exists. Choice A identifies it as a city program in Marisel, Chile, and then states its purpose from the notes: closing streets on Sundays so residents can walk, cycle, and play there.

items.stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sea butterflies are tiny marine snails, most less than one centimeter long.
• Unlike most snails, they live in open water rather than on the seafloor.
• Over time, the snail's foot evolved into two winglike flaps.
• Sea butterflies beat these flaps to swim, which gives the animals their common name.
• Their thin shells are made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.
• They are an important food source for young pink salmon.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce sea butterflies to an audience unfamiliar with them and explain how the animals got their common name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
choices: Sea butterflies earned their common name by beating a pair of winglike flaps, which lets them move steadily through the open water as they swim.
Sea butterflies, tiny marine snails that live in open water, have thin aragonite shells and are an important food source for young pink salmon.
Sea butterflies, tiny snails that live in open water, get their common name from the two winglike flaps, evolved from the foot, that they beat to swim.
Sea butterflies, tiny snails that crawl along the seafloor, are named for the two winglike flaps that extend from their thin aragonite shells.
items.explanation: This goal has two parts. Choice C covers both. It tells a new reader what sea butterflies are (tiny snails that live in open water), and it explains the name: they beat two winglike flaps, evolved from the foot, to swim.

A.why: A explains the name, so it seems to meet the goal. But it never says what a sea butterfly is. A reader who has never heard of them could think they're insects. A treats the animal as already known.

B.why: B correctly identifies sea butterflies as snails, which is half the goal. It then moves on to shells and salmon and never explains where the name comes from.

D.why: You may have liked that D both labels the animal and mentions the flaps. But it gets two facts wrong. The notes say sea butterflies live in open water, not on the seafloor, and that the flaps evolved from the foot, not from the shell.

items.subtype_name: Run-on / comma splice: join or split two full sentences
items.stimulus: Astronomers at a high-altitude observatory spent three clear nights tracking a faint comet as it swung toward the Sun, measuring how quickly its tail lengthened. items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: "On the fourth night, a bank of clouds settled over the mountain" can stand alone as a sentence, and so can "the team used the lost observing time to recalibrate..." When two complete sentences meet, a semicolon is one of the correct ways to join them, so you should pick the semicolon.

A.why: You went with the comma because the break sounds like a short pause. But both sides are complete sentences, and a comma alone can't join two sentences. This is a comma splice.

C.why: You left out the punctuation, which runs two complete sentences together into a run-on. A boundary is needed between "mountain" and "the team."

D.why: You saw that "and" can join two sentences, but a FANBOYS word between two complete sentences needs a comma in front of it. Without the comma, this is still a run-on.

A.why: You treated "each one had to line up..." as a description of the blocks. But it has its own subject ("each one") and verb ("had"), so it's a full sentence. Joining it to another sentence with only a comma makes a comma splice.

D.why: You knew a comma and "and" belonged together, but you put the comma on the wrong side. It has to come before the conjunction. Here it lands after "and," so it doesn't mark the boundary between the two sentences.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: To learn how much weight a 1920s steel bridge could carry when it first opened, engineers cut small samples from its girders and tested them in a laboratory. However, the girders have been exposed to rain and road salt for about a century, and corrosion weakens steel over time. The laboratory results therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: show that the bridge was never strong enough to carry its original traffic.
may underestimate how much weight the bridge could carry when it was new.
prove that corrosion has little effect on the strength of structural steel.
indicate that the bridge's builders chose an unusually weak type of steel.
items.explanation: The problem is a century of corrosion. Corrosion weakens steel, so samples tested today are probably weaker than the steel was in the 1920s. That means the results can't be trusted as a measure of the bridge's original strength. The only conclusion the text supports is a cautious one: the tests may make the bridge look weaker than it was when new.

A.why: You treated weakened modern samples as firm proof about the past. The corrosion only makes the results uncertain. It doesn't show that the bridge was too weak in the 1920s.

C.why: The passage says outright that corrosion weakens steel over time. This choice says the reverse.

D.why: You added a step the passage never takes. Nothing in the text is about what kind of steel the builders chose. If the samples are weak, the century of corrosion already explains it.

items.stimulus: After a school district launched a handwashing campaign, officials credited it with a 20 percent drop in illness-related absences compared with the previous winter. was unusual, since illness rates rose that winter in regions without such campaigns.
could have occurred even if the campaign had done little to reduce illness among students.

items.stimulus: Comparing a 1712 nautical chart of a stretch of the Normandy coast with modern satellite imagery, a geographer found that the charted shoreline lies about 400 meters seaward of today's. may be due as much to the limits of the early survey as to any actual erosion.
shows that the 1712 surveyors placed every coastal feature too far out to sea.
indicates that satellite imagery is less precise than estimating distances by eye.

items.stimulus: Because living floras in warm climates have a higher proportion of species with smooth-edged leaves, paleobotanists often estimate ancient temperatures from the share of smooth-edged leaves in a fossil assemblage. confirms that streamside plants mostly had smooth-edged leaves during the Eocene.
might reflect the plants' wet habitat more than the region's actual temperatures.
indicates that leaf-margin analysis cannot be applied to any fossil assemblage.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A field linguist uses the equation $T = 6r + 2g$ to estimate the total number of minutes, $T$, needed to process a recording of an endangered language. Here $r$ is the number of minutes of recorded speech and $g$ is the number of example sentences that must be glossed word by word.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $r$, and $g$. Which equation correctly expresses $g$ in terms of $T$ and $r$?
items.explanation: To get $g$ alone, first subtract $6r$ from both sides: $T - 6r = 2g$. Then divide the whole left side by 2: $g = \frac{T - 6r}{2}$.

A.why: You moved $6r$ to the other side but kept it positive. Taking $6r$ away from the right side means subtracting it from $T$, not adding it. This is the sign slip that this kind of rearranging is designed to catch.

B.why: You divided only $T$ by 2 and left $6r$ as it was. When you divide $T - 6r$ by 2, both terms get divided.

D.why: You swapped the two coefficients, as if the equation said $T = 2r + 6g$. In the given equation, $r$ is multiplied by 6 and $g$ is multiplied by 2.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A city planning office models a rider's total trip time to a downtown bus stop as $t = \frac{d}{s} + w$. In this model, $t$ is the total time in minutes, $d$ is the walking distance to the stop in meters, $s$ is the walking speed in meters per minute, and $w$ is the average wait at the stop in minutes.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $t$, $d$, $s$, and $w$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $t$, $s$, and $w$?
items.explanation: First subtract $w$ from both sides so the fraction is alone: $t - w = \frac{d}{s}$. Then multiply both sides by $s$ to clear the denominator: $d = s(t - w)$.

A.why: You multiplied only $t$ by $s$ and not $w$. Once $t - w = \frac{d}{s}$, the whole quantity $t - w$ has to be multiplied by $s$.

C.why: You lost the sign when you moved $w$. You get rid of $+w$ on the right by subtracting $w$ from $t$, so the result is $t - w$, not $t + w$.

D.why: You divided by $s$ when you should have multiplied. Since $d$ is divided by $s$ in the equation, you undo that by multiplying both sides by $s$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A sports science lab screening rowers records each athlete's body mass index using $B = \frac{m}{h^2}$, where $m$ is the athlete's mass in kilograms and $h$ is the athlete's height in meters.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $B$, $m$, and $h$. Which equation correctly expresses $h$ in terms of $B$ and $m$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $h^2$ to get $Bh^2 = m$, then divide by $B$ to get $h^2 = \frac{m}{B}$. Because $h$ is positive, take the positive square root: $h = \sqrt{\frac{m}{B}}$.

A.why: You flipped the fraction the wrong way. From $Bh^2 = m$, you divide $m$ by $B$, so $m$ goes on top. You are solving for $h^2$ itself, not for its reciprocal.

B.why: You multiplied $m$ by $B$ when you should have divided. Once $h^2$ is cleared from the denominator you have $Bh^2 = m$, and dividing by $B$ gives $\frac{m}{B}$.

C.why: You treated the exponent as multiplication by 2, as if $h^2$ meant $2h$. To undo a square, you take a square root. Dividing by 2 does not undo it.

items.stimulus: A musicologist studying archival recordings estimates how long a performance lasts with the equation $T = \frac{60n}{b}$, where $T$ is the length of the performance, in seconds, $n$ is the number of beats in the score, and $b$ is the tempo, in beats per minute.
items.stem: Which equation correctly expresses $b$ in terms of $T$ and $n$?
items.explanation: First multiply both sides by $b$ to clear the fraction: $Tb = 60n$. Then divide both sides by $T$: $b = \frac{60n}{T}$. To check, try $n = 240$ beats and $b = 120$ beats per minute. Then $T = \frac{60(240)}{120} = 120$ seconds, and $\frac{60(240)}{120} = 120$ gives back $b$.

D.why: Dividing both sides by $60n$ gives $\frac{T}{60n} = \frac{1}{b}$, so this expression equals $\frac{1}{b}$, not $b$. You stopped before taking the reciprocal, which is the last step.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A street-planning formula relates the spacing $s$ between streetlights, the number of lights $n$, and the length of the road $L$: $\frac{1}{s} = \frac{n}{L}$, where $s$, $n$ and $L$ are positive.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $s$.
items.explanation: The equation gives you $\frac{1}{s}$, not $s$. To get $s$, take the reciprocal of both sides, which flips $\frac{n}{L}$ into $\frac{L}{n}$. So $s = \frac{L}{n}$. This is the last step of many 'which equation expresses X in terms of...' questions: once you have solved for $\frac{1}{X}$, you still have to flip it to get $X$.

B.why: $\frac{n}{L}$ is the value of $\frac{1}{s}$, which is where you start. You stopped before taking the reciprocal, so this is $\frac{1}{s}$, not $s$.

C.why: You multiplied $n$ and $L$ together instead of flipping the fraction. Taking a reciprocal turns $\frac{n}{L}$ into $\frac{L}{n}$. It does not turn it into a product.

D.why: You replaced the division with a subtraction. The two sides are linked by division, and you undo that by taking reciprocals, not by subtracting one letter from the other.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A civil engineer uses $L = L_0 + L_0 a T$ to find the length $L$ of a steel beam after heating. Here $L_0$ is the beam's original length, $a$ is a positive constant and $T$ is the temperature rise.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $L_0$.
items.explanation: $L_0$ appears twice, so factor it out first: $L = L_0(1 + aT)$. Then divide both sides by $(1 + aT)$ to get $L_0 = \frac{L}{1 + aT}$. Factoring out a variable that appears twice is a step that many harder 'which equation expresses X in terms of...' questions depend on.

A.why: When you factored $L_0$ out of $L_0 + L_0 aT$, you lost the $1$ that the first term leaves behind. The bracket is $(1 + aT)$, not $aT$.

C.why: You factored correctly, but then you multiplied by $(1 + aT)$ instead of dividing. If $L = L_0(1 + aT)$, you undo the multiplication by dividing.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: In a model of fossil pollen in lake mud, $N = C - kt$. Here $N$ is the pollen count at depth $t$, $C$ is the count at the surface and $k$ is a positive constant.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $t$.
items.explanation: Add $kt$ to both sides and subtract $N$ from both sides to get $kt = C - N$. Then divide by $k$: $t = \frac{C - N}{k}$. Keeping track of the minus sign while you isolate a variable is the step these formula-rearranging questions most often test.

D.why: When you moved $N$ across the equals sign, you added it instead of subtracting it. Moving a term to the other side changes its sign.

items.stimulus: A hydrologist models the flow $Q$ over a small weir as $Q = kh^2$. Here $h$ is the water height above the weir, and $k$ and $h$ are positive.
items.stem: Solve the equation for $h$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A linguist compares a bilingual corpus in which $w$ sentences are in Welsh and $n$ sentences are in English, where $w > n$. The linguist measures the corpus's imbalance with the index $R = \frac{w - n}{w + n}$.

items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $U$, $V$, $s$, and $K$. Which equation correctly expresses $s$ in terms of $U$, $V$, and $K$?

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A linguist models how a second-language learner's reading vocabulary grows with exposure. In the model, $T$ is the number of words the learner recognizes after $w$ hours of reading, $p$ is the greatest number of words the learner could eventually recognize from the reading material, and $k$ is a constant that depends on the material.

$T = \dfrac{pw}{w + k}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $p$, $w$, and $k$. Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $T$, $p$, and $k$?
items.explanation: First multiply both sides by $w + k$ to clear the fraction: $Tw + Tk = pw$. The target $w$ now shows up in two terms, so you collect them on one side before you divide: $Tk = pw - Tw$. Then factor out $w$: $Tk = w(p - T)$. Dividing by $p - T$ gives $w = \dfrac{Tk}{p - T}$. To check, try $w = 15$, $k = 5$, $p = 8$. Then $T = \dfrac{120}{20} = 6$, and $\dfrac{6 \cdot 5}{8 - 6} = 15$.

A.why: You probably split the equation into $\dfrac{p}{T} = 1 + \dfrac{k}{w}$ and got as far as $\dfrac{k}{w} = \dfrac{p - T}{T}$, which is right. But you then solved as though the equation said $\dfrac{w}{k}$, so you never took the reciprocal. The correct result is $w = \dfrac{Tk}{p - T}$, not $w = \dfrac{k(p - T)}{T}$.

B.why: You cleared the fraction correctly to get $Tw + Tk = pw$. Then, when you moved $Tw$ across the equals sign, you kept it positive, which turned $p - T$ into $p + T$. Subtracting $Tw$ from both sides gives $Tk = w(p - T)$.

D.why: You reached $Tk = w(p - T)$ and then flipped the result upside down, so the factor you should divide by ended up in the numerator. To isolate $w$, divide both sides by $p - T$. That leaves $Tk$ in the numerator.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A city planner estimates the peak pedestrian capacity $P$, in people per minute, of a downtown corridor. Two things limit that capacity: the crosswalk signal, which allows at most $L$ people per minute, and the sidewalk, which allows $kw^2$ people per minute. Here $w$ is the sidewalk width, in meters, and $k$ is a constant.

$\dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{L} + \dfrac{1}{kw^2}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $P$, $L$, $k$, and $w$. Which equation correctly expresses $w$ in terms of $P$, $L$, and $k$?
items.explanation: Get the term with $w$ by itself: $\dfrac{1}{kw^2} = \dfrac{1}{P} - \dfrac{1}{L}$. Over the common denominator $PL$, the right side is $\dfrac{L - P}{PL}$. Take reciprocals of both sides: $kw^2 = \dfrac{PL}{L - P}$. Divide by $k$, then take the square root. Because $w$ is positive, keep only the positive root: $w = \sqrt{\dfrac{PL}{k(L - P)}}$. To check, try $k = 2$, $w = 3$, $L = 9$. Then $\dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{9} + \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{1}{6}$, so $P = 6$, and $\sqrt{\dfrac{54}{2 \cdot 3}} = 3$.

B.why: You flipped each fraction separately and rewrote the equation as $P = L + kw^2$. A sum of reciprocals can't be undone one term at a time. You can also see that this choice can't be right: $P$ is always less than $L$, so $P - L$ is negative and the square root isn't a real number.

D.why: When you combined $\dfrac{1}{P} - \dfrac{1}{L}$, you added instead of subtracting and wrote the numerator as $L + P$. Over the common denominator $PL$, the difference is $\dfrac{L - P}{PL}$.

items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $a$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $a$ in terms of $T$ and $b$?
items.explanation: Isolate the reciprocal: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b} = \frac{b - T}{bT}$. Take reciprocals of both sides: $a = \frac{bT}{b - T}$. Check: with $a = 6$ and $b = 3$, $T = 2$, and $\frac{3 \cdot 2}{3 - 2} = 6$.

A.why: You undid the sum of fractions one term at a time, as if $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ meant $T = a + b$. You can't flip a sum of reciprocals term by term.

C.why: $\frac{b - T}{bT}$ is $\frac{1}{a}$. You forgot the last step, taking the reciprocal to get $a$.

D.why: You subtracted the fractions in the wrong order and wrote $\frac{T - b}{bT}$ for $\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. Since $T < b$, your answer is negative, which can't be a number of days.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A public health team models the concentration $C$ of an airborne irritant at a distance of $d$ meters from a source that releases it at a rate $Q$. The constant $k$ depends on ventilation in the room.

$C = \frac{kQ}{d^2}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $C$, $k$, $Q$, and $d$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $C$, $k$, and $Q$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $d^2$ to get $Cd^2 = kQ$, then divide by $C$: $d^2 = \frac{kQ}{C}$. Because $d$ is positive, take the positive square root: $d = \sqrt{\frac{kQ}{C}}$. Check: with $k = 2$, $Q = 50$, $d = 5$, you get $C = 4$, and $\sqrt{\frac{100}{4}} = 5$.

A.why: $\frac{kQ}{C}$ is $d^2$, not $d$. You didn't take the square root at the end.

B.why: You isolated $\frac{1}{d^2} = \frac{C}{kQ}$ and took the square root without first taking the reciprocal. That gives $\frac{1}{d}$, not $d$.

D.why: You took the square root of the numerator only. The root has to apply to the whole quotient $\frac{kQ}{C}$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A folklorist cataloguing versions of a trickster tale records $n$ versions collected from oral storytellers and $m$ versions found in printed collections. The fraction of all recorded versions that are oral is $V$, where $V < 1$.

$V = \frac{n}{n + m}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $V$, $n$, and $m$. Which equation correctly expresses $n$ in terms of $V$ and $m$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $n + m$: $Vn + Vm = n$. Collect the $n$ terms on one side: $Vm = n - Vn = n(1 - V)$. Divide by $1 - V$: $n = \frac{Vm}{1 - V}$. Check: with $n = 2$ and $m = 6$, $V = 0.25$, and $\frac{0.25 \cdot 6}{0.75} = 2$.

A.why: You collected and factored $n$ correctly but dropped the coefficient $V$ on the $Vm$ term.

B.why: You lost a sign when you collected the $n$ terms. Subtracting $Vn$ from $n$ gives $n(1 - V)$, not $n(1 + V)$.

C.why: You set up $n(1 - V) = Vm$ correctly but divided the wrong way round. That flips the expression you need.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
An agricultural scientist measures the moisture content $M$ of harvested grain on a dry basis. A sample weighs $W$ grams when freshly harvested and $D$ grams after oven drying.

$M = \frac{W - D}{D}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $M$, $W$, and $D$. Which equation correctly expresses $D$ in terms of $M$ and $W$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $D$: $MD = W - D$. Add $D$ to both sides so every $D$ term is on one side: $MD + D = W$, so $D(M + 1) = W$. Divide: $D = \frac{W}{M + 1}$. Check: with $W = 150$ and $D = 100$, $M = 0.5$, and $\frac{150}{1.5} = 100$.

A.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $-D$ across the equals sign. It becomes $+D$, so the factor is $M + 1$, not $M - 1$.

C.why: $\frac{M + 1}{W}$ is $\frac{1}{D}$. You needed one more step: take the reciprocal.

D.why: You reached $D(M + 1) = W$ and then multiplied by $M + 1$ when you should have divided by it. This would make the dry weight bigger than the wet weight.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A printmaker centres a square linoleum block, $s$ inches on a side, on a square sheet of paper. The sheet leaves a margin of $b$ inches on every side of the block and has an area of $A$ square inches.

$A = (s + 2b)^2$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $A$, $s$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $s$ in terms of $A$ and $b$?
items.explanation: All the lengths are positive, so take the positive square root of both sides: $\sqrt{A} = s + 2b$. Subtract $2b$: $s = \sqrt{A} - 2b$. Check: with $s = 10$ and $b = 2$, $A = 196$, and $\sqrt{196} - 4 = 10$.

B.why: You subtracted $2b$ before taking the square root. The $2b$ is inside the square, so you have to take the root first and then subtract.

C.why: You treated $(s + 2b)^2$ as $s^2 + 4b^2$ and undid it term by term. Squaring a sum also produces the cross term $4sb$, so this doesn't work.

D.why: You took the square root correctly but added $2b$ when you should have subtracted it. That makes the block wider than the sheet.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
On a topographic map, two trail markers are $d$ centimeters apart. Each map centimeter represents $r$ meters on the ground. The higher marker has an elevation of $E$ meters and the lower one an elevation of $e$ meters, and a cartographer computes the average grade $g$ between them.

$g = \frac{E - e}{rd}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $g$, $E$, $e$, $r$, and $d$. Which equation correctly expresses $e$ in terms of $g$, $E$, $r$, and $d$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $rd$: $grd = E - e$. Add $e$ and subtract $grd$: $e = E - grd$. Check: with $E = 500$, $e = 300$, $r = 100$, $d = 4$, you get $g = 0.5$, and $500 - 0.5 \cdot 400 = 300$.

A.why: You dropped a sign while isolating $e$. From $grd = E - e$, you get $e = E - grd$. Your version is the negative of the correct elevation.

B.why: You mixed up terms and factors. You subtracted $g$ as though it were added to $E$, but $g$ is multiplied by $rd$, so you have to clear the denominator first.

C.why: You divided $g$ by $rd$ when you should have multiplied. Clearing the denominator $rd$ means multiplying both sides by it.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
Paleobotanists estimate past carbon dioxide levels from the stomatal index $I$ of fossil leaves. On a sample of leaf cuticle, $S$ is the number of stomata counted and $E$ is the number of ordinary epidermal cells counted.

$I = \frac{100S}{S + E}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $I$, $S$, and $E$. Which equation correctly expresses $E$ in terms of $I$ and $S$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $S + E$: $IS + IE = 100S$. Subtract $IS$: $IE = 100S - IS = S(100 - I)$. Divide by $I$: $E = \frac{S(100 - I)}{I}$. Check: with $S = 20$ and $E = 80$, $I = 20$, and $\frac{20 \cdot 80}{20} = 80$.

A.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $IS$ to the other side. It leaves $100S - IS$, not $IS - 100S$, so your count comes out negative.

B.why: $\frac{100S}{I}$ equals $S + E$, the total number of cells counted. You still needed to subtract $S$ to get the epidermal cells alone.

D.why: You divided by 100 when you should have divided by the coefficient of $E$, which is $I$.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Readers have long treated Agnes Marlowe's 1911 novel The Lexicographer's Daughter as a gentle family comedy. Its scenes of a father and daughter quarreling over word definitions are, in this view, light domestic sketches meant chiefly to amuse.

Text 2
Marlowe's novel is certainly funny. But its quarrels over definitions track a real debate of the period: whether dictionaries should record how people actually speak or dictate how they ought to. Beneath the comedy lies a serious argument about language.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The novel's dinner-table setting is its most carefully described location.
The novel's quarrels over word definitions are presented with humor.
The novel is meant mainly to amuse rather than to make an argument.
The novel takes part in a debate over the proper role of dictionaries.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the novel a comedy whose quarrels are meant to amuse, and Text 2 opens by granting that the novel 'is certainly funny.' That concession is the shared ground: both authors see the quarrels as humorous. They split over whether anything serious lies underneath.

A.why: You went to a detail from the novel itself instead of the critics' claims about it. Neither author says anything about how carefully any setting is described.

C.why: This is Text 1's view only. Text 2 rejects it and says the comedy covers a serious argument about language.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 describes the scenes as light sketches and never connects them to a debate about dictionaries.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Hester Crane's 1894 poem cycle Loom Songs is usually read as a lament. Its speakers, young women in a cotton mill, describe the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours, and critics have taken the poems as straightforward protests against factory labor.

Text 2
Although Loom Songs plainly records the hardship of mill work, its speakers also take pride in their skill, boasting of cloth woven without a single flaw. Crane portrays the weavers as craftswomen, not merely as victims.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Loom Songs presents its weavers as skilled workers proud of their cloth.
Loom Songs is best understood as a simple protest against factory labor.
Loom Songs builds its strongest effects around the sound of the shuttle.
Loom Songs depicts the difficulties of working in a cotton mill.
items.explanation: Text 1 describes the poems as a lament about the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours. Text 2's concessive clause, 'Although Loom Songs plainly records the hardship of mill work,' accepts the same point. Both agree that the cycle depicts how hard mill work is.

A.why: This is Text 2's new claim. Text 1 reads the poems only as laments and protests and says nothing about pride in skill.

B.why: This is Text 1's reading, and Text 2 argues against it by saying the weavers are more than victims.

C.why: You picked a vivid image from the poems and judged it yourself. Neither critic says the shuttle's sound is where the cycle's strongest effects lie.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Desmond Ure's 1932 novel The Bran Cure follows a town swept up by a doctor's miracle diet. Most commentators read it as pure satire, a mockery of the era's food fads with no interest in real nutrition.

Text 2
The Bran Cure does ridicule food fads, and its doctor is a fraud. Yet Ure, who corresponded with vitamin researchers, gives the novel's skeptical nurse accurate explanations of dietary deficiency. The book mocks quackery partly by contrasting it with sound science.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The novel ridicules the food fads that were popular in its era.
The novel shows no real interest in the science of nutrition.
The novel's nurse gives accurate explanations of dietary deficiency.
The novel's townspeople are its most memorably drawn characters.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the novel 'a mockery of the era's food fads,' and Text 2 grants that it 'does ridicule food fads.' The two critics disagree only about whether the book also takes real nutrition science seriously.

B.why: This is Text 1's position. Text 2 disputes it directly by pointing to the nurse's accurate scientific explanations.

C.why: Only Text 2 makes this claim. Text 1 never mentions the nurse and says the novel ignores real nutrition.

D.why: You gave your own view of the novel's characters instead of anything the critics argue. Neither text ranks the characters.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Ruth Ansel's 1928 poem "The Coal Fern" describes a fossil frond found in a lump of coal. It is often read as a meditation on mortality, with the ancient plant serving as a reminder that every living thing passes away.

Text 2
Death is undeniably present in "The Coal Fern." But Ansel had studied fossil plants at university, and her poem dwells on how precisely the frond's veins survive in stone. For her, the fossil is less a symbol of loss than a record of endurance.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The fossil in the poem chiefly symbolizes the passing of all living things.
The poem's precise detail reflects Ansel's university study of fossil plants.
The poem engages with the theme of death in some way.
The frond's delicate veins are the most striking image in the poem.
items.explanation: Text 1 reads the poem as a meditation on mortality. Text 2 concedes that 'Death is undeniably present' before making its own argument. So both critics agree that death is one of the poem's themes.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 says the fossil is 'less a symbol of loss than a record of endurance.'

B.why: Only Text 2 brings up Ansel's university training. Text 1 gives no view on where the poem's detail comes from.

D.why: You read the poem's imagery on your own terms. Text 2 mentions the veins, but neither critic calls them the most striking image.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Tomas Varga's 1958 novel Hiring Hall, set among dockworkers who gather each dawn hoping to be chosen for a day's work, is widely praised as a portrait of solidarity among workers standing together against the shipping companies.

Text 2
Varga's dockworkers certainly unite against the companies in the novel's climactic strike. Earlier chapters, however, show them competing fiercely for scarce jobs. The novel is really about the tension between solidarity and a labor market with too few openings.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The workers in the novel join together against the shipping companies.
The workers in the novel remain united with one another throughout.
The workers in the novel compete fiercely for a limited number of jobs.
The dawn gatherings at the docks are the novel's most vivid scenes.
items.explanation: Text 1 praises the novel as a portrait of workers standing together against the shipping companies. Text 2 agrees that they 'certainly unite against the companies' in the strike. That unity is the point both critics share.

B.why: This goes further than the shared point. Text 2 says the workers compete fiercely in the earlier chapters, so it would reject the idea that they stay united throughout.

C.why: This is Text 2's addition. Text 1 describes only solidarity and never mentions competition among the workers.

D.why: You reacted to the novel's setting instead of the critics' arguments. Neither text judges which scenes are most vivid.

Text 1
Clara Dunmore's 1903 novel The Night Assistant, about a young woman who catalogs stars at a hilltop observatory, has long been read as a romance. Her nights at the telescope merely set the scene for her courtship with the director's son.

items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Ines Halloway's 1967 novel Grid takes place in a newly built town of identical streets. Critics have generally read it as an attack on modern urban planning, one in which the planners' uniform layout crushes residents' individuality.

Text 2
Halloway is clearly critical of the town's designers in Grid. Her residents, though, are hardly crushed: they repaint doors, plant gardens in the medians, and rename streets. The novel suggests that people reshape even the most rigid plan to suit their own lives.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

The novel expresses a critical view of the people who designed the town.
The identical streets of the town give the novel its haunting mood.
The residents adapt the town's rigid plan to suit their own lives.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 says the residents 'are hardly crushed.'

C.why: You gave your own impression of the novel's mood. Neither critic says the streets create a haunting atmosphere.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 sees the residents as crushed by the plan, not as reshaping it.

items.subtype_name: Literary passage plus a critic's reading
items.stimulus:
Text 1
Owen Prys's 1979 poem "Aquifer" describes a farming valley in which the wells slowly run dry. Readers have generally treated it as an elegy for a vanished rural way of life, and nothing more.

Text 2
"Aquifer" is certainly elegiac in tone. Still, Prys, a former well driller, describes with technical care how irrigation pumping lowered the water table year after year. The poem mourns the valley, but it also assigns responsibility for the valley's decline.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: The poem blames irrigation pumping for the decline of the valley.
The poem's image of empty wells is its most powerful moment.

The rising water symbolizes the farmer's lack of control over his fate.
The scene of the farmer's flooded orchard is the novel's most moving.
Velasquez balances the valley's loss against the benefits of the dam.
items.explanation: Text 1 calls the orchard scene the novel's 'most affecting,' and Text 2 grants that it is 'the novel's emotional center, written with real grief.' The critics differ over the novel's overall stance, but they agree about the power of this scene.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Gauge at Pell Point is an 1894 novel by Harriet Coyle. Its main character, Nell Ambry, lives in a lighthouse on a rocky coast and keeps the daily weather log that her father began decades earlier. The log records rainfall, wind direction and air pressure for passing ships. Most of the novel takes place over one harsh winter. In an essay on the book, a literary critic claims that Nell keeps her weather records faithfully even when the conditions make the work unpleasant.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Gauge at Pell Point most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Nell loved the quiet hour after a storm, when the clouds broke apart and the harbor lay still and silver beneath them."
"Her father had kept the logbook for thirty years, and its pages had gone brown and soft from the damp of the tower."
"Though the sleet stung her cheeks and numbed her fingers, Nell climbed to the gauge at dawn and wrote down every figure."
"On mild mornings Nell would linger beside the barometer, idly tapping its glass and humming quietly to herself."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Nell keeps her records faithfully, and she does so even when conditions are unpleasant. In this line the sleet stings and numbs her (unpleasant conditions), yet she climbs to the gauge and records every figure (faithful record-keeping). It is the only choice that shows both parts.

A.why: This line has the right setting and a strong feeling about the weather, but Nell isn't recording anything, and the moment is calm rather than unpleasant. You were drawn by the matching mood and topic, but the line shows neither part of the claim.

B.why: This line describes the logbook and her father's history with it. It is about the right object, but it says nothing about Nell's own diligence or about hard conditions.

D.why: Nell is near the instruments here, but the mornings are mild and she is idling, not recording. This shows only half the claim at most and leaves out the unpleasant conditions entirely.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Valley Songbook is a 1931 novel by Tomas Varga. It follows Anselm Reiter, a musicologist who spends years collecting folk ballads from mountain villages before they are forgotten. Other scholars in the novel compete to publish first and to have collections named after themselves. Reiter is different. According to one reviewer, Reiter cares more about keeping the songs alive than about receiving credit for collecting them.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Valley Songbook most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: Reiter spent whole winters traveling from village to village, his notebook tucked inside his coat against the cold.
"I do not mind if no one recalls who wrote these tunes down," Reiter said, "so long as someone is still singing them."
Reiter was delighted when the city paper printed his portrait above a long article praising his new collection.
The oldest singer in the valley knew forty ballads, each of which she had learned as a girl from her own grandmother.
items.explanation: The claim compares two things: Reiter values the songs surviving more than he values getting credit. In this line he says he doesn't mind being forgotten (credit doesn't matter) as long as people keep singing the songs (survival matters). That puts both halves of the comparison in one line.

A.why: This shows that Reiter is dedicated to collecting, but it says nothing about credit. This is the half-the-claim trap: the line is about hard work, not about what he values more.

C.why: Here Reiter is delighted by public praise, which suggests he does care about recognition. That works against the claim.

D.why: This line describes a singer and how the songs were passed down. It has the right subject, folk ballads, but tells you nothing about Reiter's attitude.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: On the Training of Runners is a 1908 book by the track coach Walter Prentiss. At the time, many coaches assumed that athletes improved simply by running as many miles as possible. Prentiss took a different view. Historians of sports science note that he argued rest was just as necessary for a runner's improvement as hard training.
items.stem: Which quotation from On the Training of Runners most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The runner should eat plain food, take very little sugar, and avoid all rich sauces in the days before a contest."
"No athlete ever won a race by training only when the mood suited him; the work must be done daily, in all weather."
"Sleep is a pleasant indulgence for the idle, but it does nothing to build the strength that a racer truly needs."
"The hard mile and the long sleep are partners in the making of a runner; neglect either one, and he will not improve."
items.explanation: The claim puts rest and hard training on equal footing as needs for improvement. This line calls the hard mile and the long sleep "partners" and says neglecting either one stops improvement. That shows both elements and their equal importance.

B.why: This line stresses daily hard training, which is only one half of the claim. It leaves out rest completely. A quotation that matches part of the claim isn't enough.

C.why: This line says sleep does nothing to build strength, which is the opposite of the view the passage gives Prentiss.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Pump on Carrow Street is a 1952 play by Muriel Ostrander. It is set in a crowded city neighborhood during a cholera outbreak. The town physician, Dr. Imogen Hale, suspects that a shared public water pump is spreading the disease. The residents distrust her and keep using it. A theater scholar argues that the play presents Hale as someone who keeps warning the public even though her warnings are repeatedly ignored.
items.stem: Which quotation from The Pump on Carrow Street most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: HALE: "Every morning I post the notice on the pump, and every afternoon I find it torn down. Tomorrow I will post it again."
HALE: "The water from the northern spring runs clear and cold; I have tested it three times now and found nothing amiss."
HALE: "I have warned them quite enough. If they will not listen to reason, then let them drink whatever they please."
HALE: "Half the families on this street are sick now, and it is the youngest children who are suffering the worst."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Hale's warnings are ignored, and she keeps warning anyway. Her notice is torn down every day (ignored), and she says she will post it again tomorrow (she persists). This line shows both.

B.why: This line is about testing water, so it fits the public-health subject. But it describes a different water source and involves no warnings or resistance from the residents.

C.why: Here Hale gives up on warning people, which is the opposite of the persistence the claim describes.

D.why: This line comes from the right situation and has the urgent tone you might expect, but it only describes the outbreak. It shows no warning and no one ignoring her, so it misses both parts of the claim.

items.stimulus: "The Surveyor's Confession" is an 1887 poem by Edwin Marlowe. Its speaker is an aging mapmaker who has spent his life charting a small coastal town. Looking over his finished map, the speaker reflects on what his careful work achieved. In a study of Victorian poetry, one critic claims that the speaker regrets that his map, though accurate, cannot capture the life of the town.
items.stem: Which quotation from "The Surveyor's Confession" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "My ink was black, my paper smooth and fine, / And I worked by candle long into the night."
"I drew each river's bend and every hill, / But not the voices calling down the lane."
"The finished chart held all the town contained— / Its songs, its fires, the faces at the door."
"Beyond the hills there lay a land unknown, / Whose roads no surveyor ever walked."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: the map is accurate, and it still fails to capture the town's life. In the first half of the line he drew every bend and hill (accuracy). In the second half he admits the voices in the lane are missing (the life left out). This line shows the full contrast.

A.why: This line shows the speaker working hard on the map, which fits the scene. But it says nothing about what the map leaves out, so the regret half of the claim is missing.

C.why: This line says the map captured everything, including songs and faces. That reverses the claim that the map cannot capture the town's life.

D.why: This line is about unmapped land beyond the town. That is a different limitation, not the one in the claim, which is the map's failure to capture the town's own life.

items.stimulus: The Millrace is a 1928 novel by Clara Dunmore. It is set in a river valley during a spring when heavy snowmelt swells the stream that drives the local grain mill. The mill's owner, Ezra Pell, knows that the stream can overflow its banks within hours once the thaw begins. Literary critics have noted that in the novel's early chapters, Ezra keeps a close watch on the rising water even while he is busy with his ordinary work: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Millrace most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Ezra had always loved the low sound of the stream, which seemed to him the oldest and steadiest voice in the whole valley."
"Even as he stacked the grain sacks, Ezra glanced every few minutes at the notched post by the millrace, noting how far the water had climbed."
"When the spring water rose, the neighbors down the lane carried their chairs and quilts to the upper rooms and waited for it to fall."
"Ezra finished hauling the grain sacks early that evening and sat out on the porch steps, his mind drifting far from the mill."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Ezra watches the rising water closely, and he does it while busy with his ordinary work. In choice B he is stacking grain sacks (ordinary work) and checking the marked post every few minutes to see how high the water has risen (close watch). It is the only quotation that shows both parts.

A.why: You went with the right mood and vocabulary. Ezra cares about the stream here, but the line shows neither part of the claim. He isn't tracking the water's rise, and he isn't working. Feeling something about the river is a related idea. It isn't the claim.

C.why: You picked a line from the right scene, the rising spring water, but it describes the neighbors. Ezra isn't in it. The claim is about what Ezra does, so a line about other people can't illustrate it.

D.why: You matched only half the claim. Ezra is doing his ordinary work, but then his mind drifts "far from the mill." That is the opposite of keeping a close watch on the water. The line works against the claim instead of supporting it.

items.stimulus: The Span at Harlow Ferry, a 1911 novel by Edith Marrow, follows Thomas Reade, an engineer building a steel bridge across a wide and fast river. Marrow presents Reade as a man whose care for his calculations does not slip even when his body is worn out: ______
items.stem: The claim at the end of the passage has two parts. Which line from the novel shows both parts?
choices: "He was so weary by nightfall that he fell asleep at the drafting table before his supper came."
"Every rivet on the east pier, he insisted, must be counted, tested, and written in the ledger."
"Though his eyes ached and the lamp burned low, he checked each figure for the load a third time."
"From the site office he watched the river slide past, calm and grey beneath the morning fog."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Reade is careful with his calculations, AND he stays careful while worn out. Choice C shows both. His aching eyes and the low lamp show exhaustion, and checking each figure a third time shows care. This is the core step of every literary-quotation question: split the claim into its parts, then find the one line that shows all of them.

A.why: This line shows that Reade is worn out, which is half the claim. But he falls asleep instead of working, so it shows nothing about his care for his calculations. You probably matched the tired mood and stopped checking.

D.why: This line comes from the right setting, the bridge site, but it describes the river. It shows neither Reade's care nor his tiredness. Being in the right scene is not the same as supporting the claim.

items.stimulus: Letters from the Organ Loft (1874) collects the letters of Samuel Penrose, choirmaster of a small country church. Writing about the hymns his parish had sung for generations, Penrose treats them with real admiration, yet he admits they are very hard for his singers to perform: ______
items.stem: The claim at the end of the passage has two parts. Which line from the book shows both parts?
choices: "The old tunes are lovely, I grant you, but no choir of mine can reach their highest notes."
"I have loved these hymns since I first heard them sung as a small boy in the cathedral at Wells."
"Our new soprano struggles with nearly every line the vicar chooses for the Sunday service."
"The organ itself was built in 1790, and it still has to be tuned by hand each spring."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Penrose admires the old hymns, AND he finds them hard for his choir to sing. Choice A shows both. items.stimulus: "Plate and Acid" is a 1934 poem by Ines Harrow, who worked as an etcher. In etching, an artist scratches lines through a waxy coating on a copper plate, and an acid bath then bites those lines permanently into the metal. Critics have noted that the poem is less interested in the lines the etcher plans than in the ones she doesn't. According to one critic, the speaker treats the accidental marks the acid preserves as permanent and also as something she values:
items.stem: Which quotation from "Plate and Acid" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "I draw the needle slowly through the ground, / and every line obeys the hand that made it."
"The slip the acid kept, I keep as well; / by morning it is what the print is for."

"The children gathered at her hearth every evening, and even the restless miller's boy fell silent once she began."
