items.stimulus: "The Weaver's Account" is an 1851 poem by Elinor Tasker. Its speaker is a hand-loom weaver writing at a time when steam-powered mills were quickly taking over cloth production in her region. Textile historians often turn to the poem as a record of how craftspeople felt about this shift. One historian claims that the speaker takes pride in the quality of her own work while also grieving that machine-made cloth is replacing it:
items.stem: Which quotation from "The Weaver's Account" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The mill downriver hums both night and day, / And bolts of cheap bright cotton ride the cart."
"I love the clack of shuttle through the shed, / The patient rising cloth beneath my hand."
"No engine lays a thread as true as mine, / Yet I must weep to see the town in engine cloth."
"Let the mills now have the market; I am glad / To lay my shuttle down and rest at last."
items.explanation: The claim needs two things: pride in her own work and grief that machine cloth is replacing it. items.stimulus: Grid and Garden, a 1924 novel by Philip Stane, follows Lydia Marsh, an engineer hired to redesign a crowded industrial town. The book is often assigned in urban planning courses for its portrait of early zoning debates. One planning historian argues that Marsh favours straight, efficient streets only in the commercial district, and that she insists the residential quarters keep their old winding lanes:

"She drew every avenue straight across the map, from the warehouses right out to the farthest row of cottages."
"Marsh loved the old town's twisting alleys, where she had wandered as a child among the bakers and the bookbinders."
"The council argued for a full week over the cost of paving the broad new streets of the commercial quarter."
items.explanation: The key word in the claim is 'only': Marsh wants straight streets in the commercial district and winding lanes where people live. This line calls for straight market streets and crooked residential lanes, so it matches the claim's limited scope on both sides.

C.why: This line shows fondness for the winding lanes but says nothing about straight streets for business. It is the half-claim trap: the right mood and setting, but only one of the two parts.

D.why: This line is about the council arguing over paving costs. It doesn't show what Marsh prefers for either district, so it is on topic but doesn't illustrate the claim.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Harlan Vosk's 1931 play The Tally Room is set in a fish cannery where workers are paid according to the total number of cans their whole line produces, not by individual output. Under this system, one slow worker lowers everyone's pay. Labour economists sometimes use the play to illustrate group incentives. One economist claims that Nell Garrity, the play's central figure, grasps this link and presses slower coworkers to keep pace because of it:
items.stem: Which quotation from The Tally Room most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "Hurry yourself along, Tom, or the whole lot of us will be stuck here long past the evening whistle again."
"The bosses count the cans at the end of the line, and they pay the whole line together, not the single girl."
"I'll work at whatever pace suits me, Tom; my wage is my own affair and nobody else's business at all."
"Pick it up, Tom. Every can you miss on this line comes out of my pay envelope as well as out of yours."
items.explanation: The claim has a chain: Nell understands that pay is shared across the line, and that is why she pushes coworkers. Here she tells Tom to speed up, and her reason is that every can he misses lowers her pay as well as his. The line shows both the pressure and the pay link behind it.

A.why: Nell does push Tom here, but her reason is working late, not pay. You matched the urging and missed the middle step of the chain, which is the link between pay and the group's output.

B.why: This line explains how pay is shared across the line, but Nell never presses anyone to work faster. It gives the mechanism without the action, so it is only half the claim.

C.why: Here Nell calls her wage her own affair. That denies the very link between her pay and her coworkers' output that the claim says she understands.

items.stimulus: In Ottilie Farrant's 1896 novel The Blank Margin, the mapmaker Jonas Pell is commissioned to chart a northern province, much of which no surveyor has yet visited. "The duke admired maps crowded with sea monsters and would pay handsomely for an elaborately painted border."

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists have long assumed that raising the minimum wage pushes employers to cut jobs. However, a growing body of research suggests that the effect may be smaller than predicted. In a study of restaurants on either side of a state border, economist Lena Okafor found that employment in the state that raised its wage grew at nearly the same rate as employment in the neighboring state that did not. Okafor argues that employers often absorb higher wages through lower staff turnover rather than through layoffs.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study confirmed the long-held assumption that higher minimum wages lead employers to cut jobs.
Restaurants in the state that raised its minimum wage saw their employment grow during the study.
Research suggests that raising the minimum wage may reduce employment less than economists have expected.
Raising the minimum wage reliably increases employment because workers leave their jobs less often.
items.explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn in this passage. The old assumption is set up so it can be questioned, and Okafor's border study is the evidence for the newer view. Choice C covers the assumption, the challenge to it and the study, and it keeps the passage's hedge ('may').

A.why: You took the assumption in the first sentence for the conclusion. Okafor's findings challenge that assumption. They don't confirm it.

B.why: You picked a detail from the study that is roughly accurate. It describes one result, but it leaves out the passage's point that this result challenges a long-held assumption.

D.why: You stretched the claim too far. The passage says job losses may be smaller than expected. It never says higher wages reliably increase employment.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Many endurance athletes believe that stretching before a race helps prevent injury. Researchers at a Norwegian sports institute tested this belief by assigning 300 recreational runners to either a stretching routine or a light jogging warm-up for twelve weeks. The two groups reported almost identical numbers of injuries. The researchers concluded that pre-race stretching, though popular, appears to offer little protection against injury.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The runners in the study followed their assigned warm-up routines for a period of twelve weeks.
A study found that stretching before running does little to prevent injury, despite a common belief.
Light jogging is the most effective warm-up for runners who want to avoid injury before a race.
Most endurance athletes have stopped stretching before races because they doubt it prevents injury.
items.explanation: The last sentence sums up the passage: stretching before a race, though popular, offers little protection against injury. Choice B covers both the common belief and the study's finding that undercuts it.

A.why: You chose a true detail about how the study was set up. The length of the study isn't what the passage is trying to show.

C.why: You went beyond the evidence. The two groups had about the same number of injuries, so the study doesn't show that jogging works better than stretching, let alone that it's the most effective warm-up.

D.why: You reversed what the passage says about athletes. It says many of them believe stretching prevents injury, not that they have stopped doing it.

items.stimulus: For decades, archaeologists credited the stone terraces at a hillside site in the Andes to the Inca, who controlled the region in the fifteenth century. Recent evidence confirms that the Inca built the terraces soon after they arrived in the region.
New dating evidence suggests that the terraces were built by a community that predated the Inca.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the old view that the Inca built the terraces, then turns with 'However' to the dating evidence. What comes after the turn is the author's point: an earlier community probably built them. Choice D says this and keeps the hedge ('suggests').

items.stimulus: Fermented foods such as yogurt and kimchi contain live bacteria, and some researchers have proposed that eating them may strengthen the immune system. items.stimulus: Immunologists have long assumed that innate immune cells such as macrophages, unlike T cells and B cells, keep no memory of past infections. Research suggests that innate immune cells may keep a form of memory, which challenges a long-held assumption.

Trained immunity makes innate immune cells just as effective as T cells and B cells at fighting infections.
items.explanation: The passage sets up an old assumption (innate cells have no memory), says it is incomplete, and then gives Okonjo's study as evidence that macrophages can keep a kind of readiness. items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The fiddle tunes of the Ardel Valley have usually been described as a purely local tradition, handed down from player to player within the valley for generations. However, musicologist Tomas Brenner has found that several of the region's best-known melodies closely match dance tunes printed in a 1790s songbook from a port city two hundred miles away. Brenner argues that the valley's music, though shaped by local players, likely drew in part on printed sources from beyond the region.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Ardel Valley's fiddle tradition developed entirely within the valley, without any outside influence.
A songbook printed in a distant port city during the 1790s included a number of popular dance tunes.
Most folk music traditions that seem local actually began as tunes printed in city songbooks.
Evidence suggests that the Ardel Valley's fiddle tunes likely drew in part on music from outside the region.
items.explanation: The word 'However' signals the real point. The passage first gives the usual view that the tradition is purely local, then presents Brenner's evidence and conclusion that the tunes likely drew in part on outside printed sources. Choice D states that conclusion with the same level of caution as the passage ('likely', 'in part').

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the 1850s, surveyor Ines Calloway set out to map the Merrow River delta, a maze of channels that changed shape from year to year. She measured channel depths by hand, recorded which channels shifted after floods, and asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons. Because she documented how the delta moved rather than fixing it at a single moment, her map stayed useful to navigators for decades after other maps of the delta had gone out of date.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Calloway's map stayed useful for decades because it recorded how the delta changed over time.
Calloway asked local boat pilots about routes that opened and closed with the seasons.
Calloway's methods became the standard for mapmakers of river deltas around the world.
Calloway's map soon went out of date because the delta's channels shifted after floods.
items.explanation: The middle sentence lists Calloway's methods, and the last sentence sums them up: because she recorded how the delta moved, her map stayed useful for decades. Choice A states that verdict and the reason for it, so it covers the whole passage.

B.why: This is true, but it is only one of the three methods in the middle sentence. It leaves out the result the passage builds toward, so it is too narrow.

C.why: The passage says only that her map stayed useful to navigators of this one delta. It never says that other mapmakers anywhere adopted her methods.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. Other maps went out of date, but Calloway's stayed useful because she accounted for the shifting channels.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Many cities are replacing parking spaces with small public seating areas. In one riverside neighborhood, planners converted twelve curbside spaces into benches and planters. Within a year, nearby cafés reported more customers, and residents said the street felt safer at night. The project suggests that giving up a few parking spaces can make a street more useful to the people who walk along it.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: Nearby cafés gained customers after twelve parking spaces were removed.
Turning some parking into seating can make a street more useful to people.
Cities should remove all their parking to make streets safer at night.
Residents objected when planners replaced parking with benches and planters.
items.explanation: The first sentence names a trend, the middle sentences give one example, and the last sentence says what the example shows. Choice B is the only one that covers all of that: some parking becomes seating, and the street works better for people. This scope check (does the choice cover every sentence?) is the first step on every SAT main-idea question about an informational passage.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Woodcut printing is often thought of as a crude method suited only to bold, simple images. However, some eighteenth-century Japanese printers used it to produce remarkably subtle work. By carving a separate block for each color and aligning the paper with small notches, they layered as many as twenty colors into a single print with soft, precise shading.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: Some printers carved small notches into their blocks to help align the paper.
Woodcut is a crude method that is best suited to bold and simple images.
Woodcut printing, often seen as crude, could produce very subtle images.
Japanese woodcuts were the most technically advanced prints ever made.
items.explanation: The passage opens with a common view and then turns at 'However.' What comes after the turn is what the author believes: woodcut could be subtle. The last sentence explains how that was done. Choice C covers the view, the correction, and the evidence. The SAT often builds main-idea passages around a 'However' turn, and this habit helps with those.

D.why: The passage says some printers did remarkably subtle work. It never compares them with every print ever made. 'Most advanced ever' is a much bigger claim than the text supports.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Medieval music manuscripts rarely record how fast a piece should be sung, so some musicologists look to other kinds of evidence. One researcher noticed that a monastery's daily schedule set aside only about ten minutes for a certain chant. If the monks kept to that schedule, the chant was likely sung much faster than it is usually performed today.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: A monastery's daily schedule set aside about ten minutes for one chant.
Medieval manuscripts give exact singing speeds for most of their chants.
Modern singers perform every medieval chant far more slowly than they should.
A monastery schedule points to one chant once being sung faster than today.
items.explanation: The passage goes from a problem (no tempo markings) to a clue (the schedule) to a careful conclusion about one chant ('if,' 'likely'). Choice D covers all three and makes the claim no stronger than the text does. Matching a choice's strength to hedge words like 'likely' is something you will need on real main-idea questions.

B.why: The first sentence says manuscripts 'rarely record' speed. This choice says the opposite.

C.why: The passage is about one chant, and it hedges with 'if' and 'likely.' This choice covers every chant and sounds certain. It claims far more than the evidence allows.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Engineers inspecting an old stone bridge found that its arches had shifted only a few millimeters in a century. Its foundations rested on bedrock rather than soft clay. Its builders had also left channels that let floodwater pass beneath the road instead of pushing against it. Together, these features explain why the bridge has outlasted many newer ones nearby.
items.stem: Groundwork: Which choice covers the whole passage, not just one sentence of it?
choices: Several features of its design explain why the old bridge has lasted so long.
The bridge's foundations were built on bedrock rather than on soft clay.
Floodwater has slowly weakened the arches of the old stone bridge over time.
Stone bridges always last longer than bridges made from newer materials.
items.explanation: The middle sentences list separate facts, and the last sentence ('Together...') combines them into one conclusion. Choice A is that conclusion. When a passage ends by adding up its details, the main idea is usually the sum and not any single item. You will see this pattern on SAT main-idea questions.

B.why: This is accurate, but it is one of the features, not the point they add up to. You chose a single correct sentence when the passage is doing more than that.

C.why: The passage says the channels let floodwater pass beneath the bridge, and that the arches barely moved. It does not say the arches were weakened.

D.why: The passage is about one bridge and the newer bridges near it. 'Always' and 'stone bridges' in general go well beyond what it says.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Seismologists have generally regarded slow slip events, in which a fault creeps for weeks without producing noticeable shaking, as a kind of safety valve: by releasing built-up stress gradually, they were thought to lower the odds of a large earthquake. However, seismologist Mereana Tuhi's analysis of the Hikurangi margin off New Zealand found that several slow slip events shifted stress onto neighboring locked sections of the fault, where swarms of small earthquakes followed. Tuhi notes that her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, but she argues that slow slip should no longer be viewed simply as a release of danger.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Swarms of small earthquakes occurred on locked sections of the Hikurangi margin after several slow slip events.
Slow slip events release stress so gradually that small earthquakes seldom follow them along the Hikurangi margin.
Evidence that slow slip events can shift stress to nearby fault sections challenges the view that they simply reduce earthquake risk.
Tuhi's analysis demonstrates that slow slip events make major earthquakes more likely on neighboring fault sections.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the accepted view that slow slip is a safety valve. After 'However,' it brings in Tuhi's finding that slow slip can move stress onto neighboring sections, and it ends with her argument that the old view is too simple. Choice C covers the expected view, the finding and the conclusion without claiming more than Tuhi does.

A.why: You picked a detail that is accurate but only one step in the argument. The swarms are evidence. The passage uses them to challenge an assumption, and this choice leaves that challenge out.

B.why: You probably recognised 'release stress' from the opening and stopped reading. The passage says swarms of small earthquakes did follow slow slip, which is the opposite of 'seldom follow.'

D.why: You missed the hedge. Tuhi explicitly says her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, so 'demonstrates' claims something she refuses to claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fossil leaves record not only which plants once grew in a place but also the climate they grew in. Among living woody plants, species with smooth leaf edges are more common in warm regions, while toothed edges predominate in cool ones. For example, when paleobotanist Ines Varga examined a 52-million-year-old leaf bed in the Dunmore Formation, she found that only about a fifth of its species had toothed edges, pointing to a warm climate. That estimate closely matched temperatures inferred independently from chemical signatures in nearby marine sediments.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Only about a fifth of the species in the Dunmore Formation leaf bed had leaves with toothed edges.
The shapes of fossil leaves can provide evidence about ancient climates, as Varga's study of one leaf bed illustrates.
Leaf shape gives more accurate estimates of ancient temperatures than chemical signatures in marine sediments do.
Fossil leaf beds reveal much about which plants once grew in a place but little about the climates of the past.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes the general claim that fossil leaves record climate. Everything after 'For example' is one case that supports it. Choice B states the general claim and ties Varga's study to it, so it covers the whole passage.

A.why: You chose a statistic from the example. It is correct, but it is there only to support the opening claim about what fossil leaves can reveal.

C.why: You read a ranking into the passage. The two estimates 'closely matched,' and the text never says leaf shape is more accurate than the sediment chemistry.

D.why: The first half of this choice matches the opening, but the second half reverses it. The passage's point is that fossil leaves reveal climate as well as plants.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds to every threat as if meeting it for the first time. Recent studies suggest this division may be too tidy. After people receive certain vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis, their monocytes, a type of innate immune cell, can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months. The effect appears briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, but it suggests the innate branch may be capable of a limited kind of memory.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: After BCG vaccination, monocytes can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months.
Innate immune cells appear to remember specific pathogens as durably and precisely as adaptive cells do.
Vaccines such as BCG can protect people against nearly any microbe by strengthening their innate immune cells.
The innate immune branch, long thought to lack memory, may possess a limited and less targeted form of it.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the traditional split, says it 'may be too tidy,' gives the BCG evidence, and ends with a hedged conclusion that innate cells may have a limited memory. Choice D keeps both the claim and its limits: 'may' and 'limited and less targeted.'

A.why: You chose the evidence instead of what it shows. The monocyte finding is accurate, but the passage uses it to question how immunologists divide the immune system.

B.why: You kept 'innate cells remember' and dropped the qualification. The passage says the effect is briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, not equally durable and precise.

C.why: You stretched the finding into a big claim about protection. The text reports stronger responses to some unrelated microbes for months. It never says people are protected against nearly any microbe.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Print collectors have long prized the earliest impressions from a run, assuming that later ones show a block worn down by repeated pressing. The linocuts of Hedda Lorne, a printmaker active in the 1920s, complicate that assumption. Lorne regularly recut her blocks between printings, adding figures and deepening shadows, and she adjusted her inks from one batch to the next. In letters, she called her late impressions 'the finished picture.' For Lorne's work, then, a later impression may be not a degraded copy but the version she most intended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: For Lorne's linocuts, later impressions may represent the artist's intended work rather than inferior copies.
Lorne adjusted the inks she used for her linocuts from one batch of impressions to the next.
Later impressions of prints are generally more valuable than early ones, as Lorne's letters demonstrate.
Lorne's linocuts confirm that early impressions preserve details that are lost as a block wears down.

B.why: You picked one of the supporting facts. It is true, but it is only one piece of evidence behind the conclusion in the last sentence.

C.why: You widened a claim about one artist to prints in general and added a claim about value that the passage never makes.

D.why: This repeats the collectors' assumption that the passage says Lorne's work complicates. Her prints challenge that view instead of confirming it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Dietary guidelines usually treat fiber as a single nutrient, recommending a daily total in grams. However, research led by nutrition scientist Priya Anand suggests that total may be only part of the story. Different fibers feed different gut bacteria, and in Anand's trial, an inulin supplement sharply raised levels of beneficial Bifidobacterium in most participants but barely changed them in others, depending on which microbes each person already carried. Anand concludes that fiber's effects likely depend on both the kind of fiber and the eater's existing gut community.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In Anand's trial, an inulin supplement raised levels of Bifidobacterium in most of the participants.
Fiber supplements do not benefit people whose gut bacteria differ from those of most other people.
Fiber's effects may depend on the type of fiber and a person's gut microbes, not only on the total eaten.
Anand's research confirms that all types of fiber affect the gut's bacteria in much the same way.
items.explanation: After 'However,' the passage argues that a daily total is only part of the story, and Anand's conclusion names the two factors that also matter. Choice C gives both factors, contrasts them with the single-total view, and keeps the hedge.

B.why: You turned 'barely changed' Bifidobacterium levels in some people into 'no benefit' for a whole group. The passage never measures overall benefit and never makes that claim.

D.why: The passage says different fibers feed different bacteria. That is the opposite of claiming all fibers act in much the same way.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the decade after beavers were reintroduced to a river in the Scottish Borders, surveys recorded a marked rise in the number of dragonfly species along its banks. Ecologist Callum Reid considers it plausible that the beavers were responsible, since their dams create the still, plant-rich ponds in which many dragonfly larvae thrive. But the same decade also brought new limits on fertilizer runoff from nearby farms, which may have improved water quality. Establishing the beavers' role, Reid argues, will require comparing this river with similar ones where beavers are absent.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The reintroduction of beavers caused the number of dragonfly species along the river to rise.

New limits on fertilizer runoff from nearby farms took effect during the decade after beavers returned.
Reid argues that reduced fertilizer runoff, not beaver ponds, explains the rise in dragonfly species.
items.explanation: Reid grants that the beaver explanation is plausible, points out a competing cause, and says more comparison is needed. Choice B matches that structure: a limited concession ('may') followed by the call for more evidence.

C.why: You picked a detail from the middle of the passage. The runoff limits matter only because they complicate the beaver explanation, and this choice leaves that out.

D.why: You misattributed a conclusion to Reid. He says the runoff limits 'may have' mattered but does not rule out the beavers. He argues that the question is still open.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Refuse heaps, or middens, were once excavated mainly for the intact objects that might be buried in them. Archaeologists now study middens as records of changing daily life, as a study at Tel Harun illustrates.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The 1914 anthology Songs of the Northern Dales has always been credited to the collector Albert Fenwick, whose name alone appears on its title page. However, Fenwick's field notebooks, recently catalogued by musicologist Dana Okafor, tell a different story. Most of the transcriptions in them are in the hand of his assistant, Mabel Hurst, and notes in the margins show Hurst insisting on preserving singers' irregular rhythms, which Fenwick had wanted to smooth out. Okafor argues that the anthology's distinctive character owes as much to Hurst as to Fenwick.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Newly catalogued notebooks indicate that Hurst deserves substantial credit for shaping Fenwick's anthology.
Hurst insisted on preserving the irregular rhythms of singers, which Fenwick had wanted to smooth out.
Fenwick's notebooks show that he transcribed most of the songs himself before later crediting Hurst.
Most early folk-song anthologies were largely compiled by assistants whose work went uncredited.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the official credit to Fenwick. After 'However,' the notebooks show Hurst's hand and her editorial choices, and Okafor concludes that Hurst shaped the anthology as much as Fenwick did. Choice A captures that correction to the credit.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, sprint coaches prescribed long, held stretches before races, reasoning that looser muscles would move faster. Physiologist Dana Okafor tested that reasoning with thirty collegiate sprinters, who ran 40-meter dashes after either five minutes of held stretches or five minutes of leg swings and skips. The results, however, ran counter to the coaches' expectation: the sprinters were, on average, slightly slower after the held stretches. Okafor suggests that holding a stretch may briefly reduce a muscle's springiness, the very quality a sprint start depends on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study compared two five-minute warm-up routines, using thirty collegiate sprinters as its participants.
A study suggests that the held stretches coaches long recommended before sprints may slightly slow sprinters down.
Okafor's study shows that athletes should remove stretching of every kind from their training programs.
Okafor found that held stretches improved sprint times by making the sprinters' leg muscles springier.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the coaches' long-held belief, then uses 'however' to bring in the real finding: held stretches were followed by slightly slower sprints, possibly because they reduce springiness. Choice B covers both the belief and the finding that corrects it, and it keeps the text's hedge ('may').

A.why: This accurately describes how the study was set up, but it leaves out what the study found. You picked a true detail from the middle of the passage instead of the point the whole passage is building toward.

C.why: The study only compared held stretches with leg swings and skips before sprints. It says nothing about getting rid of all stretching, and leg swings are themselves a kind of dynamic stretching. You stretched a narrow finding into a sweeping rule.

D.why: The sprinters were slower after held stretches, and Okafor suggests that stretching reduces springiness. This choice turns both parts of the finding around, so you may have taken the coaches' expectation for the result.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Leaves and wood fossilize only under unusual conditions, so many ancient plants are missing from the record of large fossils. Pollen grains, by contrast, have tough outer walls that survive in ordinary lake mud. At the Harlow Basin site, for instance, paleobotanist Mei Tanaka found abundant pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments, though not a single leaf of that shrub has been found anywhere in the basin. For Tanaka, the pollen fills a gap that the larger fossils leave open.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Tanaka found pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments at the Harlow Basin site.
Pollen analysis has made the study of fossil leaves and wood unnecessary for understanding ancient plants.
Pollen grains are fragile, so they survive only in the unusual conditions that also preserve fossil leaves.
Because pollen survives more readily than leaves and wood, it can reveal ancient plants that large fossils miss.
items.explanation: The first two sentences make a general claim: large plant fossils are rare, but pollen survives well. The Harlow Basin case is an example of that claim, and the final sentence says the pollen fills the gap. Choice D states the general claim that the example supports.

A.why: This repeats the Harlow Basin example correctly, but that example only supports the passage's broader point about pollen and the fossil record. You chose the vivid case instead of the claim it illustrates.

B.why: The passage says pollen fills a gap that larger fossils leave. It never says leaves and wood are no longer worth studying. You turned 'adds to' into 'replaces'.

C.why: The passage says pollen has tough walls that survive in ordinary lake mud, and that leaves are the fossils needing unusual conditions. This choice swaps the two.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Some meteorologists have proposed that the heat radiating from large cities may trigger summer thunderstorms downwind. Radar records from the city of Aldermoor appear to fit this idea: storms form noticeably more often just east of the city than to its west. Meteorologist Priya Venkatesan cautions, however, that the prevailing winds also carry moisture from nearby Lake Tessel over the same eastern area. The lake, rather than the city's heat, could therefore account for the pattern, and separating the two influences will require further study.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Radar records fit the idea that city heat triggers storms downwind, but moisture from a lake could also explain them.
Radar records prove that Aldermoor's heat is the main reason summer storms form more often east of the city.
Prevailing summer winds near Aldermoor carry moisture from Lake Tessel over the area east of the city.
Venkatesan rejects the heat hypothesis because storms east of Aldermoor are no more common than elsewhere.
items.explanation: The passage gives a hypothesis and some evidence that fits it, then uses 'however' to bring in a second possible explanation, and ends by saying more study is needed. Choice A covers both the fit and the doubt, and like the text it does not claim certainty.

B.why: The passage says the records 'appear to fit' the idea, and then raises a competing explanation. 'Prove' and 'main reason' are much stronger than the text allows. You missed the hedge words.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it is only one step in the passage's argument. It does not mention the heat hypothesis or the uncertainty the passage is really about.

D.why: The records show storms do form more often east of the city. Venkatesan does not reject the hypothesis either. She only says another cause is possible.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists generally expect a large new employer to push up wages in a small town by competing for workers. Examining warehouse openings in forty rural counties, economist Luis Ferreira found that hourly pay at nearby retailers did rise, by about 4 percent in the first year. Many retail workers soon moved to the warehouses, though, and retailers responded by cutting staff and hours rather than raising pay further. Within three years, retail wages had drifted back close to their earlier levels. Taken together, Ferreira's findings suggest that the wage boost from a new large employer may be real but short-lived.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In the first year after a warehouse opened nearby, hourly pay at local retailers rose by about 4 percent.
Opening a large warehouse is the most effective way for a rural county to raise its long-term wages.
Research suggests that a large new employer may raise local wages at first, but the increase may not last.
Retail wages kept climbing for three years after the warehouses opened, as competition for workers grew.
items.explanation: The middle sentences give separate facts: an early rise, workers leaving retail jobs, and wages falling back. The last sentence adds them up: the boost is 'real but short-lived.' Choice C restates that conclusion and keeps its hedge.

A.why: This is an accurate statistic from the passage, but it describes only the first year. The passage goes on to show the gain fading. You stopped at one true fact instead of reading through to the final verdict.

B.why: The passage finds that the wage gain faded, and it never compares warehouses with other ways of raising wages. 'Most effective' and 'long-term' are claims the text does not support.

D.why: The passage says retail wages returned close to their earlier levels within three years. This choice reverses what happened after the first year.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Farmers across the Venn Plateau widely credit a drought-tolerant maize variety, introduced in 2015, for the sharp rise in local yields since then. However, when agronomist Hana Brisco compared records from 300 farms, she found that yields rose just as much on farms that kept planting older varieties. The rise instead tracked the spread of no-till planting, a practice that leaves crop residue on fields and helps soil hold moisture. Brisco concludes that soil management, not seed choice, likely drove most of the gains.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The yield rise widely credited to a new maize variety was likely driven more by a change in soil management.
Farms on the Venn Plateau that kept planting older maize varieties also saw their yields rise after 2015.
The drought-tolerant variety performs worse than older varieties, so farmers should stop planting it.
Brisco confirmed that the new maize variety, rather than any change in farming practice, raised yields.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the farmers' belief about why yields rose, then 'However' introduces Brisco's evidence pointing to no-till planting. What comes after the pivot is the author's real point. Choice A states it and keeps the hedge 'likely'.

B.why: This is true, and it is part of Brisco's evidence, but it is only one piece of it. It leaves out the no-till explanation and the conclusion about what caused the gains.

C.why: Brisco found that older varieties did just as well, not better. The passage also never recommends dropping the new seed. You treated 'no extra benefit' as 'harmful'.

D.why: This repeats the farmers' belief, which Brisco's findings go against. You may have read the opening sentence and missed the 'However' turn.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The loss of a single predator can reshape an entire ecosystem. Consider Lake Corvin, where heavy angling during the 1990s removed most of the largemouth bass. Freed from their chief predator, small minnows multiplied rapidly. The minnows, in turn, consumed much of the lake's zooplankton, the tiny animals that had kept algae in check. Within a decade, dense algae blooms had clouded the once-clear water, shading out underwater plants that many other species relied on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Algae bloomed in Lake Corvin after the minnows consumed much of the zooplankton that had grazed on it.
Overfishing of predators is the leading cause of algae blooms in freshwater lakes around the world.
Removing the bass from Lake Corvin had little effect beyond reducing the number of fish anglers caught.
As the case of Lake Corvin shows, losing one predator can set off a chain of changes across an ecosystem.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim, and the rest of the passage traces one example step by step. Choice D states the claim and connects it to the example the passage uses to support it.

A.why: This accurately describes one link near the end of the chain, but it leaves out the predator and the general point the example is meant to show. You picked a vivid detail instead of the passage's claim.

B.why: The passage describes one lake. It never compares causes of algae blooms or makes a claim about lakes worldwide. You turned a single example into a global ranking.

C.why: The passage says removing the bass led to minnow growth, zooplankton loss, algae blooms, and harm to underwater plants. That is far more than 'little effect'.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the mountain village of Ostrava Alta, residents can hold conversations entirely in whistles. Linguist Tomás Reyna has proposed that this whistled speech arose so that shepherds could talk across steep valleys, and his recordings show that the whistles carry about two kilometers, far beyond the reach of shouted words. Yet, as other researchers point out, showing that the system works well over distance does not show why it began. It may have started as a courtship code or a children's game and only later been put to use across the valleys.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Recordings show that the whistled speech of Ostrava Alta carries about two kilometers across the valleys.
The whistles' long range shows that they are useful over distance, but not that this is why they began.
The whistles' long range proves that villagers first developed them to speak across the steep valleys.
Shouted words carry farther than whistles, so the whistled speech most likely began as a children's game.
items.explanation: The passage grants that the whistles carry far, then uses 'Yet' to raise the stronger objection: being useful over distance does not explain how the system began. Choice B keeps both the concession and the limit.

A.why: This is an accurate detail from Reyna's recordings, but it is only the evidence the passage goes on to question. It leaves out the passage's point about the difference between usefulness and origin.

C.why: The first half, about long range, is right. The second half claims 'proves', which is exactly the conclusion the passage says the evidence cannot reach. You recognized the opening and stopped reading.

D.why: The recordings show whistles carry farther than shouted words, not the other way around. The passage also offers the game only as a possibility, not the most likely origin.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Histories of the Marren Valley's choral festivals have long credited conductor Elsa Varga with founding the tradition when she organized a gathering of choirs in 1869. However, parish records recently examined by musicologist Iván Kertész describe an earlier festival, held in 1861, at which eleven village choirs sang together under the direction of a network of local schoolteachers. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Varga's letters show that, as a young singer, she attended a festival of eleven village choirs in 1861.
Kertész's research shows that Varga played no meaningful role in the history of the valley's festivals.
Newly examined records suggest the festival tradition began earlier than credited, under local teachers.
The parish records confirm that Varga organized the valley's first choral festival in the year 1869.
items.explanation: The passage presents the accepted credit to Varga, then 'However' brings in records of an earlier festival led by schoolteachers, backed up by Varga's own letters. Choice C states the correction the whole passage builds toward.

A.why: This is true, but it is only the final supporting detail. It leaves out the passage's larger point, which is that the accepted story of how the tradition began is wrong.

B.why: The passage suggests Varga was not the first founder. It never says she was unimportant. She still organized the 1869 gathering. You pushed a narrow correction into a total dismissal.

D.why: The parish records describe an earlier 1861 festival, which challenges the claim that Varga's was the first. You mixed up the old account with what the new evidence shows.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have long described the thymus as an organ that matters mainly in childhood. It trains young T cells to recognize threats, then shrinks steadily after puberty, and by middle age much of it has been replaced by fat. However, a study led by immunologist Rania Okafor suggests that the adult thymus may not be idle. Tracking newly made T cells in 140 adults aged 40 to 70, Okafor's team found that the thymus was still producing them in every participant. Output was lower than in children, and it rose briefly after infections.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: After puberty, the thymus steadily shrinks, and much of it is eventually replaced by fat tissue.
Okafor's team found that the adult thymus produces new T cells only for a short time after infections.
Although the adult thymus has been considered largely idle, it may continue producing new T cells later in life.
Okafor's research shows that the adult thymus is the main source of the T cells that fight infections.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the traditional view that the thymus matters mainly in childhood. Then 'However' brings in Okafor's study, which suggests the adult thymus keeps making T cells. Choice C covers both halves: the old view and the finding that corrects it. It also keeps the passage's hedge ('suggests', 'may') by saying 'may continue' rather than claiming more than the study shows.

A.why: You picked a true statement, but it only repeats the setup before 'However.' The passage gives the shrinking thymus as the expected view so it can challenge that view. The finding that the adult thymus is still active is left out completely.

B.why: You stopped at 'rose briefly after infections' and missed that the thymus was producing T cells in every participant all along. Infections raised output for a while. They were not the only time it happened. The word 'only' reverses what the passage says.

D.why: You went further than the study does. The passage says the adult thymus still makes some T cells, at lower rates than in children. It never compares the thymus with other sources of T cells or calls it the main source. The passage also hedges with 'suggests' and 'may,' and 'shows' drops that caution.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marisol Ekwueme's 2019 novel The Long Rows. Ines, an agricultural researcher, is visiting her test fields after a summer without rain.

Ines had driven out expecting to find nothing. The neighboring farms were brown to the fence line, their corn folded over like paper. But at the edge of her plots she stopped. The wheat she had spent six years crossing and recrossing stood upright, thin but green, its heads already filling. She knelt and pressed a stalk between her fingers, as if to be sure it was real, and found that she was laughing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines is relieved to discover that the wheat she developed has survived the drought.
Ines is discouraged to find that her test plots fared no better than nearby farms.
Ines worries that her neighbors will resent the success of her experimental crop.
Ines notices that the corn on neighboring farms has been damaged by the dry summer.
items.explanation: You follow Ines from expecting to find nothing to kneeling in disbelief and laughing. The turn at 'But' shows her wheat has survived when everything around it died, and her laughter shows relief and joy. Choice A matches both the situation and that emotional direction.

B.why: You reversed the tone. Ines expected failure, but the text says her wheat 'stood upright' and green while the nearby farms were brown. Her laughing shows the opposite of discouragement.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests Ines is thinking about her neighbors' feelings. Their farms appear only as a contrast to her surviving wheat.

D.why: You picked a true detail from the second sentence, but it is too narrow. The dead corn is background that sets up the real focus: Ines's reaction to her own wheat.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomasz Reyna's 2008 poem "Proof." The speaker is a printmaker.

All morning I cut the block by feel,
gouging the pale wood toward a shape
I carried backward in my head.
I rolled the ink, black and slow as tar,
laid the paper, leaned my weight on it.
Only when I peeled the sheet away
did I see what my hands had meant—
the heron, facing the right way at last,
more certain than I ever was.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the tools and materials needed to cut and ink a woodblock.
The speaker is frustrated that the finished print differs from the image planned.
The speaker works without fully seeing the image until the finished print reveals it.
The speaker regrets choosing a medium that offers so little certainty to the artist.
items.explanation: In plain English: the speaker carves 'by feel' with the image held 'backward' in mind, and 'only when' the paper comes off does the heron appear clearly, 'more certain' than the speaker felt. The poem moves from working half-blind to seeing the image revealed, and choice C covers both parts.

A.why: You described only the images from the first lines (the block, the ink, the paper) and missed the turn at 'Only when,' where the poem arrives at its point.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The heron faces 'the right way at last.' The print shows what the speaker's hands 'had meant,' so it matches the speaker's intention rather than disappointing it.

D.why: You added a regret the poem never states. The speaker admits to uncertainty but never wishes for a different medium. The ending sounds like wonder, not regret.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Harriet Olumide's 2015 novel Census. Theo, a graduate student in ornithology, is conducting a morning bird count in a marsh.

Theo had been told the count would be tedious: three hours on a wet platform, tallying whatever flew past. By the first hour he had filled two pages. A pair of rails picked through the reeds below him; a harrier swung low over the water and was gone. He forgot the cold in his boots. When his supervisor's truck pulled up, Theo looked at his watch in disbelief. It seemed impossible that the morning was already over.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Theo finds the bird count just as tedious as others had warned him it would be.
Theo becomes so absorbed in the bird count that the morning passes unnoticed.
Theo hopes to impress his supervisor by recording more birds than expected.
Theo watches a harrier fly low over the marsh water before it disappears.
items.explanation: Theo was warned the count would be tedious, but he fills pages, forgets the cold, and can't believe the morning is over. Those are signs of someone absorbed in his work, and choice B captures that.

A.why: You took the warning in the first sentence as Theo's real experience. Everything after it, such as forgetting the cold and his 'disbelief' at the time, shows the count was the opposite of tedious.

items.stem: Follow Nell's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?

items.stem: Follow the narrator's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?

The narrator dives on a reef that was bleached white by a heat wave long ago.

The author's routine technical work gives way to a decision to abandon formal notation entirely.
The author's routine technical work gives way to fascination with a singer as a real person.
The author explains that one singer resumed her verse a half step higher than she began it.
items.explanation: Follow how the author feels over time. At first the work is mechanical and the singers seem far away. Then one woman's unplanned moment pulls the author in, and they stop notating and replay her laugh. Choice C describes that move from routine to fascination.

B.why: The first half is right, but the author skips notating one change on one tape. Nothing says they give up notation altogether. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

Seeing their own cells at work, the speaker fears that their immune system is beginning to fail.

To portray Ines's growing fascination with work she had expected to find dull

To reveal how Ines first became interested in studying earthquakes as a child

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Varga's 1998 poem "For the Bridge Builders."

They say the river does not remember who tamed it,
that no plaque will ever carry your names.
But you who sink the pilings in the cold brown current,
who bolt the girders while the wind leans hard,

on the strength of what your hands have set.
Build on. The far bank is waiting,
and the span you raise will hold for years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To describe the materials and methods used to construct a bridge across a river
To criticize the public for failing to learn the names of the people who build bridges

B.why: You noticed the pilings and girders and took them to be the point. The poem mentions these details only to honor the people doing the work. It never explains how a bridge is built.

C.why: You read too much into the line about no plaque. The poem mentions that the builders go unnamed only so it can answer that worry. It never blames the public. The speaker's attention stays on the builders the whole time.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Nandakumar's 2015 novel The Piece Rate. Jonah works at a garment factory where pay is about to change from an hourly wage to a set amount for each finished shirt.

The foreman announced the change as though it were a gift: from now on, every shirt would earn its own wage. Jonah, however, did the arithmetic in his head and felt his stomach tighten. He was careful, not fast, and he knew it. Around him, the younger workers were already grinning and flexing their fingers. Jonah bent over his machine and tried to make his hands move quicker, but every crooked seam he had to tear out seemed to cost him more than thread.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the younger workers' excitement about earning more under the new system
To explain why the factory's owners decided to change how the workers would be paid
To convey Jonah's anxiety that the new pay system will leave him worse off
To show Jonah's relief that his careful work will finally be properly rewarded
items.explanation: The setup line names Jonah as the focus. The foreman presents the change as a gift, and 'however' turns to Jonah's reaction: his stomach tightens, he knows he is slow, and every mistake now 'cost him more than thread.' The excerpt as a whole conveys his worry that pay per shirt will hurt him, so C is correct.

A.why: You chose a character who is in the excerpt but is not its focus. The grinning younger workers get one sentence, and they are there to contrast with Jonah. The excerpt is about his feelings, not theirs.

B.why: You chose a detail the text never gives. The excerpt says nothing about why the owners changed the pay system. It only shows how Jonah reacts to the change.

D.why: You reversed Jonah's feeling. Being careful instead of fast is exactly why he expects to lose under the new system, so he is anxious, not relieved.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Clara Wendell's 1919 novel The Gauge-Keeper. Ada has just been hired to record the daily water level of the river near her family's farm.

Each morning Ada walked down to the painted post at the river's edge and read the number the water touched. Her father called it dull work, but to Ada it was nothing of the kind. She had begun to notice how the river rose a finger's width two days after rain fell in the hills, and how it slackened in the summer heat. Writing the figures into the ledger, she felt she was learning a language the river had been speaking all along.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey Ada's father's disapproval of the work his daughter has taken on
To suggest that Ada finds the daily task tedious and wishes to give it up
To portray Ada's growing fascination with the river as she records its levels
To describe how Ada learned to predict floods before they reached the farm
items.explanation: The setup line tells you Ada is the focus. Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her noticing patterns in the river: it rises after rain in the hills and slackens in the heat. It ends with her feeling that she is learning the river's language. That is growing fascination, and choice C names both the right person and the right feeling.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ada to her father. His remark that the work is dull comes up once, and only so the text can show that Ada feels the opposite. The excerpt is about her experience, not his opinion.

B.why: You took the father's word "dull" as Ada's own view. The text says the work was "nothing of the kind" to her, and nothing suggests she wants to quit.

D.why: You added a detail the text never gives. Ada notices how the water level changes after rain, but the excerpt never says she predicts floods or protects the farm.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Hanne Ostrova's 1911 novel The Winter Conservatory. Teodor, a young cellist, is listening to his teacher, Mr. Lind, play.

Mr. Lind drew the bow slowly, and the low note filled every corner of the cold room. The other students nodded politely, as they always did. Teodor, however, sat forward with his hands clenched in his lap. He was not listening to a lesson. He was listening to the sound he had wanted to make for as long as he could remember, and he could not yet make it.
items.stem: What does this excerpt mainly show about Teodor?
choices: Teodor longs to make the sound his teacher can make.
Mr. Lind is proud of how closely his students listen.
Teodor is bored by a lesson he has heard before.
Teodor first heard a cello at a concert as a child.
items.explanation: The setup line tells you Teodor is the focus. Everything after 'however' is about him: he leans forward, clenches his hands, and wants a sound he 'could not yet make.' Put simply, he longs to play the way his teacher plays. Naming the right person and the right feeling in plain words is the step you need before you can answer a real 'main purpose of a literary excerpt' question, where the right choice will say something like 'To portray a student's longing...'

B.why: You moved the focus from Teodor to Mr. Lind. The teacher is in the scene, but the excerpt never shows what he feels. It shows what Teodor feels while he listens.

C.why: You may have mixed Teodor up with the other students, who nod politely. The word 'however' sets Teodor apart from them. He is leaning forward and gripping his hands, which is the opposite of bored.

D.why: The text says he has wanted the sound 'for as long as he could remember,' but it never says where or when he first heard a cello. You added a detail the excerpt does not give.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Ilse Marrow's 2004 novel The Field Recordings. The narrator, a linguistics student, is recording her grandmother's speech.

I had come with a microphone and a list of words to check: the old local names for a wheelbarrow, a puddle, the first frost. Gran answered each one patiently. But somewhere around the word for "puddle," I stopped writing. She was telling me about the lane where she had splashed as a girl, and I realized I wanted the story far more than the word.
items.stem: What does this excerpt mainly show about the narrator?
choices: Gran grows tired of answering her granddaughter's long list of questions.
The narrator learns the old local word that Gran used for a puddle.
The narrator comes to value Gran's memories more than her word list.
The narrator's professor had asked her to record twenty local words.
items.explanation: The setup line makes the narrator the focus. The excerpt starts with her research plan, then turns at 'But': she stops writing and wants 'the story far more than the word.' So the excerpt shows her caring more about her grandmother's memories than about her list. Saying what the whole excerpt shows about the focus person is the first step in any 'main purpose of a literary excerpt' question.

A.why: You moved the focus to Gran and got her reaction wrong. The text says she answered 'patiently.' Nothing suggests she is tired.

B.why: You picked a single detail and missed what the excerpt as a whole shows. The puddle word only marks the moment she stops writing. What matters is that the story comes to matter more to her than the word.

D.why: The excerpt never mentions a professor or a number of words. You added a background detail that the text does not give.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Rowan Ashby's 1923 poem "To a Young Birder."

Do not be troubled that the marsh is still,
That every reed looks empty to your eye.
Sit longer. Let the cold come through your coat.
The heron you were promised is nearby,
And patience is the only kind of call
A wary bird will ever answer to.
items.stem: What is this poem mainly trying to do for the person it speaks to?
choices: To warn a young birder that the cold marsh is a dangerous place
To urge a young birder to keep waiting quietly for a shy bird
To describe the first heron the speaker ever saw as a child
To describe the reeds and plants that grow in a quiet marsh
items.explanation: The title names the person the poem speaks to: a young birder. The speaker says 'Do not be troubled,' 'Sit longer,' and promises the heron is 'nearby.' That is encouragement to be patient. Working out who is being spoken to and what tone the speaker uses is the step you need for a real 'main purpose of a poem' question, where the right choice usually starts 'To encourage...' or 'To convey...'

A.why: You flipped the tone. The cold is mentioned only as something to put up with while waiting ('Let the cold come through your coat'). The poem is reassuring the birder, not warning them away.

C.why: The poem never tells a story about the speaker's own past. The heron it mentions is one the birder is about to see. You added a memory that is not in the text.

D.why: The reeds are background. The poem is speaking to a person and telling them what to do. A choice that only describes the setting misses the poem's purpose.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Corin Hale's 1998 memoir Station Weather. The narrator's father worked as a weather observer on a small island.

Every three hours, my father climbed the hill to read the instruments, and every three hours I begged to go with him. He said the wind up there could knock a child flat. I believed him, and I went on begging anyway. To me, the white box of thermometers on the hilltop was the most important place in the world, and I wanted to stand beside it.
items.stem: What does this excerpt mainly show about the narrator as a child?
choices: The father was proud of keeping careful records of the island's weather.
The narrator was too frightened of the wind to climb the hill.
The narrator grew up to become a weather scientist like the father.
The narrator badly wanted to join the father in his weather work.
items.explanation: The setup and the stem make the young narrator the focus. The narrator 'begged' every three hours, kept begging even after the warning, and calls the instrument box 'the most important place in the world.' So the excerpt shows a child who badly wants to be part of the father's work. Naming the right person and the right wish is what you will do first on a real 'main purpose of a literary excerpt' question.

A.why: You moved the focus from the child to the father. The father's routine is the backdrop, but the excerpt is about what the child wants, not about how the father feels about his records.

B.why: The narrator believed the warning but 'went on begging anyway.' That shows wanting to go, not being too afraid to go. You reversed the narrator's reaction.

C.why: The excerpt stays in the narrator's childhood and never says what career came later. You assumed an outcome the text does not give.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Hester Vane's 1921 novel The Linen Year. Ada, a young apprentice at a textile mill, has inherited her grandmother's hand loom.

For months Ada had thought the old loom a relic, fit only for the attic; the mill wove a hundred yards before her grandmother's shuttle crossed a single width. Yet one evening, smoothing a coverlet her grandmother had made, she found a tiny knot repeated at every border, placed where no mill would allow a flaw. It was, she understood, a signature. That night she sat down at the loom and did not rise until the candle guttered.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey a grandmother's pride in the distinctive marks she wove into her cloth
To portray a character whose dismissive view of an inherited loom gives way to regard for it
To contrast the speed of mill production with the slowness of weaving by hand
To depict a character's growing frustration with the demands of her work at the mill
items.explanation: The setup puts Ada at the center. The excerpt opens with what she has long believed (the loom is a relic), turns on "Yet," and ends with her working at the loom all night. The excerpt as a whole shows her contempt for the loom turning into respect, which is what B says.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ada to her grandmother. The knot is something Ada discovers, and the text never describes what the grandmother felt. The excerpt is about Ada's change of heart.

C.why: You picked a detail from the first sentence. The speed comparison only explains why Ada looked down on the loom. It isn't what the excerpt is for.

D.why: You read in a feeling the text never states. Nothing suggests Ada resents the mill. The mill only comes up as the point of comparison behind her early view of the loom.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Rydell's 1958 poem "To a Fern in Shale." The speaker addresses a fossilized fern.

You have been told, small frond, that you are gone, / pressed flat, a rumor in the stone. / But I have seen your cousins in the ravine / unrolling every April, green / as if no age had passed. So do not grieve / the weight above you: what you were still lives.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To lament that the fern's kind vanished long ago beneath layers of stone
To celebrate the speaker's discovery of living ferns growing in a ravine
To explain how ferns came to be preserved in shale over long periods
To reassure the fern that its kind has endured despite its own apparent loss
items.explanation: The poem opens with what the fern "has been told": that it is gone. After "But," the speaker offers evidence against that view (living ferns every April), and the poem ends by telling the fern "do not grieve" because "what you were still lives." The tone is consoling, and the fern is the one being consoled.

A.why: You flipped the tone. The first two lines state a belief that sounds like a lament, but the rest of the poem argues against it and tells the fern not to grieve.

B.why: You shifted the focus from the addressee to the speaker. The ravine ferns are evidence offered to comfort the fossil. They are not the poem's subject.

C.why: You credited the poem with an explanation it never gives. "Pressed flat" and "stone" name the fern's condition but don't describe how fossilization happens.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Inês Carvalho's 1987 memoir. Carvalho's father was a surveyor who drew maps for the provincial government.

My father's maps were famous in the ministry for their precision; not a stream was misplaced. As a child, I assumed he loved the land the way he loved his instruments, coolly and exactly. However, clearing his desk after he died, I found a second set of sheets, never submitted. On them he had marked where the Almeida girl drowned, where my mother first agreed to walk with him, where the best figs grew.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey the narrator's discovery that the father's bond with the land was deeply personal
To portray the father's pride in the precision that earned praise from the ministry
To suggest that the father hid the private maps for fear of the ministry's disapproval
To show that the narrator's childhood view of the father was confirmed by the desk's contents
items.explanation: The narrator describes a long-held belief (the father loved the land "coolly and exactly"), then "However" brings in the private maps full of memories and personal landmarks. The excerpt as a whole shows the narrator learning that the father's attachment to the land went well beyond the official measurements.

B.why: You focused on the father's reputation, which appears only in the opening. The text never says the father felt proud, and the passage moves past that precision to what the narrator finds.

C.why: You supplied a motive the text never gives. The sheets were "never submitted," but nothing says why.

D.why: You got the direction of the turn backward. "However" marks the discovery as a correction of the childhood belief, not a confirmation of it.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Lionel Achterberg's 1974 short story "The Trench." Maren, a graduate student, is excavating a Bronze Age site with her professor, Dr. Hale.

Dr. Hale had spent thirty seasons at the site. When Maren's trowel struck the rim of a clay bowl, he knelt beside her and said nothing for a long while. Maren waited for praise. Instead he asked her to describe what she saw, then to describe it again, more slowly. By the third telling she noticed a thumbprint pressed into the rim, and she understood that he had not been testing her; he had been giving her the find.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey Dr. Hale's long devotion to a site where he has worked for decades
To depict Maren's disappointment that her discovery went without any praise
To portray Maren's realization that her mentor's silence let her claim the find
To explain how archaeologists work out who made an ancient clay object
items.explanation: The setup and the final sentence both center on Maren. She expects praise, gets questions instead, and at last understands that Hale "had been giving her the find." The excerpt builds toward her new understanding of his silence.

A.why: You shifted the focus to the professor. His thirty seasons are background. The excerpt's point is what Maren comes to understand about him.

B.why: You stopped reading halfway through. Maren does wait for praise, but the ending replaces that expectation with understanding, so disappointment isn't what the excerpt conveys.

D.why: You treated a story as a method guide. The thumbprint is a detail Maren notices, and the text never explains any technique for identifying a maker.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Clara Ondaatje's 1996 poem "Burn Season." The speaker addresses a child walking with her through a recently burned forest.

Do not look away from the blackened hill, / the pines like struck matches, the hush where the jays were. / Look closer: beneath the ash the fireweed / has already pushed its red thumbs up. / The lodgepole cones, sealed shut for years, / opened only in this heat. / What frightens you is how a forest begins.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn the child about the destruction that fire can bring to a forest
To encourage the child to see the burned hill as a place of renewal
To mourn the loss of the birds that once filled the forest on the hill
To explain why lodgepole pines must have fire in order to reproduce
items.explanation: The poem opens on destruction, then turns at "Look closer" to new growth, and closes by recasting the frightening scene as "how a forest begins." The speaker's commands ("Do not look away," "Look closer") are encouraging, not cautionary, and they ask the child to see the burn as a beginning.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The opening images are grim, but the speaker uses them to lead the child from fear toward seeing renewal, not to warn.

C.why: You took one image as the whole poem. The missing jays are part of the opening description of damage, and the poem moves on to new growth.

D.why: You claimed more than the poem says. It notes that the cones opened in the heat but never says the pines need fire, and its purpose isn't to explain biology.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Anneliese Brandt's 1909 novel The Copyist. Teodor copies out orchestral parts from the manuscripts of the composer Voss.

Teodor had copied Voss's scores for eleven years and believed his task purely mechanical: a note in, a note out. But in the slow movement of the new symphony he found a passage that could not be right, the oboe climbing where every rule said it must fall. To correct it would take a single stroke. He copied it as written, and all night the note sang in his head, until he could not tell whether it was Voss's mistake or his genius.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray a copyist left torn over whether a passage he reproduced is a flaw or brilliance
To convey a composer's confidence in breaking the accepted rules of composition
To show a copyist correcting a composer's error despite doubts about his own judgment
To depict a copyist's resentment of years of careful work that went unrecognized
items.explanation: Teodor, the focus of the setup, starts out believing his work is mechanical. After "But," an odd passage unsettles him, and the excerpt ends with him unable to decide between "mistake" and "genius." What it shows is his being torn.

B.why: You moved the focus from Teodor to Voss. The text never shows Voss's attitude. It shows only Teodor's uncertainty about what Voss meant.

C.why: You missed the key action. Teodor "copied it as written." He considers correcting the note but doesn't do it.

D.why: You added an emotion the text doesn't give. The eleven years set up his belief that the work is mechanical, and nothing suggests he resents it.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Dorothy Quill's 1968 memoir of years spent in an industrial metals laboratory.

In the laboratory we were taught to trust the numbers: tensile strength, hardness, the exact temperature at which a steel turns brittle. I trusted them. Yet the old blacksmith who came each spring to sharpen our shop tools could judge a blade's temper by its color alone: straw, then bronze, then a blue like evening. He had never read a chart.
