items.stimulus:
The following text is from Hollis Arden's 2017 poem "To a First-Year Grower." The speaker addresses a new farmer.

You will want the seed to hurry.
Everyone does. The first spring,
you'll kneel each dawn to check the rows
as if watching could pull green from clay.
It can't. But here is what I learned
from forty harvests of beans and doubt:
the waiting is not wasted. Under you,
the roots are doing arithmetic
you cannot see, and by July
the field will show its work.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn a new grower that checking the rows too often will damage the young crop
To lament the many seasons the speaker spent doubting whether the beans would grow
To encourage a new grower to trust that growth is happening even when it is unseen
To explain the process by which bean roots draw nutrients out of heavy clay soil
items.explanation: The poem speaks to the new grower. It admits that impatience is natural, and then after 'But' comes the real message: 'the waiting is not wasted,' because the roots are working out of sight and 'by July / the field will show its work.' The tone is reassuring, so the purpose is to encourage the grower to trust growth they can't see yet.

A.why: You turned encouragement into a warning. The speaker says watching can't speed the crop up. The poem never says watching harms it.

B.why: 'Forty harvests of beans and doubt' is the speaker's credential, not a lament. The poem looks ahead with hope, so this choice gets the tone backward.

D.why: 'The roots are doing arithmetic' is a metaphor. The poem never explains how roots take up nutrients, so you've credited it with content it doesn't have.

The following text is adapted from Oona Maris's 2016 short story "The Eyepiece." Teodor is an amateur astronomer.

The following text is from Ansel Burke's 2021 poem "For the Volunteers Pulling Buckthorn." The speaker addresses people removing an invasive shrub from a forest.

To explain why buckthorn outcompetes native plants such as oak and trillium on hillsides

C.why: The poem does mention that the volunteers will move away, but only as a reason to 'pull anyway.' Reading it as a lament gets the tone wrong.

items.stimulus: Pteropods, often called sea butterflies, are snails that have abandoned the seafloor. To show that pteropods move in much the same way garden snails do

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: The theremin, invented by the Russian physicist Léon Theremin around 1920, is one of the few instruments played without being touched. The performer moves one hand near an upright antenna to change the pitch and the other hand near a looped antenna to change the volume. Its eerie, wavering tone made it a favorite of film composers in the 1950s, who used it to signal the arrival of aliens and other strange visitors.
items.stem: Which choice describes what the whole passage does, not just one sentence of it?

To explain how a theremin player controls the volume of each note
To argue that the theremin deserves more respect from trained musicians
To compare the theremin with instruments that are played by touch
items.explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first says what the theremin is, the second says how it is played, and the third says how it was used. items.stimulus: The mimic octopus, first recorded off the coast of Indonesia in 1998, survives by pretending to be other animals. To show that the octopus imitates only animals that are venomous

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: For centuries, physicians regarded the thymus, a small organ behind the breastbone, as having no real purpose. In 1961, however, the immunologist Jacques Miller showed that mice whose thymus was removed shortly after birth developed badly weakened immune systems. Researchers now know that the thymus is where T cells, a type of white blood cell, mature before they travel through the body to fight infection.
items.stem: Which choice describes what the whole passage does, not just one sentence of it?
choices: To describe how an organ once thought useless was found to matter
To explain the method Miller used in his experiments on young mice
To argue that physicians should study other organs thought useless
To show that physicians today still regard the thymus as useless
items.explanation: The passage moves from an old belief (the thymus has no purpose) to a 'however' (Miller's finding) to today's understanding (T cells mature there). All three sentences trace how ideas about one organ changed, and choice A covers that whole arc. Reading past the old belief to the correction that follows is the move you need for 'main purpose' questions built on an 'old view, then the correction' pattern.

D.why: You stopped at the first sentence and missed the 'however.' The old belief is the view the passage corrects. The last sentence shows that researchers now know what the thymus does.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: The hagfish, an eel-shaped scavenger of the deep seafloor, is known above all for its slime. That single secretion, released from glands along the animal's sides, does several jobs at once. To argue that hagfish slime is the most effective defense of any marine animal
To present a distinctive hagfish secretion and the range of uses it has
To compare the strength of hagfish slime threads with that of synthetic fibers

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Cartographer Teodora Vasić spent three decades mapping a landscape that most of her contemporaries left partly blank: the limestone highlands of the western Balkans, where rivers vanish into sinkholes and resurface miles away. Rather than survey only the ground's surface, Vasić gathered cave explorers' notes and the results of dye-tracing experiments to sketch the underground routes the water was thought to follow, marking uncertain paths with dotted lines. Her 1958 atlas, the first to show these hidden connections across the whole region, is still consulted by researchers today.

To note that Vasić's 1958 atlas was the first to show the region's hidden connections

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Few tools in sports science are as simple as the rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scale, on which athletes give a number to how hard an effort feels. Developed by psychologist Gunnar Borg beginning in the 1960s, the scale needs no equipment. Yet a subjective score can track physical strain surprisingly well: RPE values tend to rise along with heart rate and blood lactate. Coaches now use the scale to adjust daily training loads, and researchers rely on it in settings, such as remote expeditions, where laboratory measurements are impractical.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To describe a simple measurement tool and the reasons for its wide use
To demonstrate that subjective ratings are as precise as laboratory tests
To explain why remote expeditions cannot use laboratory equipment
items.explanation: The text introduces the RPE scale as a simple tool and then explains why people use it: it needs no equipment, it tracks real strain well, and it works where labs can't. Coaches and researchers both use it. Choice B covers both the tool and the reasons for its use, and its neutral verb 'describe' matches the passage's tone.

items.stimulus: A fallen tree in a temperate rainforest can look like the end of a story. In the forests of the Pacific Northwest, however, a toppled hemlock or spruce often becomes a "nurse log." items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Qanats, gently sloping tunnels that carry groundwater from beneath hillsides to distant fields, are often treated as relics of ancient Persia. Yet thousands still operate in Iran and Oman, and their design helps explain why. Because the water moves by gravity, a qanat needs no pumps or fuel. Because it flows underground, little is lost to evaporation, even in desert heat. And because a qanat collects only the water that seeps into it from the surrounding rock, it tends not to drain the aquifer it taps.

To describe a traditional water system and the features behind its continued use

items.stimulus: Collagraphy is a printmaking method in which textured materials are glued onto a board, inked, and pressed onto paper. items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Hydrologists call a river a "losing stream" when it feeds water into the ground beneath it instead of drawing water from it. Streams are not fixed in one category, though: a stream can shift between gaining and losing as the water table around it rises and falls. The Arroyo Pinto in northern Mexico is a case in point. During the summer rains, groundwater near its channel sits high enough to seep into the stream. By late winter, the surrounding aquifer has dropped so far that the arroyo's water drains downward, and the channel runs dry within a few kilometers.

To argue that losing streams are more vulnerable to drought than hydrologists have assumed
To show that the Arroyo Pinto remains a losing stream during every season of the year
items.explanation: The text defines a 'losing stream,' states the general rule that streams can switch between gaining and losing, and then uses the Arroyo Pinto to illustrate that rule. Choice A covers the definition, the rule, and the example together.

B.why: You chose one real detail. The summer rains appear only as part of the example, and the text is about the stream's changing relationship to groundwater, not about the rains.

C.why: You read in an argument the text never makes. It says nothing about drought vulnerability or about what hydrologists have wrongly assumed. It only explains and illustrates.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: For decades, the fossil plant Velatophyllum, known only from scattered leaf impressions in Antarctic rock, was assumed to be a fern. However, specimens recovered in 2019 preserve small seeds attached to the leaf bases, and ferns reproduce by spores, not seeds. Those seeds have thick protective coats, and the plant's leaves grew in tight, leathery clusters. Together, these features have led paleobotanists to reclassify Velatophyllum as an early seed plant, one apparently suited to surviving long, dark polar winters.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To argue that most plant fossils found in Antarctica have been misidentified by researchers
To describe how new specimens changed scientists' view of what kind of plant a fossil was
To show that the 2019 specimens confirmed that Velatophyllum was an unusual kind of fern
items.explanation: The text opens with a long-held assumption that Velatophyllum was a fern, turns on 'However' to the 2019 seed-bearing specimens, and ends with the plant's reclassification. Choice C covers that old-view-to-new-view structure for the fossil as a whole.

A.why: You picked a supporting fact. The point about spores is there only to show why seeds rule out a fern. It is a step in the reasoning, not the text's purpose.

B.why: You generalized beyond the text. It discusses one misidentified fossil and says nothing about most Antarctic plant fossils, and it doesn't argue a broad claim.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Metallic glasses are alloys cooled so quickly that their atoms freeze in a disordered arrangement instead of forming crystals, which makes them unusually strong and springy. For decades, however, they could be produced only as thin ribbons or small pieces, because thicker samples cooled too slowly at their centers and crystallized. Engineer Hana Okafor's team has now developed an iron-based alloy that stays glassy at thicknesses of several centimeters. Its first commercial use, in springs for precision watches, exploits the material's ability to flex millions of times without permanently deforming.

To argue that metallic glasses will soon replace steel in most kinds of industrial manufacturing
To show that metallic glasses are weaker than ordinary metals but far more flexible than them
To describe a class of materials, a long-standing obstacle to making them, and a recent advance

To show that the Ferrand Songbook's songs were copied once and never revised afterward

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: In some languages, a speaker cannot simply report that something happened; the grammar itself requires the speaker to indicate how they know it. Linguists call this feature evidentiality. In Tamuri, a language spoken by about 12,000 people in the Andean highlands, one verb suffix marks events the speaker witnessed, another marks events learned from others, and a third marks conclusions drawn from clues, such as wet ground indicating rain. Leaving the suffix off is not an option: a Tamuri sentence without one is ungrammatical.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe a grammatical feature and illustrate it with a language that requires its use
To explain how Tamuri speakers conclude from wet ground that rain must have fallen
To argue that languages with evidentiality let speakers communicate more accurately
To show that Tamuri speakers may decide for themselves whether to mark their sources
items.explanation: The text begins with a general statement that some grammars require speakers to mark how they know something, names that feature evidentiality, and then uses Tamuri's three suffixes as a concrete example. Choice A covers both the general feature and the illustration.

B.why: You picked the most vivid detail. The wet-ground example only illustrates one of Tamuri's three suffixes and is not what the text as a whole is about.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text explains the feature neutrally and never claims it makes communication more accurate.

D.why: You missed the final sentence. It says leaving the suffix off is 'not an option,' so marking the source is required, not optional.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Surviving weavers' pattern books usually preserve textile designs but reveal little about the people who made them. To argue that the spread of factory cloth drove rural weaving households into poverty
To show that Rennick's notebooks, like most pattern books, contain only design samples
To describe a weaver's records and explain why they are valuable to historians of work
items.explanation: The text contrasts typical pattern books with Rennick's notebooks, lists what she recorded beyond designs, and ends with how historians have used those records. Choice D covers both what the notebooks contain and why they matter.

A.why: You chose a detail that really is in the text but is too narrow. The woolen samples are mentioned in passing, and the text's interest is in the business records kept alongside them.

B.why: You went beyond the text. It says the notebooks show how one household earned and lost money, and it doesn't argue that factory cloth impoverished rural weavers in general.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: For decades, earthquake monitoring in rural Peru depended on a handful of costly stations spaced hundreds of kilometers apart. Seismologist Rosa Quispe Mamani has spent fifteen years filling the gaps between them. Her project, Red Escolar, installs palm-sized motion sensors in village schools, where teachers keep the devices powered and students log the readings each week. The network now includes more than 300 sites, and its records helped researchers locate a fault segment near Ayacucho that the older stations had never detected. Quispe also trains teachers to explain local earthquake risk to families.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that national agencies should replace their costly stations with sensors placed in schools
To describe a seismologist's effort to widen earthquake monitoring by placing sensors in rural schools
To explain how researchers used school-based records to locate a previously undetected fault segment
To describe how village students designed low-cost sensors to fill the gaps in a national network
items.explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first sentence names a gap in monitoring. The rest present Quispe's project: how it works, how big it has grown, what it found, and the teacher training that goes with it. Each one adds to a profile of her effort to extend monitoring through rural schools. The text informs and never argues, so the neutral verb 'describe' fits, and choice B covers the whole passage.

A.why: You picked a verb that's too strong. The text reports what Red Escolar has done but never says the older stations should be replaced, or makes any recommendation at all. 'Argue' needs an opinion the passage doesn't state.

C.why: You took a true detail for the purpose. The fault segment near Ayacucho is one result mentioned in one sentence. It can't explain why the text also covers the gap in monitoring, how the sensors are maintained, or the teacher training.

D.why: You misread who does what. Quispe's project installs the sensors, and students only log the weekly readings. Nothing in the text says students designed the devices.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Since 2009, the volunteers of the Marsh Line Atlas have mapped a stretch of Louisiana coastline that loses land nearly every year. Working from kayaks with handheld GPS units, they trace shorelines, abandoned canals, and the foundations of old fishing camps, then publish each season's survey as a free printed sheet. A map can keep a record of a place after the place itself is gone. Several islands on the group's 2011 sheet are now open water, and former residents use that sheet to find family homesites that no current map shows.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how former residents find family homesites by consulting older printed coastal maps
To argue that government agencies should rely on volunteers to map rapidly changing coastlines
To describe a volunteer group that maps a shrinking coastline and the lasting record its maps provide
To describe how a volunteer group uses satellite images to predict where the coastline will erode next
items.explanation: The text introduces the Marsh Line Atlas, explains how its volunteers work, and then states a general idea: a map can preserve a place after the place is gone. The 2011 islands and the former residents are an example of that idea. So the passage is both a profile of the group and an account of why its maps matter. Choice C is the only option that covers both parts, and 'describe' matches the passage's neutral tone.

A.why: You chose the last detail in the passage and treated it as the purpose. Former residents finding homesites is the example of the broader point, not what the whole text is for. This choice leaves out the group, its methods, and its seasonal surveys.

B.why: You read an argument into a passage that only informs. The text never mentions government agencies and never recommends who should do the mapping, so 'argue' claims more than the text supports.

D.why: You got the group's methods wrong. The volunteers survey from kayaks with handheld GPS units and record what is there now. The text says nothing about satellite images or forecasting future erosion.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Many athletes sit in cold water after hard workouts because they believe it speeds recovery. To test this belief, researchers had 24 runners complete an intense track session. Half of the runners then sat in 10°C water for ten minutes, and the other half rested on a bench. The next day, every runner ran a timed 200-meter sprint. The two groups' times were nearly identical, which suggests that the cold soak gave no advantage in next-day speed.
items.stem: What is this text mainly doing?
choices: Describing a study that found cold-water soaks did not make runners faster the next day
Arguing that the researchers used too few runners to support any conclusion at all
Describing a study that left unclear whether cold-water soaks affect next-day speed
Explaining how cold water changes runners' muscle tissue after a hard workout
items.explanation: The text sets up a belief, describes a test (cold soak or rest), and ends with a clear result: the sprint times were nearly identical. It only reports. It never criticises anything. So its job is to describe a study and give that study's actual finding. Doing this one step is what you need for the real exam question 'Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?' when the passage walks through an experiment.

B.why: You read evaluation into a text that only reports. The passage never judges the study's size or design. A 'criticize' or 'argue' choice needs the author to actually push back on something.

C.why: You stopped at 'describing a study' and didn't check the result. The last sentence gives a clear answer: the times were nearly identical and the soak gave no advantage. Saying the question was left unclear misstates the finding.

D.why: You picked an 'explain how' choice for a text that never explains a mechanism. Nothing in the passage covers what cold does to muscle. It only compares sprint times.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: When clover grows in a field, soil bacteria called rhizobia enter its roots and form small swellings known as nodules. Inside these nodules, the bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form that plants can absorb. In return, the clover feeds the bacteria sugars it makes through photosynthesis. When the clover later dies and decays, the nitrogen stored in its tissues is released into the soil, where the next crop planted in that field can take it up.
items.stem: What is this text mainly doing?
choices: Comparing how clover and other crops each take up nitrogen from the soil
Arguing that farmers should plant clover instead of buying chemical fertilizer
Explaining how clover, with the help of bacteria, adds usable nitrogen to soil
Explaining how clover removes nitrogen from soil, leaving less for later crops
items.explanation: This is a process text. Bacteria enter the roots, form nodules, and turn air nitrogen into a usable form. The clover feeds them, and when it decays the nitrogen goes into the soil for the next crop. The right choice names the whole mechanism from start to finish. On the real 'main purpose' question, a process passage almost always calls for an 'explain how' answer that covers every step, not just one of them.

A.why: This is the classic trap for process texts. The choice claims a comparison, but the text explains only one plant. 'The next crop' is mentioned only as the receiver of the nitrogen, never as something being compared.

B.why: You turned an explanation into a recommendation. The text never mentions fertilizer and never tells farmers what to do. It only describes how the process works.

D.why: You flipped the direction of the process. The text says clover adds nitrogen to the soil when it decays, so later crops get more nitrogen, not less.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Folklorists long assumed that the "drowned bell" legend, in which a sunken church bell is heard ringing beneath a lake, first spread through printed collections and was only later retold aloud. To test this, folklorist Ines Marlow compared 140 dated versions of the tale. She found that spoken versions recorded by interviewers appeared, on average, eleven years before the earliest printed version from the same region. Her results indicate that the legend traveled by word of mouth first.
items.stem: What is this text mainly doing?
choices: Describing a study whose results confirm that the legend first spread through print
Describing a study whose results challenge the view that the legend began in print
Arguing that every folk legend spreads by word of mouth before it appears in print
Explaining why the legend of the sunken bell became popular in so many regions

So the text describes a study whose result corrects the old view. When a real 'main purpose' passage starts with 'long assumed', check whether the study supports or overturns that assumption before you pick a choice.

A.why: You matched 'describing a study' and missed which way the result went. The spoken versions came about eleven years before the printed ones. That goes against the print-first view rather than confirming it.

C.why: You stretched one legend into a rule about all legends. Marlow studied only the drowned-bell tale, so the text supports a claim about that tale and nothing more.

D.why: You answered a question the text never takes up. The study is about the order in which the legend spread, not why people liked it or how far it reached.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Ecologists have traditionally assumed that earthworms in northern hardwood forests benefit tree seedlings by speeding the release of nutrients from fallen leaves. To test this assumption, ecologist Mireille Okafor fenced forty forest plots, removed the worms from half of them, and tracked sugar maple seedlings in every plot for three years. To argue that earthworms should be removed from northern hardwood forests in order to protect seedlings
items.explanation: The text opens with what ecologists have 'traditionally assumed' (worms help seedlings), then describes Okafor's experiment, and ends with a clear result: seedlings survived better without worms. items.stimulus: Most earthquakes release built-up stress within seconds. Along some subduction zones, however, the boundary between two plates can slip over weeks without producing strong shaking. In these slow slip events, fluids squeezed out of the descending plate collect along the fault and reduce the friction that normally locks the plates together. To question the view that slow slip events can add stress to neighboring segments of a fault

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: Nutritionists have debated whether eating a meal's vegetables before its starches changes how the body handles sugar. To test this, researcher Aiko Tanabe served thirty adults identical meals on two separate days; on one day they ate the vegetables first, and on the other they ate the rice first. When vegetables came first, participants' blood sugar over the following two hours rose about 30 percent less, on average. Tanabe concluded that the order of foods, not just their content, can affect the body's response to a meal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe an experiment that left open the question of whether food order affects blood sugar
To argue that adults should avoid eating rice at any meal that also includes vegetables
To explain why rice causes blood sugar to rise more quickly than most vegetables do
To describe an experiment indicating that the order in which foods are eaten can matter
items.explanation: The text names a debate, describes Tanabe's two-day experiment, and reports a clear result: blood sugar rose less when vegetables came first. The correct choice describes the experiment and states its result accurately.

A.why: 'Describe an experiment' is right, but the rest is wrong. The study found a clear difference of about 30 percent and led to a firm conclusion. Check the claim about the result, not just the verb.

B.why: You turned a finding into advice. The study was about the order of foods, not about avoiding rice, and it gives no dietary recommendation.

C.why: You went for background the text doesn't give. It never explains why rice affects blood sugar the way it does. The focus is the effect of eating order.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
items.stimulus: It has been widely assumed that workers who switch employers give up the wage gains that come with experience at one company. Economist Rosa Adeyemi examined the payroll records of 200,000 warehouse workers and found that those who changed employers at least once in five years earned, on average, 9 percent more than those who stayed, largely because new employers offered higher starting pay to attract experienced hires. Adeyemi's findings suggest that, at least in this industry, moving between employers can raise rather than reduce earnings.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To present a finding that runs counter to a common assumption about workers who change employers
To present a finding that workers who change employers lose the pay they gained through experience
To explain how warehouse companies decide what starting pay to offer the workers they newly hire
To argue that workers in every industry would earn more if they changed employers more often
items.explanation: The text starts with what has been 'widely assumed' and then reports Adeyemi's finding that workers who switched employers earned more. The study goes against the assumption, which is what this choice says.

B.why: You took the old assumption for the finding. The study found the reverse: workers who switched earned more on average.

C.why: You picked up a supporting detail. Higher starting pay helps explain the result, but the text doesn't describe how companies set pay.

D.why: You generalized past the sample. The text limits the finding to warehouse workers ('at least in this industry'), and switching more often was never tested.

items.stimulus: Folklorists have long wondered how well an oral tale keeps its shape as it passes from one teller to the next. To find out, Ilse Marrow asked a storyteller in a Frisian village to tell a local legend to a listener, who then retold it to another listener, until the tale had passed through fifteen people. Names and settings shifted almost at once, but the tale's sequence of three trials and its ending survived every retelling. choices: To describe an experiment showing that oral tales lose their plots after only a few retellings
To compare the legends told in Frisian villages with legends told in other parts of Europe

To argue that the legend Marrow studied is older than any other folktale told in Europe
items.explanation: The text opens with a question, describes Marrow's retelling chain, and reports that names and settings changed while the plot structure survived all fifteen retellings. The correct choice describes the experiment and states that result.

B.why: You assumed a comparison. The text follows one legend through one chain of tellers and never mentions legends from other regions.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A materials scientist builds a composite strip from 5 identical layered segments and then trims 4 millimeters from one end. In the scientist's model, the strip's final length, in millimeters, is given by the expression $5(2x + 3) - 4$, where $x$ is the thickness setting used for each segment.
items.stem: The expression $5(2x + 3) - 4$ is equivalent to $ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: Distribute the 5 to both terms: $5(2x + 3) = 10x + 15$. Then subtract 4: $10x + 15 - 4 = 10x + 11$. Matching this to $ax + b$ gives $a = 10$ and $b = 11$.

A.why: You multiplied only the $2x$ by 5 and left the 3 alone, which gives $10x + 3 - 4 = 10x - 1$. The 5 multiplies everything inside the parentheses, so the 3 becomes 15.

B.why: 10 is the coefficient of $x$, so it is $a$. The question asks for $b$, the constant term.

D.why: You expanded $5(2x + 3)$ to $10x + 15$ correctly but stopped there. You still need to subtract the 4 to get the constant term.

items.stem: The expression $(x + 6)(x + 2)$ is equivalent to $x^2 + bx + c$, where $b$ and $c$ are constants. What is the value of $b + c$?

items.stem: The expression $3(x^2 + 2x - 7)$ is equivalent to $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants. What is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: Distribute the 3 to every term: $3x^2 + 6x - 21$. So $a = 3$, $b = 6$, and $c = -21$, and $a + b + c = 3 + 6 - 21 = -12$.

D.why: You applied the 3 only to the $x^2$ term, which gives $3x^2 + 2x - 7$ and a sum of $-2$. The 3 multiplies all three terms.

items.stimulus: A musicologist studying string tension in early harpsichords uses the expression $x^2 - 49$ to compare a string's tension at setting $x$ with a reference tension of 49 units.
items.stem: The expression $x^2 - 49$ is equivalent to $(x + k)(x - k)$, where $k$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Expand the target form: $(x + k)(x - k) = x^2 - k^2$. Matching constant terms gives $k^2 = 49$, so $k = 7$ or $k = -7$. Since $k$ is positive, $k = 7$.

A.why: $(-7)^2 = 49$ does satisfy $k^2 = 49$, but the question says $k$ is positive, which rules out $-7$.

C.why: You divided 49 by 2 when you needed to take its square root. Since $(x + k)(x - k) = x^2 - k^2$, $k$ has to satisfy $k^2 = 49$.

D.why: 49 is $k^2$, which you get when you match the constant terms. Take the square root to find $k$ itself.

items.stem: The expression $2(x^2 + kx)$ is equivalent to $2x^2 + 10x$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: Distribute: $2(x^2 + kx) = 2x^2 + 2kx$. Setting the $x$-coefficients equal gives $2k = 10$, so $k = 5$.

B.why: You subtracted 2 from 10 when you needed to divide. The 2 multiplies $k$, so solve $2k = 10$ by dividing.

C.why: You multiplied only the $x^2$ term by 2 and then matched $k$ directly to 10. The 2 also multiplies $kx$, which makes the $x$-term $2kx$.

D.why: You multiplied 10 by 2 when you should have divided. Undoing $2k = 10$ means dividing both sides by 2.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stem: If $3(x + 4) = ax + b$ for every value of $x$, what is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: Multiply the 3 by both terms inside the parentheses: $3(x + 4) = 3x + 12$. Then line it up with $ax + b$. The constant terms have to match, so $b = 12$. This is the first step in every SAT question that says an expression 'is equivalent to' a form with unknown constants. You expand first, then compare.

A.why: 3 is the coefficient of $x$, so it's $a$. The question asks for the constant term $b$.

B.why: You multiplied the 3 by $x$ but not by the 4, so the 4 went through unchanged. The 3 multiplies everything inside the parentheses, which makes the constant $3 \cdot 4 = 12$.

C.why: You added 3 and 4 instead of multiplying. A number next to parentheses means multiply, so the constant is $3 \cdot 4 = 12$.

items.stimulus: A folklore studies student models how many variants of a regional legend appear in an archive as a function of $x$, the number of decades since the legend was first written down. The student's model is built from two parts, and combining them gives the expression $3(2x-5)^2 - 4(x+1)(x-3)$.
items.stem: If $3(2x-5)^2 - 4(x+1)(x-3)$ is equivalent to $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, what is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: First expand the squared part completely: $(2x-5)^2 = 4x^2 - 20x + 25$. The 3 multiplies all of it, so you get $12x^2 - 60x + 75$. Next, $(x+1)(x-3) = x^2 - 2x - 3$, and multiplying by 4 gives $4x^2 - 8x - 12$. When you subtract, the minus sign applies to every term: $12x^2 - 60x + 75 - 4x^2 + 8x + 12 = 8x^2 - 52x + 87$. Matching coefficients gives $a = 8$, $b = -52$, $c = 87$, so $a + b + c = 8 - 52 + 87 = 43$. Shortcut: $a + b + c$ is the value of the polynomial at $x = 1$. Substituting $x = 1$ into the original gives $3(-3)^2 - 4(2)(-2) = 27 + 16 = 43$.

items.stimulus: An astronomy student simplifies a ratio that appears in a model of how a variable star's brightness changes over time.
items.stem: For $x \neq \frac{3}{2}$, the expression $\frac{8x^2 - 2x - 7}{2x - 3}$ is equivalent to $ax + b + \frac{k}{2x - 3}$, where $a$, $b$, and $k$ are constants. What is the value of $a + b + k$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $2x - 3$: $8x^2 - 2x - 7 = (ax + b)(2x - 3) + k$. Expanding the right side gives $2ax^2 + (2b - 3a)x - 3b + k$. Match the $x^2$ terms: $2a = 8$, so $a = 4$. Match the $x$ terms: $2b - 12 = -2$, so $b = 5$. Match the constants: $-15 + k = -7$, so $k = 8$. The question asks for the sum, so $a + b + k = 4 + 5 + 8 = 17$.

items.stem: In the equation above, $p$ and $q$ are constants, and the equation is true for all values of $x$. What is the value of $q - p$?

items.stimulus: A linguist models how many distinct word forms appear in a growing transcript of an endangered language. The model uses the equation $3(x + 4)(2x - 5) = ax^2 + bx + c$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, what is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: First expand the product: $(x + 4)(2x - 5) = 2x^2 + 3x - 20$. Then multiply every term by 3 to get $6x^2 + 9x - 60$. So $a = 6$, $b = 9$, and $c = -60$, which gives $a + b + c = 6 + 9 - 60 = -45$. To check, put $x = 1$ into the left side: $3(5)(-3) = -45$.

A.why: You found $c = -60$ and stopped there. The question asks for the sum $a + b + c$, not the constant term alone.

C.why: You expanded $(x + 4)(2x - 5)$ but never multiplied by the 3 in front, so you added the coefficients of $2x^2 + 3x - 20$. The 3 multiplies the whole expression.

D.why: You made a sign error in the middle term and got $-3x$ instead of $+3x$ ($-5x + 8x = 3x$). That gave $6x^2 - 9x - 60$.

items.stimulus: A public health analyst fits a curve to weekly clinic visits during a flu season and rewrites it in vertex form: $2x^2 + 12x + 23 = a(x + h)^2 + k$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $h$, and $k$ are constants, what is the value of $a + h + k$?
items.explanation: Factor 2 out of the $x$-terms: $2(x^2 + 6x) + 23$. Completing the square inside the parentheses gives $2[(x + 3)^2 - 9] + 23$. The 2 multiplies the $-9$ as well, so this becomes $2(x + 3)^2 - 18 + 23 = 2(x + 3)^2 + 5$. So $a = 2$, $h = 3$, and $k = 5$, and $a + h + k = 10$.

B.why: You found $h = 3$ and $k = 5$ but left $a$ out of the sum. The question asks for all three constants.

C.why: You subtracted 9 instead of $2 \cdot 9 = 18$, so you got $k = 14$. The factor of 2 multiplies everything inside the brackets, including the $-9$.

D.why: You took $h = -3$ because the vertex is at $x = -3$. In the form $(x + h)^2$, the expression $(x + 3)^2$ means $h = +3$.

items.stimulus: An astronomer compares two models of the brightness of a variable star. The difference between the models is written as $(3x - 2)^2 - (x + 4)^2 = ax^2 + bx + c$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, what is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: Expand each square: $(3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 - 12x + 4$ and $(x + 4)^2 = x^2 + 8x + 16$. Subtract all three terms of the second square: $9x^2 - 12x + 4 - x^2 - 8x - 16 = 8x^2 - 20x - 12$. So $a + b + c = 8 - 20 - 12 = -24$. To check, put $x = 1$ into the left side: $1 - 25 = -24$.

B.why: You found $c = -12$ and stopped. The question asks for $a + b + c$.

D.why: You squared each binomial as the sum of two squares, for example $(3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 + 4$, and left out the middle terms.

This works because $a(1)^2 + b(1) + c$ is exactly $a + b + c$.

items.explanation: Expand the target form: $2(x - h)^2 + k = 2x^2 - 4hx + 2h^2 + k$. Matching the $x$ terms gives $-4h = -12$, so $h = 3$. Matching the constant terms gives $2(3)^2 + k = 23$, so $18 + k = 23$ and $k = 5$. So $h + k = 8$.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A materials scientist uses the expression $3(2x - 5)(x + 4)$ to model the stress in a test beam, where $x$ is the applied load, in kilonewtons.
items.stem: The expression $3(2x - 5)(x + 4)$ is equivalent to $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants. What is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: First expand the two binomials: $(2x - 5)(x + 4) = 2x^2 + 8x - 5x - 20 = 2x^2 + 3x - 20$. Then multiply every term by 3 to get $6x^2 + 9x - 60$. So $a = 6$, $b = 9$, and $c = -60$, which gives $a + b + c = 6 + 9 - 60 = -45$.

A.why: You found $c = -60$ correctly, but the question asks for $a + b + c$, not just the constant term. You stopped one step too early.

C.why: You expanded $(2x - 5)(x + 4)$ to $2x^2 + 3x - 20$ but never multiplied by 3. That gives $2 + 3 - 20 = -15$.

D.why: You multiplied the 3 into only the first term of $2x - 5$, which gives $(6x - 5)(x + 4) = 6x^2 + 19x - 20$. The 3 multiplies the whole product, so every coefficient has to be tripled.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus:
An astronomer fitting a model to a variable star's brightness curve writes the following equation.

$(kx + 3)(2x - 5) = 10x^2 + bx - 15$
items.stem: In the given equation, $k$ and $b$ are constants. If the equation is true for all values of $x$, what is the value of $b$?
items.explanation: Expanding the left side gives $2kx^2 - 5kx + 6x - 15$. Match the $x^2$ coefficients: $2k = 10$, so $k = 5$. The $x$ coefficient on the left is $-5k + 6 = -25 + 6 = -19$, so $b = -19$.

A.why: You treated the product $3 \cdot 2x$ as $-6x$, which gives $-25 - 6 = -31$. That product is positive, $+6x$.

B.why: You counted only the $-5kx = -25x$ term. Both cross-products contribute to the $x$ coefficient, so the $+6x$ from $3 \cdot 2x$ still has to be added.

D.why: This is $k$, the constant you solve for first. The question asks for $b$.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A seismologist models the ratio of two wave amplitudes recorded at a monitoring station with the expression $\frac{6x^2 + 7x - 20}{2x + 5}$, where $x$ is the distance from the epicenter, in kilometers.
items.stem: For $x \neq -\frac{5}{2}$, the expression $\frac{6x^2 + 7x - 20}{2x + 5}$ is equivalent to $ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $ab$?
items.explanation: Factor the numerator: $6x^2 + 7x - 20 = (2x + 5)(3x - 4)$. You can check this by expanding: $6x^2 - 8x + 15x - 20$. Cancel the common factor $2x + 5$ to get $3x - 4$, so $a = 3$ and $b = -4$. Then $ab = 3(-4) = -12$.

B.why: You found $a = 3$ and $b = -4$ but added them. The question asks for the product $ab$.

C.why: This is $a$, the leading coefficient of the quotient. You still need to find $b$ and multiply.

D.why: You made a sign error when factoring and used $b = 4$. Since $(2x + 5)(3x + 4)$ has a constant term of $+20$, not $-20$, $b$ must be $-4$.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A musicologist studying tuning systems uses the expression $2(x - 3)^2 + 5$ to model how far a string's pitch deviates from a reference tone, where $x$ is the string's tension setting.
items.stem: The expression $2(x - 3)^2 + 5$ is equivalent to $ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants. What is the value of $b + c$?
items.explanation: Expand the square: $(x - 3)^2 = x^2 - 6x + 9$. Multiply every term by 2 to get $2x^2 - 12x + 18$, then add 5: $2x^2 - 12x + 23$. So $b = -12$ and $c = 23$, which gives $b + c = 11$.

A.why: You doubled the $x^2$ and $x$ terms but not the 9, which gives $2x^2 - 12x + 14$. The 2 multiplies the entire square, including the constant 9.

B.why: You multiplied only the $x^2$ term by 2, which gives $2x^2 - 6x + 14$. The 2 has to be distributed to every term of $x^2 - 6x + 9$.

D.why: You computed $a + b + c = 2 - 12 + 23 = 13$. The question asks only for $b + c$.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus:
A meteorologist modeling pressure changes along a storm front writes the following equation.

$(x + 4)(x^2 - kx + 3) = x^3 - x^2 + px + 12$
items.stem: In the given equation, $k$ and $p$ are constants. If the equation is true for all values of $x$, what is the value of $k + p$?
items.explanation: Expanding the left side gives $x^3 + (4 - k)x^2 + (3 - 4k)x + 12$. Match the $x^2$ coefficients: $4 - k = -1$, so $k = 5$. Match the $x$ coefficients: $p = 3 - 4k = 3 - 20 = -17$. So $k + p = 5 + (-17) = -12$.

A.why: This is $p$ alone. You still need to add $k = 5$, because the question asks for $k + p$.

C.why: This is $k$, which you find from the $x^2$ terms. The question asks for the sum $k + p$.

D.why: You wrote the product $4 \cdot (-kx)$ as $+4kx$, which gives $p = 3 + 20 = 23$ and $k + p = 28$. That product is $-4kx$.

items.subtype_name: The sentence needs a real (finite) verb
items.stimulus: In the eighteenth century, silk weavers in London's Spitalfields district produced fabrics of remarkable complexity, using pattern-weaving techniques that refugee artisans had carried with them from France. Few of the designers' working materials survive. One pattern book from the period, now preserved in a museum archive, ______ more than two hundred hand-painted designs for brocaded silk, each annotated with notes on thread colors.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is "One pattern book," and it has no main verb yet. The phrase "now preserved in a museum archive" is only an interrupter. You need a finite verb, and "contains" is the only tensed form. It gives the sentence its main verb and agrees with the singular subject.

A.why: "Containing" sounds smooth, but an -ing form can't be the main verb of a clause. With it, "One pattern book" never gets a verb, and the sentence becomes a fragment.

B.why: "To contain" is an infinitive. It can't be a main verb, so the subject "One pattern book" is left without a predicate.

D.why: "Having contained" is a participle phrase, not a tensed verb. The sentence still has no main verb, and the perfect form clashes with a book that holds these designs now.

items.subtype_name: The sentence needs a real (finite) verb
items.stimulus: Before satellite imagery existed, mapmakers charted coastlines through a painstaking process called triangulation. On one nineteenth-century survey of a rocky northern shoreline, the field team first measured a single baseline across a flat stretch of beach with steel chains and ______ the angles from each end of that line to distant church towers and hilltops.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The word "and" joins two actions done by the same subject, "the field team." The first action is "measured," a simple past verb. The second action has to be parallel with it, so the answer is "recorded."

B.why: "Recording" is an -ing form. After "and," it doesn't match "measured," so the compound predicate is broken. You probably picked the form that sounded most fluent.

C.why: "To record" is an infinitive. It can't serve as the second verb in a compound predicate that begins with the past-tense verb "measured."

D.why: "Having recorded" is a participle, not a finite verb. It doesn't match "measured," and it suggests the recording happened before the measuring.

items.stimulus: Nutrition researchers have long debated whether dietary fiber meaningfully reduces appetite later in the day. The participants who ate a high-fiber breakfast of oats, lentils, and berries ______ significantly fewer calories at lunch than those who ate a low-fiber breakfast.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is "The participants." The clause "who ate a high-fiber breakfast of oats, lentils, and berries" already has its own verb, "ate," but the main subject still needs one. "Consumed" is finite and past tense, which matches the past-tense report of the trial.

A.why: "Consuming" isn't a finite verb. You may have taken "ate" as the sentence's main verb, but it belongs to the "who" clause. The main subject "The participants" still has no verb of its own.

B.why: "To consume" is an infinitive. It leaves "The participants" without a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.why: "Having consumed" is a participle phrase. It can't serve as the main verb, so the subject "The participants" is still waiting for one.

items.stimulus: Woodcut printing is one of the oldest ways to reproduce an image. The artist carves a design into a flat block of wood, cutting away every area that should stay white. The raised surface that remains ______ ink from a roller and transfers it to paper when the block is pressed down.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the last sentence is 'The raised surface.' The words 'that remains' only describe it, and 'remains' belongs to that small clause. So the subject still needs its own main verb. The blank also sits before 'and transfers,' so it has to match that verb. 'Picks up' is a tensed verb that matches 'transfers.' This is the first check you make on Easy questions where every choice is the same verb in a different form: does the subject already have a real verb?

A.why: 'Picking up' sounds smooth, but an -ing word can't be a sentence's main verb on its own. 'The raised surface... picking up ink' leaves the subject without a verb, and it doesn't match 'transfers' after 'and.'

B.why: You chose an infinitive. 'To pick up' names a purpose, not an action the subject performs, so the sentence still has no main verb before 'and transfers.'

D.why: 'Having picked up' is a nonfinite -ing form even though it uses 'having.' It describes something but doesn't give the subject a verb, so it can't be joined to 'transfers' with 'and.'

B.why: You swapped the starting value and the rate. This equation starts with 15 shards and loses 240 per hour.

D.why: You subtracted 15 from 240 once and then used the result as a per-hour rate. After one hour 225 shards are left, but that number is not a rate.

items.stimulus: An immunologist tracks a patient's antibody levels after a booster vaccine. On the day of the booster, the patient's antibody concentration is 12 units per milliliter. For the following weeks, the concentration increases by 3 units per milliliter each day.
items.stem: Which function $f$ gives the patient's antibody concentration, in units per milliliter, $d$ days after the booster dose?
items.explanation: On day 0 the concentration is 12, so 12 is the constant. It rises 3 units per milliliter per day, so the rate is +3. That gives $f(d) = 3d + 12$.

B.why: You made the rate negative. The concentration increases after the booster, so the rate must be positive.

C.why: You added the starting concentration and the daily increase to get 15 and used that as the rate. The 12 appears only once, as the value on day 0.

items.stimulus: Mission controllers measure that a space probe is 80 million kilometers from the planet it is traveling toward. The probe is closing the gap at a constant 2 million kilometers per day.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $D$ is the probe's distance from the planet, in millions of kilometers, $t$ days after the measurement?

items.stimulus: When a storm begins, a hydrologist records the water level of a reservoir as 18 feet. Throughout the storm, runoff raises the water level by 0.5 foot per hour.

items.stimulus: A marine biologist plants a staghorn coral fragment on a restoration frame. When it is planted, the fragment is 6 centimeters long. It then grows at a steady rate of 4 centimeters every 2 years.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $L$ is the length, in centimeters, of the coral fragment $y$ years after it is planted?
items.explanation: The length at year 0 is 6 cm, so 6 is the constant. The rate is 4 cm per 2 years, and 4 ÷ 2 = 2 cm per year. That gives $L = 6 + 2y$.

A.why: You used 4 as the yearly rate. The coral grows 4 cm every 2 years, so you need to divide by 2 to get the rate for one year.

B.why: You multiplied 4 by 2 instead of dividing. A rate given per 2 years is divided by 2 to get the rate per year.

D.why: You found the correct yearly rate of 2 and then swapped it with the starting length. This equation starts at 2 cm and grows 6 cm per year.

items.stimulus: A bird feeder is filled with 30 ounces of seed. Birds eat 3 ounces of seed each day.
items.stem: Which equation matches the description, where $S$ is the ounces of seed left after $d$ days?

items.stimulus: A wheat seedling is 5 centimeters tall. It grows 6 centimeters every 2 weeks.
items.stem: Which equation matches the description, where $h$ is the height in centimeters after $w$ weeks?
items.explanation: The rate is given per 2 weeks, but $w$ counts single weeks. Divide to get the rate for one week: $6 \div 2 = 3$ cm per week. The starting height, 5, is the constant, so $h = 5 + 3w$. Exam word problems often give a rate per several units, such as per 2 weeks, per 100 feet or per dozen. items.subtype_name: Write the linear model from a word description
items.stimulus: A meteorologist launches a weather balloon carrying a temperature sensor. At the moment of launch, the sensor reads $22^\circ\text{C}$. As the balloon rises, the temperature it records drops by $3^\circ\text{C}$ for every $500$ meters of altitude it gains. The function $T$ gives the temperature, in degrees Celsius, recorded by the sensor when the balloon is $h$ kilometers above the launch site.
items.stem: What is $T(3)$?
items.explanation: Start with the value when the input is 0. At $h = 0$ the sensor reads $22$, so that is the constant term. Next, find the rate per single unit of the input. The input is in kilometers, but the drop is given per $500$ meters. One kilometer is two lots of $500$ meters, so the temperature drops $2 \times 3 = 6$ degrees per kilometer. The temperature is falling, so the rate is negative: $T(h) = 22 - 6h$. Then $T(3) = 22 - 18 = 4$.

Made both errors: no unit conversion and a positive slope, so 22 + 3(3) = 31.

items.stimulus: A nutrition science laboratory measures the vitamin content of food samples for outside researchers. The laboratory charges a flat fee of $\$90$, which covers the analysis of up to $4$ samples. Each sample beyond the first $4$ costs an additional $\$12$.
items.stem: For $n \ge 4$, the total fee $C$, in dollars, for the laboratory to analyze $n$ samples can be written as $C = 12n + k$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
items.explanation: The $\$12$ charge applies only to samples after the first $4$, so the number of extra samples is $n - 4$. That gives $C = 90 + 12(n - 4)$. Distribute: $C = 90 + 12n - 48 = 12n + 42$. So $k = 42$. Check with $n = 4$: $12(4) + 42 = 90$, which is the flat fee, as it should be.

items.stimulus: A printmaker is producing an edition of two-color relief prints and starts with $400$ milliliters of ink. Before printing, $25$ milliliters are used to roll out the inking slab. Each print is made from two separate blocks, one for each color, and each block uses $9$ milliliters of ink for every $3$ prints. items.stem: What is the value of $b$?

items.subtype_name: Write the linear model from a word description
items.stimulus: A seismologist's field station records ground motion during an aftershock sequence. When recording begins, the station's data buffer has 1,200 megabytes of free space. While the sequence continues, the station fills 45 megabytes of the buffer every 3 minutes. Let $F$ be the free space, in megabytes, left in the buffer $t$ minutes after recording begins.
items.stem: Which equation represents this relationship?
items.explanation: The free space at $t = 0$ is 1,200 megabytes, so that is the constant term. The buffer fills 45 megabytes every 3 minutes, which is $45 \div 3 = 15$ megabytes per minute. Free space is going down, so the rate is negative. That gives $F = 1{,}200 - 15t$.

A.why: You used the 45 megabytes as if it were filled every minute. That amount is filled every 3 minutes, so you need to divide by 3 to get the rate per minute.

C.why: You gave the slope the wrong sign. Recording uses up free space, so $F$ goes down as $t$ goes up and the rate must be negative.

items.subtype_name: Write the linear model from a word description
items.stimulus: Ornithologists fitted a migrating shorebird with a tracking tag just before it started a nonstop flight over open ocean. At takeoff, the bird was carrying 400 grams of stored body fat. During the flight, it burned fat at a constant rate of 9 grams every 2 hours. Let $F$ be the amount of stored fat, in grams, that the bird has left.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $h$ is the number of hours since the flight began?
items.explanation: The starting amount is the fat at $h = 0$, which is 400 grams. That is the constant term. The rate is given per 2 hours, so divide to get the rate per hour: $9 \div 2 = \frac{9}{2}$ grams per hour. The fat is going down, so the rate is negative. That gives $F = 400 - \frac{9}{2}h$. To check, after 2 hours the bird should have $400 - 9 = 391$ grams, and $400 - \frac{9}{2}(2) = 391$.

A.why: You multiplied by the 'every 2 hours' figure instead of dividing by it ($9 \times 2 = 18$). This equation says the bird burns 18 grams each hour, which is four times the actual rate. After 2 hours it would show 364 grams instead of 391.

B.why: You found the right rate per hour but gave it the wrong sign. Burning fat makes the amount go down, so the slope must be negative. This equation has the bird gaining fat during the flight.

C.why: You divided the wrong way, $2 \div 9$, which gives hours per gram, not grams per hour. The slope has to be in output units per input unit, so it must be grams per hour, which is $\frac{9}{2}$.

items.subtype_name: “Most nearly mean” in a literary excerpt
items.stimulus:
In this text, the narrator describes how a river valley changed after wolves returned to it.

items.subtype_name: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
items.stimulus: An astronomy student models light from a distant star as two parallel rays, line $\ell$ and line $m$. The edge of a telescope mirror lies along line $t$, which crosses line $\ell$ at point $P$ and line $m$ at point $Q$. At point $P$, the angle between line $t$ (going from $P$ toward $Q$) and line $\ell$ (going to the right of $P$) measures $58^\circ$. At point $Q$, the angle between line $t$ (going beyond $Q$, away from $P$) and line $m$ (going to the left of $Q$) measures $x^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Line $t$ cuts parallel lines, so the corresponding angle at $Q$, between line $t$ going beyond $Q$ and line $m$ going to the right, is also $58^\circ$. Angle $x$ sits on the other side of line $m$ and forms a linear pair with that angle, so $x = 180 - 58 = 122$.

A.why: You treated lines $t$ and $m$ as perpendicular and took $90 - 58$. The question never says there is a right angle.

B.why: You found the corresponding angle at $Q$ and stopped there. Angle $x$ is the angle next to it on the straight line, so you still have to subtract it from $180$.

D.why: You added $90$ and $58$, as though $x$ were made of a right angle plus the given angle. Nothing in the figure supports that sum.

items.subtype_name: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
items.stimulus: On a city map, two straight roads, $R$ and $S$, cross at one point. One of the four angles formed where they cross measures $52^\circ$.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of the angle next to the $52^\circ$ angle, on the same side of road $R$?
items.explanation: The two angles sit side by side along road $R$, so together they make a straight line and add to $180^\circ$. That gives $180 - 52 = 128$. A.why: You found $90 - 52$, which treats the two angles as if they made a right angle. Nothing says the roads are perpendicular. Angles that sit next to each other along a straight line add to $180^\circ$, not $90^\circ$.

B.why: $52^\circ$ is the vertical angle, which is across the crossing from the given angle. The question asks for the angle beside it, which is supplementary to it, not equal to it.

D.why: You subtracted from $360$, the total around a point. The angle next to the given one only fills out the straight line with it, so the total to use is $180$.

items.subtype_name: What must be true from a random sample result
items.stimulus:
A hydrologist selected 200 wells at random from the 5,000 private wells in a county and tested each one. Of the wells tested, 18% had nitrate levels above the safe drinking-water limit.

I. The sample result of 18% is an estimate of the percent of all 5,000 wells in the county with nitrate levels above the limit.
II. Exactly 18% of all 5,000 wells in the county have nitrate levels above the limit.
items.stem: Which of the following must be true?
items.explanation: The 200 wells were chosen at random from the county's 5,000 wells, so the sample percent is a reasonable estimate of the percent for all 5,000 wells. That makes statement I true. A sample statistic is never guaranteed to equal the population value exactly, so statement II doesn't have to be true.

B.why: You treated the sample percent as the exact percent for every well in the county. Random selection makes 18% a reasonable estimate, not a guaranteed value.

C.why: You saw correctly that statement I is true, but you also accepted statement II. The sample only estimates the county-wide percent and can't fix it at exactly 18%.

D.why: You rejected every statement, including the hedged one. Statement I only says the sample result estimates the population value, and for a random sample that is true.

items.subtype_name: What must be true from a random sample result
items.stimulus:

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: To help a depleted grouper population recover, regulators closed one section of a Caribbean reef to all fishing. Within three years, grouper counts inside the closed section had nearly doubled. The fishing boats that once worked that section did not leave the area, however; they moved to the reef's open edges, which they now fish far more heavily than before. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: a decline in the grouper population inside the closed section.
an increase in the total number of boats fishing the region.
greater fishing pressure on the parts of the reef left open.
a shift among local crews toward species other than grouper.

B.why: The passage says the existing boats moved. It never says more boats arrived, so you added a step the text doesn't support.

D.why: Nothing in the passage says crews switched species. They kept fishing, just in a different place.

the strength of the steel cable wires and the strength of the bridge's towers.
how quickly the cable wires corrode and how quickly the deck's steel corrodes.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Many people assume that how well a vaccine protects depends only on the vaccine itself. raising the cost of producing and distributing the vaccine.
leaving older recipients less protected than younger recipients.

B.why: This is strength creep. The passage describes a weaker response in one age group only, not across every age.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Graphene is often described as the simplest of materials: a single flat sheet of carbon atoms. Making it is anything but simple. Large sheets free of defects require extreme heat, spotless surfaces, and a delicate transfer step in which the sheet can easily tear.

how thin graphene's sheets are and how much heat they can withstand

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: To protect young patients from infection, a hospital began screening every visitor to its children's ward for fever. items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Food regulators in several countries permit a "reduced fat" label on any product containing at least 25 percent less fat than its standard version. lead shoppers to buy products with more calories than the standard versions contain.
steer shoppers who use it to cut calories toward foods that barely help them do so.
lead shoppers who ignore nutrition labels to eat more fat than they did before.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Baroque keyboard scores often look sparse: a single bass line with a few numerals written beneath it. Early modern students of the repertoire took this sparseness as a sign that the pieces were easy to play. Musicologist Tomás Ruelas argues the reverse. The numerals, he shows, told performers which harmonies to improvise in real time above the bass, a skill that took years of training to master. There is thus a disparity between ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: how little of the music the page records and how much the performer was expected to supply.
how easy the pieces were to play and how complicated their notation looked.
how hard the pieces were to perform and how long improvisation took to learn.
the harmonies composers intended and the harmonies performers chose to play.
items.explanation: The two sides are a page that records very little (a bass line and numerals) and a performer who must improvise full harmonies on top of it. The disparity is between what is written down and what the player has to provide.

B.why: You reversed the contrast. The notation looks simple and the playing is hard, not the other way around.

C.why: You paired two things from the same side. Hard performance and long training both describe the demanding half, so the simple-looking notation is missing and no disparity is named.

D.why: You invented a conflict. The passage never says performers departed from what composers intended. It says the numerals told them which harmonies to improvise.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Earthen levees are built along rivers to reduce the damage floods cause to nearby communities. Hydrologists have long observed, however, that land behind a new levee tends to attract homes and businesses, since it is now regarded as safe. Each levee is designed to withstand floods only up to a specified size, and larger floods, though rare, still occur. Consequently, a levee may ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: fail during the ordinary floods that it was specifically designed to hold back.
shift the floods it prevents upstream onto communities located farther downstream.
protect the new homes and businesses behind it from most of the river's floods.
increase the amount of property exposed to floods larger than it can withstand.
items.explanation: The levee is meant to reduce flood damage, but it draws new building onto land that is still at risk from rare, larger floods. So it can increase the amount of property those big floods would damage, which is the opposite of its goal.

A.why: You ignored the design limit. The passage says levees hold up to their specified size. The risk comes from rarer, larger floods, not ordinary ones.

B.why: You added an extra step. Downstream effects may be real in some places, but the passage never mentions them. Its argument is entirely about building behind the levee.

C.why: You stated only one side of the tension. Protection from most floods is the levee's intended benefit. The question asks what follows from the gap between that safety and the rare large flood.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Nineteenth-century collectors who transcribed oral folktales saw themselves as rescuing a tradition from disappearance. Folklorist Maren Aalto observes that oral tales had survived precisely by changing, since each teller adapted plot and detail to the audience at hand. Once a printed version circulated in a region, however, villagers increasingly treated it as the correct telling and corrected storytellers who departed from it. The unintended effect of the collectors' work was thus to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: preserve tales that would otherwise have been forgotten within a generation.
weaken the very variability that had allowed the tradition to survive.
make villagers lose interest in hearing tales performed by local storytellers.
encourage tellers to adapt printed tales more freely to suit their audiences.
items.explanation: The collectors wanted to keep the tradition alive, and Aalto says it survived by varying. Print made one version the "correct" one and discouraged variation, so the collectors undermined the thing that had kept the tradition going.

A.why: You gave the intended goal, not the unintended effect. Preservation is what the collectors hoped for, and "within a generation" is a claim the passage never makes.

C.why: You went beyond the text. Villagers kept listening closely enough to correct tellers, so nothing shows they lost interest.

D.why: You reversed the effect. Villagers corrected tellers who departed from the printed version, which discouraged free adaptation.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: A city offered free flu vaccinations at clinics open only on weekday mornings, aiming to narrow the gap in vaccination rates between its low-income residents and everyone else. Clinic records showed that most people who came were retirees and salaried workers with flexible schedules, few of whom were low-income. Hourly workers, who make up most of the city's low-income population, rarely attended. As a result, the program may have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: overburdened clinics with more retirees and salaried workers than staff could serve.
led hourly workers to distrust health programs that are run by the city.
lowered vaccination rates among low-income residents below their earlier level.
widened rather than narrowed the gap it was designed to close.
items.explanation: The program set out to close a gap, but most of the people it vaccinated were not low-income. Raising rates mainly among people already better off would make the gap wider, the opposite of the goal. "May have" matches how cautious the evidence is.

A.why: You looked at the side the program already favoured. The passage never mentions staffing problems, and the question is about the group the program was meant to protect.

B.why: You added a motive. Hourly workers stayed away because of the hours, as far as the passage shows. Nothing points to distrust.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. A program that failed to reach low-income residents doesn't lower their rate below where it was. It only fails to raise it.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Backyard bird feeding is often promoted as a way to support declining songbird populations. A survey by ornithologist Priya Venn found, however, that the birds visiting feeders most often were house sparrows and other common generalist species, while several declining insect-eating species almost never used feeders at all. The generalists also compete with those declining species for scarce nest cavities. People who feed birds in order to help vulnerable species therefore risk ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: strengthening the competitors of the very species they mean to help.
depriving common generalist species of food they need in order to survive.
driving declining insect-eating species to abandon their nest sites entirely.
drawing declining species to feeders where too few insects are available.
items.explanation: Feeders mostly feed the generalists, and the generalists compete with the declining species for nest cavities. So people trying to help vulnerable birds end up supporting those birds' competitors, which hurts the group they meant to protect.

B.why: You aimed the harm at the wrong side, and in the wrong direction. Generalists are the birds feeders benefit most, not birds that lose food.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. Competition for cavities doesn't establish that the declining species abandon their nests "entirely."

D.why: You missed a stated detail. The declining species almost never use feeders, so feeders don't draw them anywhere.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Linguists documenting endangered languages increasingly rely on audio recordings, which are inexpensive to make and easy to archive. Yet a recording captures only what speakers happen to say. It cannot show whether a rare construction is ungrammatical or merely unused. Settling that question requires lengthy sessions in which a trained linguist asks speakers to judge invented sentences, and few fluent speakers of most endangered languages remain. Thus there is a disparity between ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the number of recordings linguists make and the number they can archive.
the sentences speakers say naturally and the sentences they judge acceptable.
the evidence that is easiest to gather and the evidence some questions require.
the low cost of making recordings and the effort of transcribing them accurately.
items.explanation: Recordings are cheap and easy to collect, but they can't answer questions about grammaticality. Those need judgment sessions, which are slow and depend on speakers who are scarce. The disparity is between the evidence that is easy to get and the evidence certain questions actually need.

A.why: You built a gap the passage rules out. Recordings are described as easy to archive, so making and archiving them aren't in tension.

B.why: You paired the wrong two things. The passage contrasts two kinds of evidence, not speakers' speech with their judgments, and it never says those two differ.

D.why: You matched only one side. Cheap recordings are in the passage, but transcription never is. The real other side is the scarce judgment sessions.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Land managers in parts of the American West have used controlled burns to clear sagebrush, hoping to reduce the fuel available to large wildfires. Ecologist Ruth Calder reports that on burned plots, invasive cheatgrass, which dries out early each summer and ignites easily, often established itself faster than the sagebrush could regrow. Her findings suggest that in these areas, controlled burns may ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: eliminate sagebrush permanently from every plot on which they are used.
favor the very vegetation that makes wildfires more likely to start.
reduce the fuel available to wildfires for many years after each burn.
fail because cheatgrass is more resistant to fire than sagebrush is.
items.explanation: The burns are meant to reduce wildfire fuel, but they let in cheatgrass, which dries early and catches fire easily. So the burns can encourage plants that make fires more likely. "Suggest" and "may" fit this hedged claim.

A.why: You fell for strength creep. Cheatgrass establishing "faster than" sagebrush regrows doesn't mean sagebrush is gone "permanently" from "every" plot.

C.why: You gave only the policy's goal. Calder's findings point the other way: the burns may replace sagebrush with a more flammable fuel.

D.why: You reversed the trait. The passage says cheatgrass ignites easily, which is the opposite of fire-resistant.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: No-take marine reserves, which ban all fishing, are meant to let fish populations recover and then replenish surrounding waters as adult fish swim across the boundary. When marine ecologist Talia Ruano tracked fishing boats after a coral reef in the Visayan Sea was closed, however, she found that the displaced boats clustered tightly along the reserve's edge. There they caught many of the large, egg-producing adults leaving it. This suggests that such a reserve may, contrary to its purpose, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: harm the fish populations living deep within the reserve's protected interior
drive fishing boats away from the waters surrounding the closed reef
limit the restocking of nearby fishing grounds that it was designed to provide
lead fishers near the reserve to catch mostly small, immature fish
items.explanation: Put the two sides in your own words. The reserve is meant to send breeding adults out to restock nearby waters, but boats wait at the edge and catch those adults as they leave. The unintended effect works against the reserve's goal: fewer of the fish that were supposed to restock the surrounding fishing grounds survive to do it. 'Contrary to its purpose' points you to the side the policy was meant to help.

A.why: You picked a harm to the side the reserve already protects. The boats fish at the edge, not inside, and the passage says nothing about the interior population suffering. The harm in the passage falls on the outside waters the reserve was meant to restock.

B.why: You reversed what Ruano found. The displaced boats did not leave the area. They crowded along the reserve's boundary.

D.why: The passage says the boats caught large, egg-producing adults, not small, immature fish. You swapped in the opposite kind of catch.
